Sony has a collection of colorful, translucent cosmetics for its PlayStation consoles and controllers. Announced Wednesday, the Prism collection brings three new, gorgeous color options that conjure a nostalgic, transparent tech feel.
They come in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. (Based on the pictures, the gray looks more like a blue to me.) You can get Sony’s DualSense PlayStation 5 controllers in the Prism design or opt for PS5 console covers. On the controllers, translucent plastic wraps around almost the entire device’s frame, letting you view the components inside. On the console cover version, the transparency is more limited—you can see only the fan and a few other components.
The Prism Collection DualSense wireless controllers cost $85, while the console covers cost $75. Preorders start on November 10, but the collection won’t ship until February 4. Those are roughly the same prices as existing controllers and covers, though on the higher end. Basic color controllers start at $74 on the PlayStation website. Covers start around $59. The more colorful options on both products go up from there.
Apple’s original iMac largely popularized translucent, colorful tech that lets you see inside the machine. The look was en vogue for a while in seminal devices like the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo’s Game Boy Color.
That see-through aesthetic was a signature in the early 2000s. (My first CD player had a translucent top, and you could see the disc spinning around the whole time.) Twenty-some years later, it’s being revived as nostalgia bait in a transparent tech renaissance. You can find the transparent look in everything from gaming handhelds to a Theragun. Sony also has a transparent pair of earbuds.
Reminiscing about the good ol’ days might also remind you that Sony’s old consoles used to have disc drives. In July, Sony made a controversial decision to end production of physical game discs starting in 2028. Ownership advocates have decried the choice, noting that Sony’s own terms of service state that buying a digital copy of a game does not mean the customer owns it. It’s yet another move toward the end of physical media.
Still, the Prism collection sure looks pretty.

Quick Answer
The Fitbit Edge is a $179.99 fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, built-in GPS, ECG, replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It also offers Google Maps navigation, Gemini-powered coaching, advanced health tracking, and a special Stephen Curry edition.
The fitness world may be in a “to screen or not to screen” state, with fitness bands without screens gaining popularity, but Google is clearly keeping its Fitbit feet in both screen and screenless fitness trackers. Days after launching its Fitbit Air screenless tracker in India, the Search giant has launched the Fitbit Edge, a fitness tracker with a display that sits right in the middle of the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, both in terms of pricing (it starts at USD 179.99, well above the USD 99.99 of the Fitbit Air but well below the USD 399.99 of the Pixel Watch 5) and display size. Only time will tell whether it will hit the golden middle ground between “lots of display” and “no display at all,” but while we wait for the Fitbit Edge to hit stores later this month (and indeed, hopefully arrive in India soon), here are twelve points worth noting about the latest Fitbit in fitness town:
Table of Contents
A big display in an increasingly no-display zone
In a fitness band world that seems to be aiming to become more and more screen-less, the Fitbit Edge comes with a big-gish display for a fitness tracker. It has a 1.34-inch AMOLED, always-on display, which is 46 percent bigger than the one on the Charge 6, its predecessor. It is also much brighter and has Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Fitbit actually claims it is the brightest and biggest display on a Fitbit fitness tracker. Should the Fitbit Air be jealous?
Wear it without Wear OS: Fitbit OS onboard
It comes from Google and also has a display on board like the Pixel Watch 5, which has led many to assume that the Fitbit Edge must be running on Wear OS, but that is not the case. The Fitbit Edge actually runs on Fitbit OS. And like all Google fitness devices, it also uses the Google Health app to keep track of your data and give you fitness inputs. While this means you get relatively less distraction and only basic notifications, it also means you do not get access to third-party apps on the device.
Bye bye Haptic, Hello real button!
One of the biggest headaches of the Fitbit Charge 6 was its pressure-sensitive, haptic touch button, which many of us struggled to use (it almost had a vibe of its own). Thankfully, the Fitbit Edge fixes that and brings a physical button on the side for controls. We couldn’t be more glad. The haptic control on the Charge 6 was a bit of a pain and messed up what was (and still is) a superb fitness tracker.
A battery that can be removed and replaced
Most modern devices have given up on the concept of a removable battery, which was sad because once the battery of a device died, it tended to render an otherwise perfectly good device useless, unless one went in for complex engineering. That, however, has been changing thanks to regulations from the EU, and the Fitbit Edge comes with a removable battery. Which means you can simply remove the battery and replace it if its health deteriorates, increasing the life of the fitness tracker.
Very Air-y battery life
In terms of battery life, the Fitbit Edge rather surprisingly has the same battery life as the display-less Fitbit Air – about a week. However, keeping the always-on-display feature on reduces this to a rather low two days.
Metal frames that can take an ECG…and save your life (in select countries)
The Fitbit Edge’s metal frame can be used to take a 30-second manual ECG. This can highlight heart rate irregularities and can also spot signs of AFib. The tracker also has an optical PPG heart rate sensor that continuously tracks one’s heart and pulse rate and alerts the user if their heart rate is unusually high or low. The catch is that the ECG is only available in select countries, but it is still great to see an ECG on a fitness tracker – a feature seen generally in premium smartwatches.
Take it swimming
Much like its screen-less sibling, the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge too is pretty sturdy. The device comes with 5 ATM water resistance, which means you can easily take it along for your swim sessions. The device also features IP68 dust and water resistance, and as we mentioned earlier, Gorilla Glass 3 protection.
Comes with GPS and is stair-worthy
The Fitbit Edge has an improved and built-in GPS, something the Air lacks, so you do not need to carry your phone along to cover outdoor workouts and activities. It has multi-constellation support, which is paired with a new antenna and chip, making the device up to 40 percent better at tracking locations than the Charge 6. The Edge has another edge over the Air – an integrated altimeter, which can detect changes in altitude, and comes in handy not only while counting stairs but also during hikes and trekking, where you can accurately measure altitude change.
Get Google Maps directions on your wrist:
The Fitbit Edge might not have Google Wear, but it works in sync with Google Maps on your phone and can show you turn-by-turn directions on your wrist. The feature requires you to have an active Bluetooth connection between your phone and the Fitbit Edge, and directions will start popping up on your tracker screen when you start walking, running, cycling, or even driving. That big display really helps!
Quick Notifications, quicker actions but no call support:
The Edge has a mixed relationship with your smartphone. It is a few steps ahead of the Air in terms of notifications, or some might say behind it in terms of a distraction-free experience. You get basic call, message, and app notifications on the tracker, and also get quick reply and navigation access on it. However, you cannot use it to handle calls because the device does not have a mic or a speaker. You can accept a call from the tracker, but it will be directed to your smartphone.
Google Health Guardian’s on your wrist
Earlier limited to the more expensive Pixel Watches, Google’s Health Guardian is available on the Fitbit Edge. This comes with cardiovascular tracking and alerts, alerts for potential breathing and pulse issues, and tracking of trends in the background to create monthly reports on blood pressure and even insulin resistance. It also unlocks premium features of the Google Health app, like personalized coaching and deeper tracking and analysis.
Gemini present, but cannot be summoned:
The Fitbit Edge comes with personalized Gemini coaching to help you meet your health and fitness goals. But complete access to all of Gemini’s features requires a subscription, and you cannot summon the AI assistant on your tracker – you have to use your phone for it.
And one more thing: There is a Stephen Curry edition:
The Google Fitbit Edge comes with a special edition, designed in collaboration with 4-time NBA champion Stephen Curry. It pairs the regular tracker with a Satin Pyrite aluminum case and also features a custom moisture-wicking, water-repellent, recycled polyester yarn band. Also on board are special basketball watchfaces. Mind you, all that extra goodness will set you back by an additional USD 40 – the Stephen Curry edition starts at USD 219.99.

Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
- Published
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.
Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.
He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.
The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.
Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.
"The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.
The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

He will succeed Hitesh Oberoi, who will step down as managing director and CEO at the close of business on December 2, ending nearly 27 years in a full-time executive role at the company.
Info Edge said Oberoi had decided to step down to devote more time to his interests in education, entrepreneurship, institution building, investing and philanthropy, and to spend more time with his family.
Oberoi will remain associated with the company as a non-executive, non-independent director from December 3
The announcement came alongside Info Edge’s Q2 FY27 results. Its consolidated net profit rose 87% to ₹649.8 Cr in the September quarter from ₹347.5 Cr a year earlier. Net profit increased 32.6% QoQ from ₹490.1 Cr.
Revenue from operations grew 12.2% YoY and 2.6% QoQ to ₹903.9 Cr. Other income rose 164.8% YoY to ₹428.4 Cr from ₹161.8 Cr, contributing to the increase in net profit.

- The claim that U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was married to her brother is unfounded.
- The latest rumor stems from a New York Post story claiming Omar's father's name was Nur Said Elmi — not Nur Omar Mohamed — and the Omar has a sister in the United Kingdom named Leila Nur Said Elmi who allegedly lived with Omar's ex-husband Ahmed Elmi, suggesting they were all siblings. A legal motion from the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia also referred to Omar as "llhan Nur Said Elmi."
- Snopes found that the claims lack evidence because they appear to be entirely circumstantial and unsubstantiated. Having possibly similar names does not prove that Omar is related to Leila Nur Said or Ahmed Elmi. Additionally, the claims did not confirm Ahmed Elmi's parentage or his relationship to Leila Nur Said. The claims also ignore Somali naming conventions in which children receive first names tied to their paternal lineage.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Omar, the U.S. attorney's office and an individual believed to be Ahmed Elmi, and are waiting for responses.
For years, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has been the subject of claims that she committed immigration fraud by marrying her brother, which Snopes has determined were unfounded. In October, President Donald Trump's administration reopened an investigation against Omar in which it claimed to have more evidence about her family history and alleged she had committed identity fraud, leading to federal agents raiding her home in Washington, D.C.
Following this development, Snopes readers asked us to once again determine whether Omar married her brother to commit immigration fraud and whether the U.S. government had DNA evidence to substantiate that claim.
The accusations continued to claim that Omar had married her brother, a man named Ahmed Elmi. New reporting from The New York Post claimed Omar's father's name was actually Nur Said Elmi, not Nur Omar Mohamed. According to the Post, a U.K. marriage certificate showed that Omar's ex-husband lived in London with a woman named Leila Nur Said, who was believed to be Omar's sister and whose father's name also also Nur Said Elmi.
A Fox News story, citing anonymous sources, claimed Omar's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Motions filed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, related to the search warrant also referred to Omar as "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."
In an X post, responding to allegations about her name, Omar wrote: "So let's make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar."
A NewsNation report claimed the federal agents went through Omar's garbage in the hopes of obtaining DNA samples during the raid on her house. Omar told MSNOW that she did not believe they had taken DNA samples, nor was she asked to provide any. Without DNA testing Elmi and Omar, there is no definitive proof they are siblings.
In an interview with MSNOW, asked directly whether she was related to Elmi in any way, Omar said, "Not to my knowledge."
We found that this was not evidence enough to support the claim she married her brother or committed immigration fraud. We have reached out to Omar's office for a response to the above allegations, as well as to Pirro's office, and will update this report accordingly.
Below, we break down all the claims about Omar's past marriages, her father's name and her alleged sister:
What is the timeline of Omar's marriages?
As we have reported previously, Omar was married twice before her current marriage to Tim Mynett: to Ahmed Hirsi (who was Ahmed Aden before he gained U.S. citizenship) and to a U.K. citizen, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — the subject of the above claims.
According to a statement Omar released in 2016, she and Hirsi applied for a marriage license in 2002. The couple married in an Islamic ceremony but never completed the process for a civil marriage, according to Hirsi. By 2008, Hirsi and Omar had separated (per Islamic custom). After that relationship ended, Omar had a civil marriage with Elmi in 2009. When that relationship ended, Elmi moved to England and they divorced per Islamic practice in 2011, but without receiving a legal divorce.
Omar and Hirsi reconciled in 2011 and remarried in an Islamic ceremony, according to her statement. In 2017, Omar formally petitioned for divorce from Elmi, and legally wed Hirsi in 2018. Minnesota court records show Omar and Elmi's marriage was legally dissolved on Dec. 4, 2017. Minnesota court records show Hirsi and Omar legally divorced on Nov. 22, 2019. Hirsi and Omar have three children together, according to court documents.
Who is Omar's father?
Nur Omar Mohamed died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications, according to a report in Sahan Journal, a Minnesotan news organization focusing on immigrant communities. The obituary described him as a prominent Somali military officer during the late-1970s Somalia-Ethiopia war.
The report noted Mohamed was a colonel during the dictatorship of Mohammed Siad Barre, who was removed from power in 1991, after which the country descended into civil war. Mohamed and his family subsequently became refugees.
In a statement announcing his death, Omar referred to her father as Nur Omar Mohamed. However, in a deleted 2013 tweet about Father's Day, Omar referred to her father as "Nur Said." Many jumped on this as evidence that Omar's father could also be the father of her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
In 2019, after Omar's account deleted the tweet about her father, Omar's spokesperson said (archived):
When people write vile things on posts about people she loves—including posting disturbing doctored images of her father—she takes them down. Nur Said means 'Happy Light' and it's been her dad's nickname since he was a kid. He has a public page with the same name. She isn't deleting it for the disturbing and hateful reasons that are being implied by conspiracy theorists.
According to the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center, part of the Defense Department, Somalis have names with three or more components and don't commonly use hereditary surnames. A Somali often receives a personal first name at birth, followed by their father's first name, and then their grandfather's first time. So most children, male or female, share their father's and grandfather's first names. However, many Somalis also have additional names based on their lineages or clans. The institute noted, "Because all three names come from a shared pool of personal names, many Somalis have names that are the same or similar."
Omar's tweet referring to her father as "Nur Said" on its own does not establish that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was her brother. The names Said, Nur, and Elmi are extremely common among Somali Muslims. Further, according to a 2016 profile of Omar, her paternal grandfather's name was Abukar.
Snopes was unable to find Mohamed's original Facebook account. It is likely the account has been deleted.
Is Omar related to Leila Nur Said?
The New York Post connected Omar's father's Facebook account to Leila Nur Said, saying she frequently left "hearts" on his pictures. Snopes was unable to locate either account and thus cannot independently verify this connection.
The Post's pool of evidence that established these connections is flimsy. A U.K. marriage certificate obtained by the Post for Leila Nur Said lists Nur Said Elmi, a military officer, as her father. Ahmed Elmi is not mentioned on this certificate. The Post reported: "Elmi's parentage is not known, but he lived in London with Leila Nur Said, a Somali woman who is thought to be Omar's sister, who possibly raised him."
Neither the Facebook connection to Omar's father, nor the marriage certificate, can effectively establish Ahmed Elmi's relationship with Leila Nur Said.
Media reports claim Elmi is a doctoral researcher at the University of Bristol. We reached out through an email listed on the university website and will update this post accordingly.
Our previous coverage
As we reported before, Omar showed a reporter from the Minnesota Star Tribune photos of documents from her family's entry into the U.S. after fleeing the civil war. She did not provide the reporter with copies of these papers but showed that they listed her father and showed her as the youngest of seven children. There was no one named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi listed in the documents.
We previously noted that Omar and her siblings all arrived in U.S. with refugee statuses. Omar was a minor when she became a naturalized U.S. citizen. How one sibling could end up with a completely different immigration status from the others remains unexplained by the claims.
According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policy, immigrants can apply for permanent residency status (opening the pathway to naturalization) if they are siblings of a U.S. citizen, or if they are married to a citizen. Any sibling of Omar would not have to marry her in order to secure a path to citizenship. If Elmi desperately wanted U.S. citizenship, he would not have immediately returned to England after his split with Omar.
In sum …
There is not enough evidence establishing familial ties between Elmi and Omar. Media reports are relying on similar names to establish connections — disregarding Somali naming conventions in which unrelated people can share common names. Until we know more, we leave this claim unrated.
For further reading, we are have reported on numerous rumors about Omar, including that she allegedly fled to Morocco after the raid on her home and that she changed her birth year in official records.

లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, చైనా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని అసఫిలా, లాంగ్జు, తక్సింగ్ సర్కిళ్లను తన ఆధీనంలోకి తీసుకుందని, ఈ విషయంలో కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం తగిన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం లేదని చెబుతున్నట్లు ANI లోగోతో ఉన్న ఒక వీడియోను సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ వీడియోను ఇదే వాదనతో సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదనలో నిజమెంతుందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, చైనా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని అసఫిలా, లాంగ్జు, తక్సింగ్ సర్కిళ్లను తన ఆధీనంలోకి తీసుకుందని, కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఈ విషయంలో తగిన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం లేదని తెలిపిన వీడియో.
ఫ్యాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియోను డిజిటల్గా ఎడిట్ చెయ్యబడింది. అందులోని ఆడియో డీప్ఫేక్. ANI 2023 అక్టోబర్లో ప్రచురించిన అసలు వీడియోలో, మేజర్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా జమ్మూ కశ్మీర్లోని నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LoC) వెంబడి చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాల గురించి మాట్లాడారు. ఆయన అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని ప్రాంతాలపై చైనా నియంత్రణ గురించి మాట్లాడలేదు. ఈ వీడియో డీప్ఫేక్ అని భారత సైన్యం ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ విభాగం, ANI కూడా స్పష్టం చేశాయి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్ల రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, 2023 అక్టోబర్ 27న ది స్టేట్స్మన్ ప్రచురించిన అదే వీడియోకు సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియో లభించింది. ఈ వీడియోలో లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా, నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LoC) వెంబడి పాకిస్థాన్కు చెందిన ఉగ్రవాద బృందాలు పదేపదే చొరబడేందుకు ప్రయత్నించడం గురించి మాట్లాడారు. గత ఎనిమిది నెలల్లో భద్రతా దళాలు 10 చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాలను అడ్డుకున్నాయని, ఈ ఘటనల్లో 27 మంది ఉగ్రవాదులను హతమార్చాయని తెలిపారు. అలాగే, ఆయుధాలు, ఇతర యుద్ధ సామగ్రి, మాదకద్రవ్యాలను స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నట్లు చెప్పారు. ఈ వీడియోలో ఎక్కడా అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ను చైనా ఆక్రమించిందని ఆయన ప్రకటించలేదు.
అంతేకాకుండా, ANI కూడా ఇదే వీడియోను 2023 అక్టోబర్ 27న తన Xలో పోస్ట్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఎనిమిది నెలల్లో 10 చొరబాటు ప్రయత్నాలను భద్రతా దళాలు అడ్డుకున్నాయని, ఈ ఘటనల్లో 27 మంది ఉగ్రవాదులను హతమార్చి, ఆయుధాలు, మాదకద్రవ్యాలను స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్నాయని ANI తన పోస్టులో పేర్కొంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని ఆడియోను Hiya AI, Resemble AI టూల్స్తో విశ్లేషించగా, అది కృత్రిమ మేధస్సు (AI) ద్వారా రూపొందించిన డీప్ఫేక్ ఆడియో అని గుర్తించాం.
భారత సైన్యం ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ విభాగం, ANI కూడా ఈ వీడియోను డిజిటల్గా మార్చారని స్పష్టం చేశాయి. లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా చేసినట్లుగా చూపిస్తున్న వ్యాఖ్యలు కల్పితమైనవని తెలిపాయి.
చివరిగా, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోని కొన్ని ప్రాంతాలపై చైనా నియంత్రణ సాధించిందంటూ లెఫ్టినెంట్ జనరల్ గిరీష్ కాలియా వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వీడియో డీప్ఫేక్.

Valorant’s 9th Duelist, Hush, arrives as Agent 31 with a high-skill kit centered around telekinesis and purple crystal powers. Unlike pure speedsters like Jett or Neon, Hush plays as an Initiator-Duelist hybrid. She combines the longest dash in the game with guided crowd control, adaptable flashes, and long-range object manipulation. If you want to master Hush in Valorant, here are all her abilities, along with quick tips and tricks to use them effectively.
All Valorant Hush Abilities Explained
When we first witnessed the revelation of Hush in Valorant, her kit seemed quite overwhelming. Well, before we jump into the tips to play the agent, here is the list of all her abilities:
Telekinesis (Passive / F)
Align your crosshair and press your interact key (F) to grab weapons, pick up the Spike, or hit map switches from around 36 to 37 meters away. Telekinesis has a 30-second cooldown.
The target must be in your direct line of sight (it won’t work through walls or smokes). However, items will phase through closing doors if you trigger the switch and grab the item immediately.
The range for grabbing weapons and the Spike is slightly longer than the range for triggering door switches. Telekinesis makes Hush one of the best objective-securing agents in Valorant.
Flow (C)
Place an anchor anywhere and propel yourself toward it. Using it mid-air lets you hover and curve your movement path around obstacles.
Flow is the longest dash in Valorant, surpassing Jett, Raze, and Waylay. Depending on where you aim, you can execute high aerial entries (by jumping before dashing) or fast, low-to-the-ground slides by aiming directly at the floor.
Flashbulb (Q)
EQUIP a flash device similar to KAY/O. FIRE (left-click) to throw it directly, or ALT-FIRE (right-click) to prime it on your shoulder for quick use while keeping your weapon out. When thrown or primed, press Q again to redirect the projectile toward your crosshair and detonate it.
This functions as one of the most versatile flashes in the game. You can bounce it off walls for fake flashes, set up one-ways, or prime it before dashing to blind enemies the exact second you enter a site.
Displacement (E)
EQUIP a gravity projectile that uses the same firing and guiding mechanics as Flashbulb (FIRE to throw and redirect, ALT-FIRE to prime). Upon detonation, it pulls players toward the center. The ability refreshes every 2 kills, similar to how Raze gets paint shells and Neon gets slide back.
Note that the pull itself from Valorant agent Hush’s Displacement does not stun enemies by default. To concuss opponents, they must collide with another player or a solid surface like a wall or box. It also affects Hush, meaning you can throw it at your own feet to sling yourself out of a corner for a fast peek.
Suspension (X) – Ultimate
Launch a guided orb that moves in the direction of your crosshair. Reactivate or FIRE to detonate the orb early, lifting all caught enemies into the air, disarming them, and preventing them from using Valorant weapons or abilities.
Enemies caught in Suspension are left completely defenseless. Keep in mind that while the orb cannot be shot/destroyed by regular gunfire and can brush against vertical walls without popping, it will automatically detonate the moment it touches any walkable surface (floors, boxes, or ledges).
Best Tips and Tricks to Master Valorant Agent Hush
To get the most out of Hush’s high skill ceiling, use these practical tips and tricks in Valorant and rank up faster:
- Dual-Prep Before Entries: You can prime both Flashbulb (Q) and Displacement (E) on your shoulder via right-click at the exact same time while keeping your gun out. Prep both before dashing into a site to blind and pull defenders simultaneously. Just watch the prep timer so they don’t expire.
- Master Dash Tech (Quick Slide, Pagani Peek & Momentum Cut): A regular high dash leaves you floating in the air for too long. Pull your crosshair down mid-dash to cut momentum and hit the ground faster. To execute a Neon-style Quick Slide, aim slightly above a surface, jump before the dash pops, and hold crouch at the peak of your jump. You can also aim Flow (C) at a 30-45° angle against a wall to slide across it for an unreactable Pagani Peek. Otherwise, place the anchor at 45° and turn your screen so it sits at the edge of your monitor while holding S + A/D for a Super Dash.
- Use the Minimap to Guide Redirects: Because redirected Displacement (E) and Flashbulb (Q) projectiles travel in a dead-straight line toward where you face, watch your minimap while the projectile is flying to time your second key press accurately around corners. On defense, prep Displacement to yank Jett or Neon players straight out of their smokes on audio cues, or pull enemies completely off ledges on maps like Abyss.
- Dive-Bomb With Ultimate Immunity: Hush is completely immune to her own Suspension (X) ultimate. You can fire the orb, immediately fast-dash directly onto the enemy’s position, and detonate it right at your feet to levitate everyone around you while you shoot freely.
- Deny Clove and Sage Revives: When your team gets a pick and an enemy Clove has their ultimate ready, or Sage is looking to resurrect a teammate, use Telekinesis (Passive) from up to 36m away to steal the dead player’s primary weapon. When they revive, they will be stuck with only a Classic. You can also hit door switches from across the map on Lotus or Ascent. This helps for early-round Odin wallbangs, Operator angles, or rotation fakes.
- Bait Out Veto’s Interceptor: Agent 29, Veto, is Hush’s biggest hard counter in Valorant. His Interceptor destroys Flashbulb, Displacement, and even her otherwise unbreakable Suspension ultimate. Never initiate a site hit with your loud ultimate if Veto is alive. Instead, play default and have teammates use rechargeable utility (like Skye flashes) to bait out Veto’s Interceptor before committing.
And that’s everything you should know about the abilities and tricks for Hush, Valorant’s new Duelist agent. Before you head into your first match, make sure you have the best Valorant crosshair codes set up for a cleaner aim experience.
What role is Hush in Valorant?
Hush is a Duelist (the 9th Duelist in the game) who plays as an Initiator-Duelist hybrid.
When does Hush release in Valorant?
Hush was released alongside Season 26, Act VI on October 27, 2026.
Is Hush a good agent for beginners in Valorant?
No, Hush has a very high skill ceiling that requires managing projectile redirection, prep timers, and directional dash physics.
Where is Hush from in Valorant?
Hush is from Guangdong, China.
Who is the voice actor of Hush in Valorant?
The Japanese voice actress for Hush in Valorant is Aino Shimada. Riot Games has not yet officially announced the English and Chinese voice actresses.

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory.
The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group.
So Wheeler and Johnson figured that a methylated version of cytosine might also exist in nature.
In 1925, Johnson, while working with another scientist named Robert Coghill, finally discovered 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Two more decades later, Rollin Hotchkiss found 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of cows. Soon, scientists found that it existed in nearly all animals.
However, nobody knew why it existed — or why some of the cytosines in DNA were methylated while others were not.
Genes on and off
That insight came in 1975, when Robin Holliday and John Pugh proposed that the methylation of the cytosine could be a way for the body to use the information stored in DNA.
DNA is segmented into genes, and each gene contains the information necessary to make a particular protein. These proteins perform their specific functions in the cells. Since every cell in the body has two copies — one from each parent — of all human DNA, all cells technically have the blueprint to make a whole organism.
However, cells also have specialised functions. A brain cell will not need the genes for the proteins used to digest food. So Holliday and Pugh suggested that chemical modifications such as the methylation of cytosine could help establish and activate genes that a cell wants while silencing those it does not.
This idea, that cells could use chemical tags on DNA to control which genes were active, has come to be called epigenetics. (The British biologist Conrad Waddington had actually coined the term in 1942 itself.) Soon, scientists found enzymes that could add and remove these chemical tags to and from DNA.
Today, we know that cells use many other chemical tags, not only on DNA itself but also on the proteins around which DNA is wrapped like a vine around a stick.
Together, all these chemical marks help control which genes are switched on or off. Problems in this system can lead to changes in gene activity, which in turn can lead to diseases like cancers.
Functional cure
Now, according to a paper that appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21, scientists have used this epigenetic control to treat a hepatitis B infection.
This is a remarkable development because, instead of targeting the virus directly, the work silenced the viral DNA. This is promising because current treatments rarely eliminate the DNA, which allows the virus to rebound. By silencing this residue, the treatment could offer a path to a lasting functional cure for hepatitis B.
The hepatitis B virus mainly infects liver cells. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. In many people, the immune system clears the infection, but if it does not, the viral DNA can persist for years or even decades in the host’s liver.
In this time, the virus can remain silent, meaning the viral DNA is still present in the cell but its genes are not active to produce new viruses. This allows the virus to ‘hide’ from the immune system. Then, at a later point, the virus can activate again and produce new virus particles.
And studies have shown that one of the mechanisms by which the virus stays silent is by methylating the cytosines.
Locator and effector
The authors of the new study have reported a new experimental therapy called CRMA-1001, which, they have claimed, can silence the DNA of the hepatitis B virus by selectively adding methylation marks to the viral genome.
The study is innovative because it uses several different technologies to overcome three major challenges. To epigenetically silence viral DNA, scientists first need to be able to target the virus’s DNA without methylating any of the cytosines in the host’s DNA. Then, the silencing mechanism must switch off the virus’s DNA effectively. Finally, all of this should happen without causing any unwanted side-effects to the host.
The study authors solved the first two problems by combining two substances called a ‘locator’ and an ‘effector’. The locator used the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool to find and bind to a specific DNA sequence: in this case, that was a sequence within the viral DNA. This allowed the CRISPR system to take the ‘effector’, the methylation machinery, to the correct location. The effector had proteins that could add methyl groups to nearby cytosines in the viral DNA and proteins that help switch off genes.
Finally, the researchers packed the entire system and delivered it on an mRNA platform (similar to the mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic). This made the system transient: once a cell had read the instructions to make the required proteins, it degraded them, stopping the production of those proteins too.
Novel therapy
The researchers gave mice infected with hepatitis B virus either a single dose of CRMA-1001 or three doses, one month apart, and regularly tested them for six months for the signs of infection. They reported that after one dose, the levels of several hepatitis B virus markers, including the viral DNA and two viral proteins called HBsAg and HBeAg, dropped significantly. When they tested the viral DNA, they found new methyl groups, suggesting that the treatment was working as intended. The effect was even stronger after three doses: six months after the first dose, as many as 90% of the animals had less viral DNA than could be detected.
CRMA-1001 is not a cure in the traditional sense of the word. The hepatitis B virus DNA is still present in the liver cells. Instead, the study demonstrated a functional cure: when the virus is not necessarily eliminated but is kept so thoroughly suppressed that, for all intents and purposes, the patient has no active signs of disease.
In this study, the team followed up with the mice for six months after treatment, and the researchers found sustained suppression of the virus in that period. However, the study did not establish whether the virus could eventually become active again after those six months, since the viral DNA was still present.
Further studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of CRMA-1001, including whether the silencing effect can persist over many years and whether the virus can ever become active again after treatment. An ongoing phase I/II clinical trial includes these among other questions.
If CRMA-1001 is eventually approved as a therapy for the market, it will represent a novel way to tackle a viral infection: where instead of fighting the threat, the cell ignores it.
Arun Panchapakesan is an assistant professor at the Y.R. Gaitonde Centre for AIDS Research and Education, Chennai.

Anthony Albanese has ruled out major cuts to health, education and essential services in December’s mid-year budget update, but conceded savings are required as Labor struggles to curb accelerating inflation.
Amid growing pressure from within Labor’s own ranks, as well as from the opposition and business, Albanese said the Coalition was hypocritical in not supporting existing savings proposals, including the government’s plan to reduce the private health insurance rebate for people over 65.
Privately, Labor MPs admit the strong likelihood of the Reserve Bank delivering the year’s fifth interest rate increase next week will compound the government’s political problem over the high cost of living, with some calling for radical moves from the federal government. Ed Husic, the former industry minister, this week said price controls on essential groceries items were needed, calling for caps on the cost of bread, milk, meat and fresh produce.
Australia’s headline inflation rate rose to 4.3% on Wednesday, dramatically increasing expectations of another interest rate rise on Melbourne Cup day.
The cash rate already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four rate hikes in 2026. A move to 4.85% would bring rates to their highest levels in 18 years, putting further pressure on household budgets.
As the Coalition criticises Labor for the rate of government spending, Albanese said he understood frustration in the community and efforts to find savings were under way.
“We will continue to meet over coming weeks as well, as we do consistently, looking for, making sure that appropriate savings are made,” he said, ahead of the budget update due in mid-December.
“What we won’t do is rip tens of billions of dollars out of health and education. That’s what happened last time when the Coalition came into office.
“We’re not looking at cutting funding for hospitals and schools and essential services because we’re a Labor government that understand that people are under pressure.”
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, on Thursday accused the Coalition of being consumed by “weird post-truth stuff” by refusing to acknowledge the global fuel shock as the biggest contributor to inflation.
Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.
Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%.
“The issue with inflation in our economy right now is really a function of two things. First of all a much quicker–than–anticipated recovery in the private sector,” Chalmers told parliament.
“Secondly, obviously, the escalation in fuel prices that came from the biggest oil shock in the history of the world.”
The government’s plans to wind back the private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 would save about $3bn over four years, money earmarked for aged care services. But the plan appears friendless in parliament, with the Coalition opposed.
Coalition MPs believe they have Labor cornered over the budget and rising interest rates, with the budget update expected to be further buffeted by higher costs for government debts due to conditions in the global bond market.
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Labor’s budget settings were “forcing Australian families to pay more for everything”.

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

Parents of spinal muscular atrophy(SMA)-afflicted children coming to the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital had been counselled several times about the government introducing the generic version of Risdiplam, instead of the Evrysdi brand by Roche, said V.H. Shankar, Head of the Department of Medical Genetics, who is also in charge of the treatment of children with rare diseases at the hospital, here on Friday.
Dr. Shankar, who attended a press conference along with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, said several meetings had been held with the parents of SMA-afflicted children, during which time all their queries on the efficacy of the generic drug were clarified.
He was answering queries on whether the parents had been told about the introduction of the generic drug for SMA and whether their concerns had been assuaged adequately by the authorities.
Dr. Shanker said he himself had spoken at several of the meetings with the parents. He added that the new generic drug Natsmart was given to six children and the parents were clearly told that the drug being dispensed was not the same brand (Evrysdi) that used to be dispensed earlier.
He said the technical committee had evaluated the decision to shift from Evrysdi to Natsmart several times. The purchase procedure was initiated in February 2026 itself.
Chairperson of the technical committee and Director of Medical Education K.V. Viswanath said the medicine bottles bore the sticker “Physicians’ sample/ for clinical trials”, which is just an indication that the bottles were not for open sale.
The SAT Superintendent had earlier clarified that they were awaiting the government supply of Natsmart, when on Monday, patients had arrived at the SMA clinic seeking the medicine. He had also clarified that rather than asking them to come another day, the hospital had contacted Natco and secured some samples from them to be given to the SMA patients.
The government supply arrived on Tuesday evening itself, but by which time, the campaign that clinical trial medicines were being given to SMA patients was already raging.
Former Health Minister, Veena George, had demanded on Thursday at a press conference that the government should explain how “drugs meant for clinical trials” had been supplied through the hospital. She also alleged that after the controversy broke, the parents had been “threatened” into returning the medicine bottles by the SAT Hospital authorities.
Mr. Muraleedharan said the authorities took back the medicines and replaced it with the lot from the government supply to put the controversy and concerns at rest. He said the doctors at SAT Hospital had spoken to the parents and explained everything and the so-called “concerns” were the creation of some news channels. He said it was also possible that the controversy was deliberately raked up by some along with pharma majors.
He said the government intended to purchase only the generic version of Risdiplam so that the treatment can be provided to more patients.
Meanwhile, many public health experts have expressed concern over the manner in which the issue is being politicised by the Opposition, which has continued to perpetuate the concerns and misgivings of parents of SMA patients by raising the allegation that “clinical trial drugs” were distributed to children.

Ellie Kildunne has been named on the England bench for their fixture against the USA, despite head coach John Mitchell making six changes to his side.
The 27-year-old full-back was dropped for the 31-22 defeat by Canada last Saturday, with Mitchell saying she needed to show "greater consistency".
Despite the loss in Ottawa, Bristol Bears star Kildunne will once again have to settle for a place on the bench for Friday's match against the USA in New Jersey, with Emma Sing retaining her spot.
With 67 England caps to her name, Kildunne was named World Rugby's player of the year in 2024, and starred in the Red Roses' 2025 World Cup victory.
Four of Mitchell's changes are to the backs, with Tatyana Heard, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Flo Robinson and Holly Aitchison handed their first starts of the tour, while forwards Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir replace Hannah Botterman and Sarah Bern.
"Our intent is to start this next phase strongly against the USA, with six months until our next Test in the Women's Six Nations," said Mitchell.
"We're rotating some positions this week to refresh the group, create opportunities and continue building our depth.
"Selection is driven by what the team needs against the USA, the behaviours we value and the performance we're preparing to deliver.
"Everyone has a role, and everyone is accountable for our standards."

Is the double drop from the Premier League becoming more common?
- Published
One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.
It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.
With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop,
For the 1,450 Burnley supporters who made the trip to Lincoln City last weekend, the threat is all too real.
Head coach Nicky Hayen was never likely to survive a 4-1 defeat by a Lincoln team who were in non-league football 10 years ago.
With Diego Lopez appointed as Burnley's new chief football officer, and Fabio Celestini installed as their new boss, the Clarets must now hope for a change in fortunes.
Is the Championship becoming ever-more competitive as well-run clubs like Lincoln make an impact?
Or it simply a case of clubs from the Premier League imploding after relegation?
'Mismanagement of the playing squad' to blame
Fifteen years ago, the suggestion a top-flight club could be relegated in successive seasons was unthinkable.
After all, in the first 20 seasons of the Premier League it happened just the once.
That was to Swindon Town, and even then there were special circumstances.
The Robins finished fourth bottom of the second tier in 1994-95 but were relegated because of the rebalancing of the divisions to reduce the Premier League to 20 teams.
In any other season they would not have suffered the double drop.
As such, it could be argued that Wolves were the first team to suffer a double drop from the Premier League after being relegated in 2011-12.
Since then it has happened four times in 14 seasons.
Or, after Sunderland went down in 2016-18, three times in nine seasons.
And then back-to-back seasons with Luton and Leicester.
Meanwhile, Wigan and Portsmouth were relegated to League One after a second season in the Championship, Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday after a third.
For Wolves, Sunderland and Leicester there was considerable turmoil on and off the pitch which contributed to their demise.
Burney fans may fear there are similarities at Turf Moor.
During their double drop descent, Wolves - who remarkably suffered a treble drop to the bottom tier in the 1980s - burned through four managers and made a series of poor transfers.
Sunderland did so with the ignominy of being the only club to finish bottom of both divisions, winning just 13 of 84 league matches.
The Black Cats had been in the top flight for 10 seasons - though they had only reached the 40-point barrier, usually the target to remain in the division, three times.
Leicester's relegation to League One was a direct result of poor boardroom decisions, with a six-point deduction for breaching profit and sustainability regulations ultimately sealing their fate. The Foxes finished 23rd in the Championship, five points from safety.
It took Sunderland four years to return to the Championship, and such is the turmoil at Leicester an immediate promotion looks unlikely. Russell Martin's Leicester side sit 13th in League One, with the club up for sale.
"Despite the fact we've seen Luton and Leicester suffer back-to-back relegations in recent years, I don't see it as a trend that will continue," former Watford and Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff, now an EFL pundit, told BBC Sport.
"For both of those clubs, in my opinion, it was a case of mismanagement of the playing squad.
"From Luton's perspective, there were a few players there who maybe felt an entitlement to stay in the Premier League. They didn't readjust to being back at the Championship, where most of their players had actually been previously.
"And for Leicester City, they kept hold of too many that didn't really want to be there and then obviously weren't equipped to deal with a relegation battle."
While Luton may have got their recruitment wrong, they were much more responsibly run compared to the other double drop clubs.
The Hatters' progress off the pitch remains progressive rather than regressive, with work advancing on a new 25,000-capacity stadium at Power Court which is due to be completed for the start of 2028-29.
The fine line for success is shown by Luton's relegation from the Championship in 2024-25. They went down because of their inferior goal difference compared to Hull City, with the Tigers then promoted to the Premier League the following season.
Championship will become 'a much more competitive league'
Burnley had earned a reputation as the archetypal yo-yo club - relegated from or promoted to the top division in each of the past five seasons.
But after a leveraged buyout by Alan Pace's ALK Capital in 2020, the Clarets were carrying £142m in loans in the 2024-25 accounts - the year they went up - which was the highest debt level in the Championship.
This week Burnley set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win. When they host Portsmouth on Saturday, it will be 378 days since their last home victory.
Being humbled by a well-run, up-and-coming club like Lincoln, with far fewer resources but savvy ownership, will not be lost on Burnley supporters.
And the financial gap is huge.
Burnley's total revenue for 2024-25 was £71.7m, which dwarfed Lincoln's £7.81m.
The Clarets then received £48m in parachute payments. Lincoln can expect about £5.5m in solidarity funding.
Off the pitch there should be no contest, but football is not played purely on balance sheets.
In its State of the Game report, published earlier this month, the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said a new financial deal between the Premier League and the EFL must "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship".
The solution is merit payments, which would mirror the Premier League's model of prize money by final league position.
At present, every club in the Championship receives the same payment, regardless of where they finish.
"The amount of money paid in parachute payments will reduce and the amount of money going into the Championship will vastly increase," IFR chair David Kogan said.
"The delta between parachute payment clubs and non-parachute payment clubs is going to significantly reduce, which makes the Championship a much more competitive league."
Parachute payments are paid to clubs relegated from the Premier League to help them adjust to the financial realities of the second tier - £48m in year one, then £39m in year two,
Could this make the double drop more common as the revenue gap closes? Much will depend upon just how "significantly" the gap is closed.
The IFR report found that parachute payment clubs were more than four times more likely to be promoted. In 2024-25, four clubs were in receipt and they were almost 27 points better off, and filled the top three places (with Luton relegated).
"If you look at the numbers of teams that go back up or finish in the top places, there's a huge correlation between those clubs and the ones that are parachute payment clubs," McAnuff said.
"Even with a reduction in parachute payments, I still feel that advantage will prove to be massively significant for those teams."
It may yet be that Burnley escape the double drop, that the financial advantage of parachute payments outweighs poor decision-making.
But the double drop has generally become far more common. And that should concern any club that gets relegated and is not prepared for life in the Championship.

The story so far
An initiative launched by Keralam government to make the treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) accessible to more patients is now courting controversy.
SMA is a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function. While a complete cure remains elusive, the launch of Risdiplam, marketed as Evrysdi by Roche Pharmaceuticals, the first at-home, oral treatment for SMA, gave hope to thousands of SMA patients. Risdiplam was found to have a significant effect on the progression of the disease, by slowing down motor degeneration, improving physical milestones and stabilising respiratory function.
Risdiplam was launched in India in July 2021, making it the first and only approved drug in the country to manage SMA. But the drug’s astronomical cost made it inaccessible to most families.
Keralam, which has been giving Risdiplam free of cost to eligible children since 2022, made a switch to the less expensive generic version of the drug in October this year . But since then, a section of parents of children living with SMA children have urged the government to switch back to the expensive, branded version.
Last week, when the generic drug was dispensed for the first time at SAT hospital, a Centre of Excellence for Rare Diseases in Thiruvananthapuram, a sticker on the bottle which said “Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials” reopened the branded versus generic debate and a new allegation, that drugs meant for clinical trials were being used on children
How Keralam began SMA treatment
Keralam was the first State to give Risdiplam free of cost through government hospitals in 2022 and an SMA clinic was subsequently opened at SAT hospital. Though initially Risdiplam was given free only to children under 12, in 2026 the government announced an extension of coverage to genetically confirmed SMA Type 2 patients up to age 25, with ₹30 crore allocated in the State budget for this. However, as of now, 109 Type 1 and 2 children with SMA below the age of 12 are being given Risdiplam, free.
Risdiplam, under its trade name Evrysdi, used to cost ₹6.3 lakh for a bottle (current price ₹4.44 lakhs), which the State was getting at a negotiated price of ₹5.4 lakh per bottle. Under the patient assistance programme, Roche used to give 11 bottles free of cost to the State for every four bottles it purchased. The State’s annual requirement was estimated at around 2,500 bottles and the annual financial commitment was around ₹23 crore. The State, therefore, was up against enormous cumulative expenditure as more children became eligible and existing patients required continued treatment.
The decision to switch to generic
A technical experts committee in Keralam met several times to evaluate if the generic alternative, Natsmart, which has all regulatory approvals, and which was ready for commercial distribution in October 2025, could replace Roche’s Evrysdi. Natco Pharma, through a historic Delhi High Court verdict, had won the right to marker the generic alternative of Risdiplam at a dramatically reduced price of ₹15,900 per bottle, against Roche’s Rs. 6.3 lakhs per bottle.
A bottle of Evrysdi on which Roche holds a patent, typically lasts 12 days, meaning the annual maintenance cost for a patient would amount to a crushing ₹60-70 lakh. With Natsmart, the generic alternative, the cost would be under ₹5 lakh. In February 2026, the Keralam government gave the go ahead for Natsmart, and purchase processes were initiated.
What are parents’ concerns?
Parents and advocacy groups including the Cure SMA Foundation of India claim that the branded medication, Evrysdi, has a proven, long-term track record of safety and efficacy, while the new generic version lacks dedicated human bioequivalence or long-term clinical studies specific to paediatric patients. They claim that a sudden switch to an unverified or less effective generic formula could reverse the critical motor and survival progress already achieved by children who are currently stable on the original drug. They have been continuously petitioning the government asking that their children be allowed to continue on Evrysdi.
What do doctors say?
Public health experts have hailed the government’s decision to switch to the generic drug. They say that arguments challenging the efficacy of the generic formulation and alleging a lack of ‘bioavailability’ are entirely unscientific and baseless.
Bioavailability denotes the rate and extent to which an administered pharmaceutical substance enters systemic circulation through the digestive tract. A bioequivalence study normally compares the rate and extent of absorption of the generic with the reference product. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises this as an important way to establish interchangeability. However, bioequivalence studies are not required for every generic medicine. The WHO’s guidance on generic medicines explicitly recognises circumstances in which equivalence studies can be waived. One such circumstance is when the generic and reference products are pharmaceutically equivalent oral solutions containing the same active ingredient at the same molar concentration, subject to the applicable requirements for excipients.
In this case, both products contain Risdiplam. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Natsmart and the regulator’s position is that a bioequivalence study is not required for this particular oral solution. Public health experts also say that the absence of a conventional bioequivalence study does not necessarily mean the regulator approved the drug without adequate evidence. A regulator may accept a scientifically-justified waiver.
Doctors also point out that Natsmart is being prescribed by many premier teaching hospitals in the country and several patients are already using it in Keralam too, for the last five months, without any complaints.
Public health is about maximising access to people, and unless credible scientific evidence demonstrates that the approved generic is less safe or less effective than the original molecule, regulatory approval should remain the primary basis for procurement decisions in publicly-funded health programmes, experts have argued.
The current controversy
The current controversy centres around an alarm raised by parents of children with SMA, after they pointed out that the bottle of Natsmart dispensed to them was labelled, ‘Physicians’ sample/for clinical trials’. Though the authorities clarified later that these were drug sample bottles they were forced to source directly from Natco and not part of the government supply (which was delayed), the issue has become something for Opposition parties, particularly the CPI(M), to latch on to. It has also served to perpetuate fears and misgivings about the generic drug among SMA families.
What is happening at present?
SAT Hospital authorities, who are responsible for the SMA clinic, have now decided to hold a meeting of families to assuage their concerns. They say that several meetings had been held earlier too, to reassure parents about the switch from Evrysdi to Natsmart. However, the new controversy over ‘clinical trial’ drugs may have undone some of the previous work. The labelling issue is clearly separate from the concerns about the switch to generic medicine and the families’ demand for scientific evidence and transparent communication is valid, authorities admit.

Horses, farming and a bad injury - McNabney's rise to Ireland
- Published
"Will you ever be home to the farm again?"
That was the light-hearted response from James McNabney's father after he was called into the Ireland squad for the first time.
When the news came, the 23-year-old back row was in South Africa with Ulster and, without an eSIM in his phone, was trying to connect to WiFi when out for coffee.
When finally online, he saw the email that said he had earned an Ireland call-up from Andy Farrell.
"I was delighted. It was a big moment for the family as well," McNabney said.
"My mum was very proud and I don't think my dad knew what way to take it at the start.
"But no, they're both delighted for me and I appreciate the support they've given me."
- McNabney keen to show Ireland coaches 'what I'm all about' 
  - Published2 days ago
- Ringrose set to miss Ireland's November games 
  - Published1 day ago
McNabney's route into the Ireland set-up is not the traditional path taken by most players.
Growing up on a farm in Ballymena, he did not watch a lot of rugby growing up and only started playing in school. At the time, horses were his focus.
Long before he had even dreamt of becoming a professional rugby player, he had represented Northern Ireland and Great Britain's equestrian teams.
"I rode horses from when I was about six until I was 16," he said.
"Horses was sort of a main hobby, then it became a sport for me."
At 16 he was given an ultimatum over his sporting future.
"Michael Black [a provincial talent coach] from Ulster was like, 'you need to make the decision whether you're going to put on a bit of timber and play rugby or stay lean and ride a horse'.
"I decided to play rugby. I was enjoying it, I stuck at it and here I am."
As for equestrian, there's no more horsing around for the big back row.
"We've still got one at home. If I'm taken to the field then I'll maybe jump on it.
"Other than that, I only do it for the craic. I haven't been on a horse in, I'd say, six months."
Given his other interests, McNabney says he did not have a lot of rugby heroes growing up and instead simply "enjoyed playing it".
"I didn't really watch it that much. That probably went against me because I was quite green, and didn't know much about it.
"But it wasn't until I was getting to Ireland Under-20s that I really thought this is what I'm going to do for a job."
'There are going to be setbacks'
An Under-20 Six Nations Grand Slam winner in 2022 and 2023, McNabney's senior Ireland chance came more than a year later than he initially hoped.
After an impressive season with Ulster, he had been included by Farrell as a training panellist for the 2025 Six Nations.
He was set to be included again for the summer fixtures against Japan and Georgia when the bulk of the front-liners were away with the British and Irish Lions, but he did not get to meet up with the squad after he sustained an ACL injury.
He only returned to action for Ulster in pre-season this summer after a year on the sidelines, and the fact Farrell has included him in the Ireland panel again at the first time of asking shows how highly he is rated by the coaching group.
At 6ft 5in and almost 19 stone, it's easy to see why Farrell described him as "some specimen of a man".
McNabney said it was the worst injury you can get as a player, but that "you just have to be patient".
"I tried to set a goalpost of where I wanted to be to get back. And then different things happened. I learned to just take it a day at a time.
"Each player is different and their bodies react differently to everything. So I just had to learn that there are going to be setbacks.
"We've got it here now and I'm delighted that I pushed through."
'I don't have the expectation of being capped'
Now in a position to impress Farrell and his coaching team, McNabney could make his Ireland debut in November's Nations Championship matches against Argentina, Fiji, South Africa or during the finals weekend in London at the end of the month.
He says he is "delighted" he has got a chance, but even if he doesn't get any minutes on the pitch he is more than happy to play a role this autumn.
When asked what his goal was for the camp, he said to "learn as much as possible and hopefully earn my first cap".
"I don't have the expectation that I'm going to get capped. I'm here to work hard, show what I'm about.
"Just because I'm picked in the squad doesn't mean I'm necessarily going to play.
"Hopefully I train hard, get picked, and hopefully Faz [Farrell] sees what I see in myself and backs me.
"I'll just work hard and prepare the team as best as I can for the games coming up."
Given his laid-back demeanour, it's no surprise to hear that McNabney "hasn't been too fixed" on whether he will or will not make his Ireland bow in the next five weeks.
"Every young player wants to play for Ireland someday. It's hard to get into the team, that doesn't just happen," he added.
"Someday I might wear the green, but I still haven't worn it yet."

Panic at federal nuclear site as raging blaze shuts down air, rail and ground travel
A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is in a complex where key parts for nuclear bombs were once made triggered an emergency declaration Wednesday

A fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory in South Carolina prompted an emergency declaration on Wednesday, halting incoming traffic and restricting air and rail service in the surrounding area. Firefighters extinguished the blaze by Wednesday night, and the site returned to normal operations.
A Savannah River Site statement said it found no detectable levels of contamination. The laboratory sits within the U.S. Department of Energy's Savannah River Site, a massive complex where the federal government once produced materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily tritium and plutonium-239.
The lab occupies the northwest corner of the site, near its edge. The complex opened in the early 1950s as the Cold War was heating up and was built near Jackson, South Carolina.
According to the U.S. Department of Energy, it is used today for environmental stewardship and cleanup, nuclear waste management, and the disposition of nuclear materials. Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the lab currently conducts experiments with nuclear materials and processes radioactive material, including operating a facility for radioisotope recovery from used nuclear fuel.
Lyman said it is reassuring that officials said there has been no off-site contamination, noting that a buffer zone separates most of the facilities from public areas. But if you have a fire involving radioactive material, “you need to take extreme precautions because of the potential dispersal of that material and the potential for contamination, potential for the public to be exposed,” he said.
The emergency declaration issued Wednesday is the second-highest of three emergency categories at the site and indicates “something more serious has occurred,” according to the site's community preparedness information.
It ended on Wednesday night after the fire was extinguished. A U.S. Department of Energy spokesperson said one person suffered minor injuries in the fire. The spokesperson, citing officials at the Savannah River Site, said the person injured was an employee who was taken to the hospital.
The spokesperson said the fire was extinguished and no contamination has been reported. The Savannah River Site did not say what caused the fire. According to its website, the Federal Aviation Administration temporarily restricted flights in the area because of the fire.
The Savannah River Site said rail, river and ground travel in the area also was restricted. It said employees not involved in emergency response or shutdown operations were sheltered as a precaution. The fire prompted a "site area emergency." After producing material for nuclear weapons during the Cold War, the Savannah River National Laboratory now focuses on waste cleanup and nuclear materials management.
