The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States.
The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia.
“It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it’s being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.”
The project has gained official support after repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were finally settled through a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark in September 2026. The agreement preserves Greenland’s autonomous territory status within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. But relations have grown increasingly strained between the United States and its allies in Europe and Canada since President Trump initiated trade wars with multiple countries and has taken an increasingly pro-Russia stance on the war in Ukraine.
Europe has also been eyeing new Internet cable routes to Asia because more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia run through undersea cables in the Red Sea, according to TeleGeography. Maintaining such cables has become riskier since open warfare resumed between the Yemeni government and Houthi faction this year, with Houthi forces having fired missiles and drones at commercial ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint and the broader Red Sea.

The question of when India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) will finally be monetised has remained at the centre of the fintech industry’s conversations over the past month. The debate intensified after the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) deferred the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions. Earlier reports suggested that the rollout could be pushed to January 2027. However, the framework now appears likely to be introduced after Diwali, with the industry awaiting a final announcement. Under the proposed framework, eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR fee of 0.40%, capped at ₹300 per transaction. The proposal has drawn resistance from retail traders, who argue that the charges would add to their operating costs. The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) also called for a ‘No UPI Day’ protest, but eventually withdrew the proposal following a meeting with finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Separately, advocate Anjan Datta filed a public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the policy in the Supreme Court. The apex court, however, declined to stay the proposed MDR charges. Meanwhile, UPI transaction volumes and values declined month-on-month (MoM) in September. The number of transactions fell nearly 1.8% to 24.07 Bn, while their cumulative value dropped 1.5% to ₹29.37 Lakh Cr. However, the decline that followed August was met with an all-time high in monthly transaction volumes. Average daily UPI transactions increased to 802 Mn in September from 791 Mn in August, while the average daily transaction value rose to ₹97,913 Cr from ₹96,205 Cr. For banks, payment companies and third-party application providers (TPAPs), the proposed MDR framework could open up a new revenue stream in a market where monetisation has remained a persistent challenge. Meanwhile, the uncertainty around the rollout has also weighed on listed fintech companies. Reports of a delay in MDR implementation triggered declines in the stocks of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik, underlining the potential impact of UPI monetisation on the broader payments ecosystem. As the industry awaits greater clarity on the future of UPI and the economics of digital payments, we are back with the October edition of Five Fintech Startups To Watch. This monthly series spotlights startups operating in some of the most promising and fast-evolving segments of India’s fintech ecosystem. With that, here are five interesting ventures that caught our attention this month. Editor’s Note: The list below is not a ranking of any kind. Startups have been listed alphabetically. Credfix | Helping Distressed Borrowers Falling behind on loan repayments can quickly turn into a stressful cycle of recovery calls, mounting worries about credit scores and uncertainty over what to do next. For many borrowers, negotiating with lenders, exploring settlement options and dealing with legal notices can be just as daunting as the debt itself. In India’s about $200 Mn debt collection software market, Bengaluru-based Credfix is trying to help borrowers deal with debt through an AI-powered platform. Founded in 2025 by Ranjan Agarwal, Neeraj Kulkarni and Ayush Kedia, Credfix helps borrowers understand their financial situation and explore ways to repay or settle their outstanding loans. It also helps lenders recover money from borrowers who are struggling to pay. The startup currently serves over 2 Lakh borrowers with total outstanding debt of more than ₹4,000 Cr. Around 40% of its users are from tier II and tier III cities. Credfix combines AI-powered tools with human support to help borrowers at different stages of the debt repayment process. Its Risi AI assistant offers guidance on available settlement options, responding to legal notices and dealing with recovery agents. The startup also helps borrowers negotiate one-time settlements, where lenders agree to close a loan for less than the total amount owed. In addition, it explains borrowers’ rights and provides step-by-step guidance on rebuilding their CIBIL scores after settling their loans. FOLO | Bringing Entire Wealth Into One View A person’s wealth is often spread across multiple bank accounts, investments, insurance policies and other assets. Keeping track of everything can make it difficult to know how much they own, how much they owe and how their overall financial position is changing. FOLO, short for Family Of Loved Ones, is trying to solve this problem with an app that brings a person’s financial information together in one place. Founded in 2022 by Munmun Desai and Vishal Purohit, the startup operates in India’s $171.2 Bn wealth management market, which is projected to grow at over 10.6% annually over the next eight years. It has raised over $2.9 Mn in funding so far. FOLO is a SEBI-registered investment adviser that collects financial information from more than 650 sources, including bank accounts, mutual funds, stocks, fixed deposits, property, loans, credit cards and insurance policies. This gives users a consolidated view of their assets and liabilities, without having to manually track everything. The platform uses the account aggregator framework to access financial information in a read-only mode, with users’ consent. It also allows users to share selected financial details with up to four trusted individuals, such as family members or financial advisers, without revealing their account login details. Beyond tracking wealth, FOLO offers an offline service, called LYNC, to help users transfer their assets to nominees after their death. The startup claims to have connected assets worth more than ₹20,000 Cr on its platform and crossed 1 Lakh app downloads. Spring Street | Making Global Investing Accessible To Indians India’s investors are increasingly looking beyond domestic markets to diversify their bets. However, investing in foreign stocks and other assets can be complicated, with hurdles around research, money transfers, taxes and regulatory compliance. Founded in 2026 by Nishant Bansal, Spring Street is building a platform that gives Indian residents and non-resident Indians (NRIs) access to international markets through managed investment portfolios. Backed by Nexus Venture Partners, the startup is targeting a growing appetite for overseas investments. Indian residents remitted around $2.6 Bn (₹22,000 Cr) for overseas investments in FY26, up nearly 56% from $1.69 Bn in FY25. Its flagship product, Prisma, offers professionally managed portfolios investing in international stocks, bonds and commodities. These portfolios provide exposure to markets across North America, Europe, Asia and Latin America, with options tailored to investors’ risk appetites and financial goals. Spring Street also handles overseas investing, from onboarding and identity verification to remittance paperwork and investment tracking. To facilitate investments under the Reserve Bank of India’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), the startup has partnered with GIFT City-based ViewTrade, which is regulated by the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA). ViewTrade acts as the broker and custodian. Spring Street charges an annual portfolio management fee of 1.25% to 1.50% of assets managed, depending on the portfolio, with no additional commissions on individual trades. Investors need to start with a minimum investment of $500. UpTik | Unlocking Invoice Discounting For SMEs Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) often struggle with cash flow when customers take weeks or months to pay their invoices. This can leave businesses short of money to cover everyday expenses or fund their next order. At the same time, retail investors looking beyond traditional investment products have limited access to opportunities linked to short-term business financing. Hyderabad-based UpTik is trying to bridge this gap by connecting investors with businesses seeking working capital. Founded in 2025 by Ainampudi Vinod Varma, Mudunuri Dileep Varma, Phanindra Kumar and Uma Mukesh Ponduru, the startup allows businesses to raise funds against unpaid invoices, while investors can earn returns when those invoices are paid. UpTik claims to have grown its assets under management (AUM) from ₹6.5 Cr in March 2026 to over ₹25 Cr in September 2026. Monthly disbursements also rose from ₹3.6 Cr to ₹13.3 Cr over the same period. Through its platform, UpTik offers retail investors, HNIs and institutional investors opportunities to finance verified business invoices. The startup lists investment opportunities with defined tenures and provides details about the underlying transactions, expected returns and associated risks. Investors must complete KYC checks, while each deal undergoes due diligence and legal screening. Users can also track their investments and request withdrawals of returns to an in-app wallet. UpTik provides additional protection against defaults on select deals. The startup plans to expand beyond invoice discounting into other alternative investments, including corporate bonds and startup investments. Zomint | Democratising Wealth Management While wealthy individuals can hire wealth managers to guide their financial decisions, professionals and families with smaller portfolios often have to navigate investment choices on their own. Chandigarh-based Zomint aims to bridge this gap by helping professionals and families manage their wealth through personalised financial advice. Founded in 2025 by Aman Mittal and Shavir Bansal, the wealthtech startup draws on Bansal’s earlier venture, the personal finance content platform Bekifaayati, which claims a community of over 50 Lakh and more than 80 Lakh monthly views. This audience has also helped Zomint build its customer base. According to a market assessment published in an NSE-hosted document in November 2025, India’s investment and wealth management sector had an estimated annual addressable market of ₹1.1 Lakh Cr in FY25. The assessment projects this to reach ₹2.2 Lakh Cr to ₹2.6 Lakh Cr by FY30. The startup assigns each customer a dedicated financial expert who uses AI tools and research to track investments, recommend suitable mutual funds and guide financial decisions over time. Its relationship managers currently serve more than 250 families each. Zomint lets customers start with a monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) of ₹25,000 or a lump-sum investment of ₹5 Lakh. Its investment options include equity, debt and hybrid mutual funds, gold and silver funds, and global investment products available through GIFT City. Beyond helping customers choose investments, Zomint actively monitors their portfolios and can recommend changes based on market conditions, developments affecting individual funds or shifts in customers’ financial circumstances. This allows the startup to offer ongoing guidance rather than one-time investment recommendations. Edited by Shishir Parasher

Lokayukta Case Against Ramesh Thete: Retired Madhya Pradesh-cadre IAS officer Ramesh S Thete was arrested in Nagpur on Wednesday by Bhopal's MP Nagar police in connection with a fraud and cheque bounce case. The arrest was made in the Manish Nagar area with assistance from Beltarodi police.
Police are bringing Thete to Bhopal, where he will be produced before a court after questioning.
Court Had Issued Permanent Arrest Warrant
Thete's arrest follows an order passed by Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) Kalpana Kotwal's court in Bhopal on March 23, 2026. The court declared him an absconder and issued a permanent arrest warrant after he repeatedly failed to appear for hearings.
According to the court order, Thete had been given several opportunities to appear but failed to attend the proceedings. Previous arrest warrants could not be executed.
The court observed that the circumstances suggested he was deliberately avoiding the warrant. The complainant also informed the court that Thete had failed to comply with its directions, while requested a permanent arrest warrant.
The court accepted the application and issued the warrant. It also directed that the case file be placed in the archives until his appearance.
Other Cases Registered Against Thete
The retired IAS officer faces separate cases registered at Habibganj and MP Nagar police stations, as well as a case with the Lokayukta.
An FIR registered with the Lokayukta in February 2023 also named his wife, Manda Thete, as an accused.
The cases include allegations related to disproportionate assets, bank-related fraud and cheque bounce incidents. These are separate matters, and their legal status will depend on the respective proceedings.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

The pros and cons of a stuttering run-up are under debate after two crucial penalty misses in the Carabao Cup last 16.
Chelsea midfielder Valentin Barco missed the Blues' fourth penalty in their entertaining shootout defeat by Liverpool when he hit the post after a stuttered run-up.
Xabi Alonso's side would be in the EFL Cup quarter-finals had he scored, but they crashed out as defender Wesley Fofana sent one in sudden death high into the Kop at Anfield.
Barco's miss came after Arsenal midfielder Bruno Guimaraes had his spot-kick saved after a similar 'stutter' run-up as the Gunners crashed out against League Two Fleetwood Town on Tuesday night.
Both were shown how to do it by Liverpool defender Joe Gomez - a player who has never scored a senior goal in 319 professional appearances - who rifled the winning penalty into the top corner after a simple run-up.
Players opt for the stutter in a bid to trick the goalkeeper into giving them a clue as to which way they will dive.
The problem is it can backfire spectacularly if the goalkeeper holds their nerve or - in Barco's case - the taker fails to hit the target.
Former Chelsea defender Cesar Azpilicueta told ITV: "Every player picks his style where he feels confident, and for Valentin Barco, I believe that is his way of shooting it. I don't believe that was his first time, I hope not!"
The 'stutter' penalty became a theme of this year's World Cup. There were 26 at the summer's tournament but 11 were missed.
The stop-start run-up technique does not have a strict definition but a player is allowed, under Fifa rules, to stop or feint in the run-up as long as they don't do it directly before kicking the ball.
Even Harry Kane tried it in the summer and missed. His stuttering run-up led to Croatia goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic saving his penalty in England's 4-2 win.
But because Livakovic came off his line early, Kane got a retake and smashed it home with a straightforward approach.
Arsenal and Brazil midfielder Guimaraes was one of those 11 to miss at the World Cup but did not change his approach at Fleetwood.
Some players have used it to their advantage. Brazil icon Pele was famous for it while Cristiano Ronaldo has used it with both success and failure.
Manchester United's Bruno Fernandes, former Chelsea and Arsenal midfielder Jorginho and Wolves striker Raul Jimenez are others who often use the 'stutter' style.
"I wouldn't allow it if I was a manager," former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told TalkSport on Wednesday after Arsenal's defeat the night before.
"It is ridiculous, self-indulgence, a player trying to be the centre of attention.
"When they do the stutter they think the keeper might go, but they aren't going that early, they aren't being tricked any more. It is naive."
But former Liverpool and Chelsea full-back Glen Johnson had a different view and pointed to the fact that Barco missed by mere inches.
"I like the technique," he told ITV. "It gives the players a bit of time.
"W what confused me about that one [from Barco] is usually players are watching the keeper. He has moved, he has got it right and gone the right way but lifted it in the air for no reason.
"You have the whole goal to shoot at and that is the surprising part. He has already beaten the goalkeeper, he doesn't have to hit it into the top corner.
"If he puts that ball three inches to the right you would say it is the best penalty you have seen."
Gomez breaks his goal duck - kind of
It will not go down as a goal in the record books but Gomez got the feeling of seeing one of his shots hit the back of the net for the first time as a senior player.
It is remarkable that in 319 games for Charlton Athletic, Liverpool and England, the 29-year-old defender has never got on the scoresheet.
But Gomez looked like a veteran finisher when he powered his penalty - which was the penultimate of the shootout before Fofana missed - into the top corner in front of the Kop.
"Everyone is on edge and we want to win," Gomez told ITV.
"For me it is the moment I was thinking about and anticipating. It was nice it went in."

Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration.
The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy’s Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a “big fan.” But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they’re effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk.
Kennedy’s new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register, with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month.
Questionable rationale
Along with the notice in the Federal Register, HHS also posted a more detailed explanation of the policy today that includes more of Kennedy’s rationale for easing enforcement of the six select peptides, which are: BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500.

SEM court directs Delhi police to give Neha Bora copies of 6 FIRs by November 20
The direction by Special Executive Magistrate Raj came after Bora’s counsel, advocate, argued that the documents earlier supplied by the police were deficient.
A Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on Wednesday directed the Delhi police to provide AISA president Neha Bora with copies of six FIRs registered against her during the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, which were cited as her criminal antecedents while initiating proceedings to make her furnish a peace bond.
The direction by Special Executive Magistrate Ritu Raj came after Bora’s counsel, advocate Abhik Chimni, argued that the documents earlier supplied by the police were deficient and did not contain complete details of the FIRs, which were required by them to furnish a reply.
Also read | After Delhi HC order, Neha Bora gets documents behind peace bond notice
He submitted that despite relying on these cases as criminal antecedents to issue a show-cause notice asking Bora to execute a peace bond, the police had not provided copies of the FIRs.
High Court had directed police to share all material
The fresh direction follows the Delhi High Court’s dismissal of Bora’s challenge to the peace-bond proceedings on October 23.
While upholding the notice, the high court had directed the police to furnish all material relied upon to initiate the proceedings and asked the SEM to ensure that the principles of natural justice were followed before passing any order requiring her to furnish a bond.
Also read | ‘Nothing wrong with regime change’, Neha Bora tells Delhi HC; cops counter her
The police had earlier supplied Bora with documents, including a kalandara (a police report submitted to a magistrate) dated October 17 and three general diary entries from different police stations.
However, Chimni argued that the material provided did not adequately disclose the details of the six FIRs cited against her, leaving the defence without copies of the cases being relied upon by the authorities.
The police, represented by legal consultants Prashant Prakash and Bhagwan Dass , meanwhile, told the court that the FIRs lodged against Bora were sensitive in nature and hence they shall be provided by the next date of hearing on November 20.
Bora detained during protest march on October 16
The proceedings stem from Bora’s detention on October 16 during a protest march at Mandi House, where she and other AISA activists were demanding the resignation of Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
After her release the following morning, the police initiated preventive proceedings and issued a notice requiring her to explain why she should not be directed to furnish a personal bond of ₹10,000, along with one surety, to maintain peace.
The police have cited alleged provocative sloganeering, demonstrations near Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders and allegations that Bora instigated people to join a protest in Connaught Place as grounds for apprehending a breach of peace.
The Delhi High Court, while rejecting her plea, held that sufficient material was available before the SEM to initiate proceedings under Sections 126 and 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). It also directed that all material on which the authorities intended to rely during the inquiry be furnished to Bora.
Bora has opposed the demand for a peace bond, maintaining that it infringes upon the right to democratic dissent. She has said she would not sign the bond and would continue to challenge its use against peaceful protesters.
The direction came after Bora’s counsel, advocate Abhik Chimni, argued that the documents earlier supplied by the police were deficient and did not contain complete details of the FIRs.
He submitted that despite relying on these cases as criminal antecedents to issue a show-cause notice asking Bora to execute a peace bond, the police had not provided copies of the FIRs, hampering her ability to respond to the proceedings.

With days to go before the midterms, data shows the U.S. economy is doing well
The U.S. economy grew faster in the summer compared to the spring, driven by consumer spending as well as investments in AI.
Gross domestic product, which broadly measures economic activity, grew at an annual rate of 3.4% July through September, according to a report from the Commerce Department released Thursday. The previous quarter GDP grew at a 2.2% annual pace.
A big driver for GDP growth in the third quarter was the strong investments from AI companies, which continue to build out data centers and spend big money in developing the technology.
Meanwhile, consumer spending was another of the big drivers of GDP growth, led in part by higher-income Americans who are better able to withstand stubbornly high inflation.
The sturdy GDP data comes just days before the midterm elections, with many Americans saying they feel gloomy about the economy as inflation jacks up the costs of many day-to-day necessities, while the ongoing conflict with Iran drives up energy costs like gasoline.
Although consumer spending has been growing steadily, it has not spread out evenly across households, with lower-income Americans struggling more than high-earners. Wage growth has also fallen behind inflation, further squeezing many Americans.
Siri Steven, a manager at a resale store in Decorah, Iowa, says she and her husband are putting off fixing up their more than 130-year-old house.
"We barely go out to eat now," Steven said. "I really have to be mindful of our budget and make sure that we can pay all our bills and not overdraft."
She also says her family hasn't been able to save, going paycheck to paycheck. The personal saving rate for the U.S. in September is 3.8%, according to a separate report from the Commerce Department, down from 4.1% in August.
Prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, according to the same report, faster than the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The Fed watches the Commerce Department's inflation measure closely, particularly when deciding what to do with its benchmark interest rates.
Fed holds rates
Still, the central bank decided against raising rates Wednesday, with added pressure to raise rates during the next meeting in December after Thursday's reading on prices.
Economists also are concerned about the country's long term fiscal health. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, warns that despite solid GDP figures, economic growth feels delicate. That's due to business and consumers having to navigate around Trump Administration policies, such as tariffs and the U.S. war against Iran.
"We're growing," Zandi said. "The economy is moving forward but it's a very, very fragile growth. It doesn't feel like we're kicking it in on all cylinders."

Abdul El-Sayed doesn’t make headlines as the Senate candidate who wrote a book on applying systems science to public health, or who worked to rebuild Detroit’s health system, or who researched the ways social circumstances can impact maternal mortality.
With six days left in his bruising, contentious campaign, El-Sayed is known for his comical social media videos, his advocacy of “Medicare for All” and his controversial stance on U.S. policy toward Israel. As the man Vice President JD Vance called “a little weasel.” As the Egyptian-American who President Trump has said would “open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
But El-Sayed’s medical and public health background is likely to figure prominently if he is elected as a senator from Michigan. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has pitched El-Sayed as the future standard-bearer for Medicare for All, the policy Sanders popularized in the American consciousness. He would be the first epidemiologist to make it to the upper house, and the first holder of a medical degree to represent the Democratic party in the Senate since 1969. He would also be the first Muslim senator.
And at a moment when there is no clear challenger to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s remaking of the agencies that are the bedrock of public health, he is the candidate many supporters hope will push back.
“Public health is really under attack now, and the situation really needs response. Currently there is almost no public health person in the administration,” said Alfredo Morabia, an epidemiologist at Columbia University who taught El-Sayed in a class on the history of public health while El-Sayed was earning his doctoral degree.
As a second-generation immigrant, a federally funded health equity researcher, a former local public health director, and an evangelist for single-payer health care, El-Sayed stands for much that is under siege by the Trump administration.
El-Sayed’s time in academia and health departments, and his description of himself as a doctor, have come under scrutiny during this race. His opponent, former FBI agent and Republican representative Mike Rogers, has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed for not being “a real doctor.” While El-Sayed has both a DPhil and an M.D., he never completed a medical residency, and cannot see patients. Rogers has also criticized El-Sayed’s Medicare for All proposal, saying it would force Americans to ration care while raising costs.
On Monday, at an event with Rogers, Kennedy said “there’s 500 million Arabs in the world and yet they don’t produce science.” He went on to say “they don’t win the Nobel Prize. They don’t win the Fields prize.” (The Fields Medal is awarded every four years to honor outstanding mathematical achievement.)
El-Sayed responded in an interview with STAT Wednesday that “it’s ironic to hear a guy who’s trafficked in eugenicist terms, who rejects science outright, come to Michigan to lecture voters about an Arab American scientist with two doctoral degrees who believes in science, like vaccines.”
He said he views Kennedy as “truly the most incompetent HHS secretary we’ve ever had.”
Beyond advocating Medicare for All legislation, El-Sayed has said he would seek an assignment to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which sets budgets for the Department of Health and Human Services.
From that position, El-Sayed has said, he “can’t wait to sit across [from] RFK Jr. and actually grill him.” He told STAT he is “looking forward to sitting down with public health leaders and scientists and researchers … and being ready with a package on day one in 2029 for the next Democratic administration to start building what we need.”
In the meantime, he said he would be holding the Trump administration “accountable for all of the failures.”
But El-Sayed also shares some priorities with the current administration. His platform includes capping overhead costs for universities receiving federal research funding and finding ways to incentivize high-risk, high-impact scientific research.
If there is a silver lining in the Trump administration’s remaking of the federal health agencies, El-Sayed told STAT, it’s that “we get an opportunity, I think, right now, to build what we need.”
At the National Institutes of Health, he said, that means ensuring that funding goes to projects that are responsive to the needs of Americans, rewarding new ideas, and shoring up training programs. At the Food and Drug Administration, FDA, he wants to speed up drug approvals. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, El-Sayed said, must be “more responsive to the future.”
Many who knew El-Sayed in academia in the 2010s sensed his frustration with the pace at which research can help those most in need. That pushed El-Sayed toward the centers of power, where he believed he could have more impact, though some of his critics have questioned how much he changed in his short time leading public health departments.
El-Sayed ran the Detroit health department for nearly two years before launching a failed bid for governor of Michigan in 2018. He later led the separate public health agency in Wayne County, which encompasses Detroit and some of its suburbs, until again leaving to pursue his political ambitions. His allies hope 2026 can be his moment.
“This guy, man, he just has this energy about him that just gets people around him excited,” said Katelyn Jetelina, the founder and CEO of Your Local Epidemiologist, who joined El-Sayed as a co-host on his podcast, “America, Dissected,” at the end of 2024. Part of his appeal, she said, is that he envisions an improved public health system, rather than one that simply attempts to walk back changes the Trump administration has enacted.
“He’s not just complaining, but coming up with solutions,” Jetelina said.
Shaped by his immigrant identity
El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills, Mich., in 1984 to two Egyptian immigrants. His father came to the United States to attend graduate school at Wayne State University and then became an engineer, while his mother worked as a nurse practitioner.
El-Sayed often recounts visiting his teta, or grandmother, in Kardasah, Egypt, where he was exposed to some of the inequities he would later try to address. “You can imagine me walking into that apartment, my hat backward with my American kid swagger,” El-Sayed said at a campaign event in Kalamazoo, Mich., in September 2025. “You can imagine her pointing to one of my cousins, ‘That one is smarter than you.’ Points to the next one: ‘I don’t have to tell you, is taller and better looking.’ Points to a third one: ‘Nicer, kinder-hearted. Fourth one is more athletic, fifth one works harder than you.’”
“By the end of this, I am like ‘Teta, what do I have going for me?’ and she’s like, ‘Habibi, [my beloved, in Arabic] you have the best thing of all.’ And I am like ‘What’s that?’ She goes ‘You get to go back to America at the end of the summer.”
In his memoir, “Healing Politics,” El-Sayed refers to this as a “matched-pair epidemiological study of sorts.” The difference between him and his cousins, he writes, is privilege: clean water, political rights, and life in a high-income country. Being able to witness what poverty looks like, and having the ability to address it, he said, is something he viewed as a “profound responsibility.”
His identity would also spark his foray into academic research. Like many Muslim-Americans, El-Sayed saw the 9/11 terror attacks change his reception in the predominantly white suburb where he lived. A high school student at the time, he endured racial slurs, was bullied by other students on the football field and told to “go back to your own country.” It’s a line of attack that has extended to the current campaign.
His opponent, Rogers, wrote in a statement the day after the Aug. 10 Democratic primary that “never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” There is no record of El-Sayed saying that.
By his senior year at the University of Michigan in 2007, El-Sayed would be named valedictorian of his class, and was bound for medical school in Ann Arbor. He hoped to combine his growing interest in politics with academic training in the medical sciences.
The path to merging those two passions seemingly presented itself after El-Sayed sat down with Sandro Galea, a professor of epidemiology at the school who studied the ways social factors impacted health outcomes. El-Sayed asked to volunteer in Galea’s lab to learn the ropes of social science research. Unfortunately, Galea told El-Sayed, he didn’t take volunteers and didn’t have funding for another research assistant.
El-Sayed was undeterred. He showed up the next morning to Galea’s lab and told him, “I’m ready to work.” The two went on to collaborate for years, and two decades later, Galea is still a mentor.
“I think everything he’s done has been evidence of his hard work, strategic hard work,” said Galea, who now leads the Bursky School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis.
Early in El-Sayed’s apprenticeship in Galea’s lab, he read a paper on the effect of intensified Islamophobia on birth outcomes in the wake of 9/11 in California, which found that the risks for preterm birth and low birth weight infants increased for women of Arabic descent, but had not for any other group.
“In that paper, science, social science, and my own life experiences collided in a way I had never known was possible. It was exhilarating and devastating at the same time,” El-Sayed wrote of the study in his memoir.
In 2008, El-Sayed was chosen for the prestigious Rhodes Scholarship, which would take him to England’s University of Oxford for two years of research. While there, he worked on using AI-based modeling to simulate the many social factors that created racial disparities in rates of obesity in England.
El-Sayed then made his way to New York, where he began the clinical side of his program to become a clinician-scientist. He figured out how to navigate the emergency room where he worked, but often felt at odds with a system that perpetuated the disparities he wanted to work toward ending.
His breaking point was watching the treatment of Martha, as he refers to her in his memoir, who had slipped and hit her head in a subway station. His colleagues had not ordered a CT scan, which should have been the first step in assessing the unhoused woman, and were preparing to discharge her. He spent two weeks caring for Martha, learning that she was also HIV positive and a person with alcoholism and diabetes who had been in and out of the medical system, and arranging for her to go to a rehabilitation facility.
Instead, she went to live with her daughter. Several weeks later, as El-Sayed was boarding a subway, he found Martha sleeping there. Feeling that he, and the medical system, had failed her, he pulled his residency application that day.
“Practicing medicine wasn’t the path to solving the problems I cared about, as scared as I was to admit it after so many years of training,” he wrote.
As a professor of epidemiology at Columbia University, El-Sayed focused his academic work largely on health disparities, with an emphasis on maternal mortality. He also studied the health of Arab Americans.
One paper that found Arab mothers had better birth outcomes when the father was also Arab was labeled as “racist” by Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. “Scary stuff,” he wrote on X. That paper had not received much attention from the scientific community before that criticism, but El-Sayed’s work on Arab Americans was seen by some as pioneering.
“I think he brought this population into the health disparities literature in a way that many folks before him had trouble doing,” said Nadia Abuelezam, an epidemiologist at Michigan State University who has worked with El-Sayed. Before working with him, doing research on Arab populations had been “very discouraged at my institution because there wasn’t a lot of funding for it and folks didn’t see it as a priority population.”
In a 2011 study, El-Sayed, working with Galea, found that marriage was not as protective against poor birth outcomes as many had thought. Galea said the study illustrated El-Sayed’s research approach: “A searching mind, one that is not willing to accept that things are static, and that we should be always thinking about our world and how it may be shifting.”
Katherine Keyes, a former Columbia colleague who published several papers with El-Sayed on infant mortality and on the public health impacts of incarceration, agreed. “He thought of the idea, he located the data, he analyzed the data, he brought together experts who knew how to interpret the data,” she said. “Every step of the way was Abdul creating something out of nothing, some knowledge that didn’t exist before.”
Lofty ideas and political realities
To those close to him at Columbia, it was obvious El-Sayed was destined for bigger things. Some wondered whether he would lead a university or school of public health. The answer came a little over a year after he became a professor there. He was tapped by the mayor of Detroit for a homecoming of sorts, leading the Detroit Health Department.
To his colleagues, it seemed like an obvious transition. El-Sayed was frequently frustrated at the slow speed by which academia can make a difference in people’s lives. Academics “are much more ready to study than to act as a rule, and that’s been true for generations. I think Abdul was uncomfortable with that,” said Steven Mooney, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington who previously worked with El-Sayed.
In taking the job, El-Sayed was facing an uphill battle. In what was the poorest major city in America, he was tasked with rebuilding the health agency after a prior administration had privatized it. He had lofty ideas: He launched a program to provide up to 5,000 children with free eyeglasses, increased testing for lead in water following the water crisis in nearby Flint, and launched an initiative to help residents pay off their medical debt, which has paid off over $95 million in debt, according to a local government dashboard. (El-Sayed has claimed on the campaign trail it has paid for $700 million).
But the progress he was able to make didn’t feel like enough. Mooney recalls El-Sayed’s dissatisfaction with a project studying the potential impact of building demolitions on blood lead levels of children living nearby. It was a difficult problem. “We couldn’t say the demolitions weren’t a problem for kids, but we couldn’t say they were either,” Mooney said “You could feel him being disappointed in that result.” The data were not compelling enough to spur action.
That frustration grew with the election of Donald Trump in 2016.
“So many of the programs that we had instituted were funded, directly or indirectly, by federal grant programs,” El-Sayed wrote in his memoir. “Those programs would likely face cuts or consolidations that would likely hurt the poor Black communities like Detroit that Trump would characterize as ‘American carnage’ in his inauguration.”
A few months later, he submitted his resignation and launched a campaign for governor.
“As an appointed public official,” El-Sayed told STAT, “you sit behind an elected politician who gets to set that frame of the debate. I think it’s just really important, as a scientist and public health leader, to be able to engage in the conversation about what that public mandate ought to be, about where public health ought to go.”
He said he hopes to embolden public health leaders to “pick broad, righteous fights” with private corporations that have been “hurting people.” The hesitation to do so, he believes, has harmed trust in the field.
During the Covid pandemic, he recalled, there was a “gentleman who was like, ‘Look, man, I’m going to take this vaccine. I get it, but you’re asking me to take a vaccine that didn’t exist a year ago for a disease that didn’t exist a year ago, but … I can’t afford my insulin, which is a medication that’s existed for 100 years for a disease I had my whole life.’
“We’re not standing up to the paywall that sits in front of a lot of the incredible things that science can produce for people,” he said.
‘Carefully analyzed the health care system’
El-Sayed garnered national attention as the possible first Muslim governor in the U.S., but lost in a primary to Gretchen Whitmer. He would remain a fixture on the national stage.
While campaigning, El-Sayed had appeared on the popular, left-leaning podcast, “Pod Save America.” Believing there were few forums left for discussion of public health, El-Sayed flew out to Los Angeles and pitched the same network on the idea of a public health-focused podcast. He did 10 episodes about what he saw as the most pressing issues.
Plans for what was to be a limited series changed as news of a novel coronavirus spread across the globe. El-Sayed was asked to do a biweekly show. He also campaigned with Sanders, who was running for the Democratic nomination for president.
He has incorporated Sanders’ Medicare for All initiative as one of the policy pillars of his Senate campaign. The proposal remains an uphill battle. But the public may be increasingly receptive to the idea: Support is at its highest since Sanders introduced it in 2016, according to a recent KFF poll. Two-thirds of respondents said they back a national health plan, with support higher among Democrats and independents.
That figure is likely the result of growing concerns about the affordability of health care, said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “I would not interpret our poll as some indication that the public is knowledgeable about Medicare for All,” he said. The poll also found that support dropped when people were told Medicare for All would eliminate private health insurance, lead to delays in treatments, and require higher taxes.
Joel Zinberg, director of the public health and American well-being initiative at Paragon Health Institute, a free market health policy think tank, and a critic of the proposal, said El-Sayed “relies very heavily on the idea that there’s going to be these tremendous administrative savings, you’re getting rid of complexity, whereas in fact, that’s sort of an illusion.”
Allies of El-Sayed, however, hope that as someone who has written a book on Medicare for All and has seen many sides of the health care system, El-Sayed can legitimize the discussion around the proposal.
“A common critique of Medicare for All folks is that it’s just a slogan. It’s not serious, not rigorous on the policy. For Abdul that’s certainly not the case,” said Hayden Rooke-Ley, a friend of El-Sayed’s and a professor of health services policy and practice at Brown University.
“He’s somebody who has carefully analyzed the health care system, and asked what is the most efficient, just, and democratically accountable way to finance it and insure people,” he said. “And he’s concluded, I think correctly, that it would be to expand Medicare to everybody.”

Worried about artificial intelligence destroying all of humanity soon, or, alternatively, turning your toaster or other home appliances against you?
For the moment, I’m most concerned about what it might be doing to science, specifically the biomedical sciences and especially us biologists. I’m excited about how useful AI can be. However, I’m also deeply concerned about its potential impacts, especially for new and future biologists who “grow up” doing science with AI.
There’s reason to think that overdependence on AI could make us less capable as researchers. Then there are potential job losses in science due to AI.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Good morning. We’ve got a big investigation into Epic for you today. Yes, that Epic. Refill your coffee to read the great story from Casey Ross and Brittany Trang, who managed to interview more than 50 people, despite widespread fear of speaking out against such a powerful company.
Trump admin wants credit for fewer overdose deaths
It’s one of the biggest questions facing addiction experts right now: Why are drug overdose deaths declining? After years of steep increases, especially amid the pandemic, U.S. overdose deaths decreased 27% in 2024, and preliminary data from 2025 show another meaningful drop, though overdose mortality is still too high. Yesterday, an HHS press release credited both Trump administrations with driving down deaths, citing two new reports authored by its own officials and staff. But addiction experts say the factors are far more complicated than one administration’s policies.
“The decline started years ago, with many states peaking during the COVID pandemic, and the continued downward trajectory deserves credit from Trump 1, Biden, and Trump 2 admins,” epidemiologist and harm reduction advocate Nabarun Dasgupta told me in an email. He published a thorough report last week breaking down the factors that likely played a role in the decline, including changes in the drug supply, behavioral shifts among drug users, and public health and harm reduction interventions. (Something that experts agree didn’t actually help: closing the border.)
And there’s an important caveat: Dasgupta and others emphasize that impending Medicaid cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill could reverse a lot of the progress that’s been made when it comes to addiction treatment. “The paperwork burden associated with maintaining coverage is unrealistic for many in chaotic phases of drug use, namely those who need help the most,” Dasgupta said.
Two deaths in autoimmune cell therapy trial
Artiva Biotherapeutics said yesterday that it’s winding down after two patients died during a trial testing its cell therapy for autoimmune diseases, the latest in a series of safety events that have rocked this promising research field.
The deaths appear unrelated to the therapy, the company said. Still, they highlight the growing questions about the safety of the approach and what risk is tolerable for people with autoimmune conditions. Read more from STAT’s Elaine Chen.
How Epic’s iron grip chokes innovation in health tech
There’s a single, privately held business in charge of most patient data in the U.S. You’ve almost certainly heard of it — you’ve probably also logged into the company’s MyChart software to message your doctor or look at test results. Epic Systems Corp. holds data on some 8 in 10 Americans, and its hospital record-keeping software covers more than half of the country’s inpatient beds. A new STAT investigation found that the company selectively withholds access to these data to the disadvantage of rival software tools, leaving its own products unchallenged.
“It has killed innovators left and right,” one senior executive at a longtime Epic hospital customer said. “It’s time for a change.”
STAT’s Casey Ross and Brittany Trang conducted more than 50 interviews with leaders of health technology companies, hospital executives, consultants, investors, and former Epic employees. It’s not only competitors who voiced complaints, but also some of Epic’s own hospital customers. The investigation came out of the pair’s previous reporting on antitrust lawsuits and inquiries into the company, as well as the increased willingness of concerned sources to supply documents and other information demonstrating a pattern of behavior by Epic, Casey told me. Read the first story of a new series, Inside Epic’s Empire, that will investigate the company’s growing dominance and its impact on competition and innovation amid the AI boom.
(And if you’ve been impacted by Epic’s actions in the health technology marketplace, Casey and Brittany want to hear from you. Share your experience here.)
‘Even as a pediatrician of 18 years, I have never seen a case of measles outside a textbook’
That’s pediatrician Katie Lockwood, who wrote a First Opinion essay published today about how doctors can help families stay both calm and informed about measles. Despite never having seen a patient with measles, Lockwood hears from parents nearly every day who are scared of the disease and want to know how to protect their children.
“The symptoms of measles sound like every illness a child could bring home from day care,” Lockwood writes. “Therefore, understanding what measles is, and isn’t, becomes even more important.” Read more.
Is the fertility industry anti-feminist?
In a new First Opinion essay, an internal medicine physician says yes. Pooja Yerramilli froze her eggs a few years ago, “and the experience was anything but empowering,” she writes. In the last decade, the number of patients freezing their eggs has increased exponentially. That’s likely due in part to positive factors like increased awareness and accessibility, Yerramilli acknowledges. But her own experience was something else.
“From the moment I entered the doctor’s office, I felt reduced to nothing more than a vessel for reproduction — a severely flawed, cracked vessel, through which my eggs were rapidly escaping and deteriorating with every passing day,” she writes. Read more about what Yerramilli characterizes as a sort of coercive, complicated process (which at one point involved, I was shocked to read, venmoing a nurse for administering a precisely timed “trigger shot”).

Potential gang involvement in the fatal drive-by shooting of a 19-year-old woman is being investigated by police.
Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, from Jimboomba, was hit in the head and neck when masked gunmen opened fire into a crowd outside Fitzy’s Loganholme, a pub in Brisbane’s south, on Saturday night.
She died in the Princess Alexandra hospital on Thursday morning.
Three men, aged 27, 37 and 38, were also hospitalised. One is recovering from surgery while the other two have been released.
Police are searching for those responsible for the attack, which happened on a night when the venue was hosting a boxing event.
Det Insp Ian Galpin was visibly emotional as he announced the young woman’s death to the media.
He offered his condolences to Schuster-Togiatau’s family and friends, adding that about 80 police officers were involved in the murder investigation.
“We will not stop until these people are identified and taken into custody,” he said.
“I’d ask our community to reflect on the fact that a 19-year-old woman, in the prime of her life, was simply going out for a night out with friends and has had her life taken from her in the most cowardly way.
“There are people out there who know exactly who was involved in this offence and exactly why this occurred.
“I’m asking those people to be brave enough to come forward with that information.”
Det Insp Galpin said the young victim’s family was “not doing well” and had requested their privacy be respected.
“It’s an incredibly difficult time for them, I can’t imagine the hurt that they’re going through,” he said.
He also said police were keeping an open mind in relation to possible gang involvement.
“We will not stop until these people are identified and taken into custody,” he said.
“If that leads to the identification of gang members, their associates or other forms of organised crime, then that will certainly expand the scope of our investigation.”

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.
Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Even with a discount, Google offers a free trial for all new Workspace subscribers. Your first 14 days are free, regardless of which plan you choose. Planning a trip during the festive season can be expensive this year, thanks to strong demand and higher operating costs for airlines. According to a report by The Economic Times, average one-way fares for travel between September 1 and November 10 rose 68% year-on-year on the Delhi-Hyderabad route, while Mumbai-Kolkata fares increased 51%. Fares on Delhi-Goa and Mumbai-Bengaluru routes were up 39% and 37%, respectively. The rise comes as airlines grapple with higher aviation turbine fuel (ATF) costs and fewer flight options on some routes. With the rising cost of flights, one might consider taking a train to visit their hometowns or take a holiday during Diwali or Dhanteras. But chances are, train tickets are all sold out. Hence, booking at the right time can be beneficial for travellers. Wondering how to find cheaper flights or train tickets this festive season? Cleartrip recommends planning ahead, tracking flight fares and using flexibility in travel dates to find cheaper tickets. Booking flights two to three months before travel is generally advisable, according to Cleartrip. Early booking can help travellers secure lower fares before demand rises closer to the departure date. It can also offer a wider choice of flight timings and seats, particularly on popular routes during festivals. The company also offers a domestic flight date-change option for its Elite loyalty members at ₹9. For international travellers, it provides Visa Rejection Cover at no additional cost, with a full refund if the visa is rejected, subject to terms and conditions. Travellers should check the eligibility criteria and terms of such offers before booking. Instead of booking immediately after finding a fare, travellers are recommended to compare prices across different dates and evaluate the fare. The company offers a price trends feature that uses pricing data from the previous 30 days to indicate whether a fare is lower than usual, typical or higher than average, helping travellers decide whether to book immediately or explore other dates. However, historical fare trends are not a guarantee that prices will fall further. During peak travel periods, fares may rise as seats become unavailable. On the other hand, last-minute seats may see low prices as well. Travellers who can adjust their departure date by a day or two may have a better chance of finding lower fares. According to Cleartrip, early-morning and mid-week flights tend to cost less than flights on more popular travel dates and timings. Airlines offer different fare categories, including lower-priced options that may exclude checked baggage or impose limits on baggage allowances. Travellers carrying only cabin baggage could consider such fares to reduce the upfront ticket cost. However, passengers should check what is included in the fare before making any purchases. A low-priced ticket may not necessarily be the cheapest option after baggage, seat selection and other fees are added. Travellers can also compare bank card offers, loyalty points and flight-plus-hotel deals before making a booking. Depending on offers, combining eligible bank credit card offers, loyalty coins and flight-plus-hotel packages can significantly bring down ticket prices. Airline loyalty programmes can benefit frequent domestic flyers. Passengers should compare the final payable amount across booking options and check the minimum transaction value, eligible cards and other conditions attached to discounts. Train travel can be a more affordable alternative to flying during the festive season. However, popular trains often see heavy demand around festivals, and confirmed seats can become difficult to find. Indian Railways currently allows reservations for most trains up to 60 days in advance, excluding the date of journey. The advance reservation period was reduced from 120 days to 60 days with effect from November 1, 2024. For travellers planning festive journeys can check the reservation opening date and book as soon as the booking window opens. If a preferred train is already fully booked, passengers can check availability on other trains running along the same route. Travellers may also consider nearby railway stations, provided the additional travel time and cost are reasonable. For example, passengers struggling to find Delhi to Howrah train tickets, can try looking for Delhi to Sealdah options. The Railways also operates special trains during peak travel periods to accommodate additional demand, if needed. Passengers can check official railway announcements and booking platforms for updates on special services. Paying through wallet apps, UPI, and bank card offers can reduce the cost of train tickets as well. However, passengers must remember that confirmed seats matter more than a discount.
