A report merged on Thursday claimed that the contents of at least three documents in the massive tranche of Epstein files indicate classified information was included in files collected by the Department of Justice.
What exactly was classified and why, it remains a mystery.
One of the documents shows Todd Blanche's Office of the Deputy Attorney General itself received classified material related to Epstein in March 2025, CBC News reported. By law, material can only be classified for national security purposes.
This comes despite Attorney General Blanche long maintaining that the so-called Epstein files, even those kept from the public, contain no secret information related to national security.
When the document releases began last winter, Blanche noted that the Epstein Files Transparency Act authorised withholding information in the interest of national security or foreign policy, but said, "no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis."
"There's not some tranche of super-secret documents about Jeffrey Epstein that we're withholding, we're actually not withholding anything based upon [national defense information]," Blanche, who was deputy attorney general at the time, was quoted by CBS News as saying.
The Department of Justice reportedly claimed that it collected 6 million pages of material and ultimately released over 3 million of those pages after reviewing for duplication, attorney-client privilege and relevance to Jeffrey Epstein.
Congressional challenges and a lawsuit are casting doubts on the DOJ's claims and demanding the release of more documents that were held back.
Included among the Epstein files is an eight-page timeline of the FBI's New York office's initial efforts last year to track down and deliver its voluminous files to the Justice Department's Washington headquarters.
On March 25, 2025, one document shows delivery of "16 Epstein items to ODAG," referring to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General. Among them, items No. 2 and No. 6 are described as "Epstein Transparency Project - Classified Material" and "CDs with classified materials (x2)," CBS reported.
The Epstein Transparency Project refers to the Justice Department's effort to review the files and redact, withhold or clear them for release.
It is not clear what exactly was identified as classified. Each CD was likely capable of holding hundreds of megabytes of material.
The files also contained an email sent that same day from the unit chief of the National Security Classification Operations Unit — an office whose role is to review FBI documents for classification or declassification.
The email includes an attachment labeled "Epstein - Classified Document Memo.docx."
The body of the email says there were three documents "identified that remain classified." One was described as an "FBI document which is classified when see-through." A redaction obscures the unit chief's description of the other two documents, the report claimed.
The identity of the email's recipient was also redacted.
It's also not clear whether the two documents — the email and the list — are referring to the same classified material.
A CBS News analysis of a numerical coding system used by the DOJ to organise the Epstein files offers clues about some of the documents the department has withheld.
The codes don't reveal what's missing, but they do show where gaps exist, raising questions about the DOJ's explanation for why documents were withheld.
Among the missing documents are pages from Epstein's own financial records collected as evidence in a federal prosecution.
Here's how it works: Documents from the Epstein files are labeled with a string of numbers beginning with the letters EFTA stamped on the bottom right-hand corner; EFTA stands for Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Those are called Bates numbers — a common way of organizing massive document batches in legal cases. Every page receives its own number. In the Epstein files, the sequence goes from 1 to 2,858,498, which is the tally of approximately how many pages of documents were released
According to the DOJ, other documents — including court records and investigative files they've previously released — bring the total to over 3 million.
Alongside the Epstein files' Bates numbers are other, older coding numbers that appear on many documents. This indicates that those documents had previously been used in federal legal cases, potentially collected as part of an earlier subpoena.
For instance, Bates coding on some of the documents is from the Ghislaine Maxwell criminal case and was used to organize files given to Maxwell's legal team ahead of her 2021 trial as part of the discovery process.
Other Bates numbers indicate documents were collected from Epstein's banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, during the FBI's investigation into his trafficking activities.
Similar gap analyses have been done in the past by independent researchers.
Finding gaps in these documents is a simple process of counting.
In tens of thousands of instances, the main EFTA number will advance by one but the other Bates numbers advance by two or more. Those gaps indicate pages that had been there before were likely removed at some point after the DOJ obtained them.
In another example, a series of around 4,500 images of checks from Epstein's accounts has gaps where 66 of those check images should be. Oftentimes the missing image is only the front or the back of the check, although in several cases both are missing.
Comparing all of these numbers against the final EFTA page numbers, it is possible to calculate that there are tens of thousands of pages of documents that are missing from these sections, with no clear reason why.
"Financial records were not a permissible category for removal," Barbara McQuade, the former U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, told CBS News.
Like every federal prosecutor, she says she is very familiar with Bates numbers. "It's the reason you have Bates numbers, so you notice something like that," she said.
The DOJ hasn't responded to CBS News' recent inquiries about the Epstein files, but it has previously said that every document required to be released by the Epstein Files Transparency Act has been released, and the remaining files were unrelated, privileged, or were duplicative.
Another sequence of Bates numbers that provide a map to where documents were removed appears to be from a preliminary processing of the files.
One large sequence of those have "R1" in between EFTA and the page number.
This R1 numbering is found across approximately 995,000 released pages, between p. 61 and p. 2,214,171 in the files. Each page is also labeled with an EFTA page number.
While the EFTAs are sequential, the R1s have gaps which range from 1 page to hundreds of pages. Each time a gap appears — for example, if the EFTA advances by 1 but the R1 advances by 2 — it's evidence that pages were removed.
By comparing these sequences it's possible to identify gaps where documents, mostly emails, were removed between that earlier review and the final release. No partial emails turned up in the thousands of documents we examined, so the removals appear to be entire email exchanges.
The emails are not sequential in date and jump by days, months and years, so knowing what was removed from context is simply not possible.
But the results of calculating the differences between the first and last of the numbers in this earlier sequence versus the later sequence is 1.2 million pages, which is the total number of identified gaps from just this one section.
Most of the documents in this section are emails to or from Jeffrey Epstein, including communication with young women who would later accuse him of abuse; email exchanges with his business associates; messages to or from his assistant, Lesley Groff; or emails sent or received by Ghislaine Maxwell.
There is one possible explanation for many of the email gaps. Instructions given to DOJ attorneys working on processing the redactions state:
"If the document is an email chain and the most-inclusive email (i.e., containing all the back-and-forth) has already been reviewed and redacted as appropriate for production, the interstitial back-and-forth can be marked as duplicates."
In other words, all emails exchanged prior to the last email in a chain can be considered a duplicate, because the last one should include all of the messages, and eliminating the duplicates will speed up the redaction process. Once a document is marked as a duplicate, it would likely be excluded from the files.
If that was the case, this was only partially accomplished because duplicate emails still exist throughout the files.
There's also the possibility that errors in the process could have resulted in crucial emails mistakenly being deleted.

Mourinho and chaos - is Real Madrid boss misunderstood?
- Published
Barcelona fans have long teased Jose Mourinho, with their insult of choice being traductor - Spanish for translator.
It is their way of mocking the Real Madrid manager's humble beginnings.
Learning his future trade while serving as an interpreter for the legendary Sir Bobby Robson, Mourinho followed Robson from Sporting to Porto, before the pair reached Barcelona in 1996.
Four years later Mourinho was the manager of Benfica, the first steps in a coaching career that would lead him to Champions League glory, twice, and success in England, Italy and Spain.
So much more than merely a translator, even while at Barcelona, the Portuguese boss' wide and varied success best illustrates the true qualities that underpin him - diligent, determined, introspective, able to thrive in chaos, and tactically brilliant.
Last weekend, that eager tactical mind was in full force as Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1.
As the footballing world praised the tactics Mourinho used, it was an apt moment to reflect on his 26 years in management.
This Clasico featured Real Madrid playing in a 4-4-2 shape with winger Vinicius Jr suspended.
Federico Valverde played at right-back. Bernardo Silva came into the side partnering Aurelien Tchouameni in midfield. Arda Guler and Yan Diomande manned the flanks and Jude Bellingham played up top alongside Kylian Mbappe.
Like he has often done in big games, Mourinho asked one of his more industrious players, Silva on this occasion, to man-mark Barcelona's Pedri. Not an easy task, but it was one that minimised the Spaniard's influence.
1 of 2
Noting Barcelona's intense press and the fact that they converged towards the ball, Real's players drew opponents on to them in wide areas before exploiting space that opened up on the far side – either through impressive dribbling or long switches.
This was particularly noticeable when the ball was played from the right side of the pitch to the left flank as Marc Cucurella snuck behind Lamine Yamal.
After the match, Mourinho broke habit.
Not one to normally dwell on the tactical details of his game publicly, he decided to explain how it was the deep runs from his midfielders that Barcelona found hardest to track.
A master in using news conference as a continuation of what happens on the pitch, perhaps Mourinho revealed his methods in the hope that future opponents of Barcelona would take note.
By running into space behind Barcelona's high line, Real undid Hansi Flick's famed front-footed approach.
1 of 3
Masterminding individual wins in big games tend to garner Mourinho warranted praise, but his wider approach does not always get the recognition it probably deserves.
In recent years, coaches with more clearly defined tactics, patterns of play, or fixed positional references have been lauded as the geniuses of the sport.
Mourinho hasn't taken this approach, opting for one that leans on the quality of his players and tactics that look different depending on the club he finds himself leading.
This less fixed style is more difficult to analyse from the outside looking in, which can result in misunderstanding his work entirely.
Mourinho is a follower of tactical periodisation, a way of football thinking pioneered by Vitor Frade.
While Mourinho was working alongside Robson at Porto in the mid-1990s, Frade was also part of the coaching staff.
Pulling on threads from psychology, sociology, neuroscience, and systems theory, Frade's thinking rejected the common belief that technical, tactical, physical and psychological parts of football should be treated as separate things.
Part of the thinking behind this was that these factors were not drawn on separately in a match but instead all at once.
When Mourinho took charge of Real for this season, the Athletic reported that training sessions had become shorter but more intense, always carrying a focus on the ball.
Even getting players match fit was a job done with the ball at their feet.
In football, coaches seem to veer one of two ways.
Some look to minimise the effect of a match's chaos while others - including followers of tactical periodisation - accept and adapt to it.
Mourinho started his career as impressively as anyone, winning the Uefa Cup and Champions League with Porto, turning Chelsea into a dominant force in England, guiding Inter to a treble and then winning La Liga at Real Madrid.
But between 2019 and 2025, he took jobs at teams with more modest expectations compared to his earlier work.
Since EFL Cup and Europa League success at Manchester United in 2017, Mourinho's only trophy has been the Conference League he won in 2022 with Roma.
During that decade it was the coaches who minimised chaos that thrived.
As fans watched 'chess-like' matches, successful coaches looked to keep lots of the ball, setting their team up in predictable and symmetrical shapes with fixed player roles, such as touchline wingers or inverted full-backs.
Opponents often defended in a zonal manner, as players blocked specific areas of the pitch.
This allowed the attacking team to plan to move players into areas that gave them overloads on the pitch.
In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressing which has removed the ability for teams to find overloads. Pressing puts pressure on the attackers on the ball which hurries their decisions, too.
This has made games look more chaotic, which may be to Mourinho's benefit.
Students of Frade believe chaos is inseparable from the game. By training in a holistic manner, the hope is that players become better equipped to solve problems on the fly.
Perhaps this is why Mourinho's teams have typically thrived in difficult conditions, as underdogs, when the stakes have been high, or when games move away from pre-planned patterns.
Mourinho doesn't seek to control every decision his players make but instead looks to prepare them to find solutions for themselves; with better players, these solutions should, in theory, be better.
It's why, against Barcelona, we saw excellent footballers in Bellingham, Mbappe and Silva excel, all playing in their own unique style, but in a way that came together – when the stakes were highest.
Mbappe attacked the last line and finished moves. Bellingham was combative in duels and elegant on the ball to dribble past players. And Silva slowed down the game under Barcelona's press, before getting the ball to his team-mates higher up the pitch once the opposition had committed.
Mourinho embodies the sequel. He began his managerial career at Benfica, returning 25 years later in September 2025.
He won back-to-back league titles at Chelsea, before returning six years after his departure to win a third. And now, 13 years on from his first tenure at the Bernabeu, a second spell at Real Madrid.
It is fitting, then, that the changing footballing landscape might be offering him another sequel, this time in his tactical approach.

Time is brain, when it comes to the treatment of strokes. But a stroke occurring during sleep may go unnoticed until a person wakes up with symptoms, leaving doctors without a clear timeline of its onset. This is where brain imaging helps doctors identify patients with wake-up strokes and assess the extent of injury to pave the way for prompt treatment. Neurologists underscore the need to seek medical care immediately to ensure timely treatment.
M. Radha, head of department and professor of neurology, Government Kilpauk Medical College (KMC) Hospital, Chennai, said that the prevalence of wake-up strokes is 20% - one in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body,” she said.
If a patient arrives at a hospital within 4.5 hours of stroke symptoms, then thrombolysis can be done, she said, adding: “However, in wake-up stroke, we cannot calculate the time of the onset of symptoms. We do not know the window. So, acting fast is important. In case of any symptoms, patients should reach the hospital on time.”
The role of imaging
In wake-up strokes, imaging helps give a clear picture for the doctors. “An MRI brain scan should be taken immediately. If it is not available, a CT angiogram should be taken. The scans help us assess the extent of brain injury and blood flow to different parts of the brain. They can determine whether there is diffusion-perfusion mismatch. The difference may represent brain tissue that is still salvageable and can be potentially saved. Like in regular strokes, ‘time is brain’ in wake-up strokes too, making prompt diagnosis and treatment crucial,” she explained.
Shubha Subramanian, senior consultant - neurology, Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai, said that in ischemic strokes, thrombolysis is used to dissolve the blood clot if a patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. “In cases involving a large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is performed within 24 hours of symptom onset, depending on the patient’s eligibility. In wake-up strokes, we do not know when the stroke started; it could be at night or early in the morning. What we do next is crucial. This is why we rely on imaging techniques,” she added.
“MRI has a lot of sequences. If you compare the diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) imaging, a mismatch in that shows that the brain tissue is still salvageable. So even if we do not know the time of onset of stroke, we can still go ahead and thrombolyse the patient. In the same way, MRI perfusion or CT perfusion studies will also give us a clue regarding salvageable brain tissue. This will help us in taking crucial decisions regarding thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or whether to go for conservative management,” she elaborated.
Effective coordination
Under the Tamil Nadu Accident and Emergency Care Initiative and Stroke Care and Rapid Intervention with Plasminogen activator and Thrombectomy (SCRIPT) programme implemented by the Tamil Nadu government and with facilities available at the new JICA building at KMC, patients with with wake-up strokes are regularly treated, Dr. Radha noted.
“There is effective coordination between the administration, the emergency department, radiology and neurology departments. We have a green channel in place. As a result, once the patients with symptoms of stroke enter the Emergency Department, the neurologist is intimated. Our doctor goes to the radiology department which has significantly reduced the door to needle time,” she said.
Awareness is crucial
BE FAST is the acronym to spot the warning signs of stroke, denoting Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech and Time. “We do see that the awareness of stroke symptoms is increasing and the referral system has also improved,” Dr. Radha said.
Dr. Shubha Subramanian said that in wake-up strokes, the person may not realise that he/she has symptoms of stroke when they wake up from sleep. “They may face difficulty in getting up and may also fall as a result. It is important for family members to identify the symptoms and rush for medical help,” she added.

Jammu, Oct 29: Jammu and Kashmir Deputy Chief Minister Surinder Choudhary on Thursday said the government would extend all possible assistance to those who suffered losses in the devastating blaze in the Shiva market here, and help them restart their businesses.
A massive fire had ripped through the market early Sunday, gutting around 40 shops and reducing a bustling commercial stretch to rubble.
Choudhary, who visited the market and interacted with shopkeepers, said the fire had destroyed the livelihood of several middle-class traders who had invested beyond their means in stocking goods ahead of Diwali and other festivals.
“This is a prominent and very old market near the railway station. I have visited this market many times and purchased goods here. These are mostly middle-class shopkeepers who had invested beyond their capacity in their businesses,” he told reporters here.
“The government will extend whatever special assistance is possible. It is the government's responsibility and duty to stand by people in their time of distress,” he said.
The deputy chief minister said he had visited the market on the directions of the chief minister, who was currently in Delhi for important meetings and was expected to return to Jammu on November 2.
He said he had interacted with Chamber of Commerce and Industry president Arun Gupta, the market president and members of the market committee to assess the losses and understand the concerns of the affected traders.
“I will arrange a meeting of the affected shopkeepers with the chief minister. I will also call the deputy commissioner and the Jammu Development Authority vice chairman to the Secretariat to discuss what can be done to help them,” he said.
Acknowledging that the assistance available under the existing guidelines might be limited, the deputy chief minister said the government would explore the possibility of extending relief on a special-case basis.
“If we strictly go by the MHA guidelines and the existing rules, these poor traders may not receive much assistance. But this is a special case because their livelihood is at stake,” he said.
However, he cautioned against making unrealistic promises.
“To say that we can compensate them 100 per cent for their losses would be impossible and would amount to making a false promise. But I can assure you that the government will extend full cooperation, to the extent possible, as a special case to help them restart their livelihoods,” he said.
He noted that the timing of the fire had compounded the losses as traders had stocked up on goods for Diwali, Vishwakarma Puja and Bhai Dooj.
The deputy chief minister said he was informed that one trader had stocked goods worth Rs 50 lakh just two days before the incident.
“Imagine what he must be going through. The goods have been destroyed, and the damage to the shops is also extensive. Iron rods have come out of the roofs, which gives an idea of how intense and devastating the fire was,” he said.
The deputy chief minister urged the affected shopkeepers to prepare a memorandum outlining their demands and submit it to the chief minister during the proposed meeting.
He also said traders could undertake minor repairs to their shops ahead of Diwali, which falls on November 8.
Stressing that the issue should not be politicised, he said his visit was motivated by humanitarian considerations and the responsibility of an elected government towards those affected by the tragedy.
“This is not a political statement. It is a matter of humanity and the duty of a responsible government. We will try to find a solution so that these traders can resume their businesses,” he said.

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
- Published
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the Johannismühle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
Johannismühle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

US and Japan agree to establish missile-production facility
The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said
CEBU, Philippines -- The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said late Wednesday. It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China’s growing aggression in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called “Operation Supercharge" are “essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, without elaborating or providing other details of the agreement. The U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets are one of the world’s most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he “shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before.”
“We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means,” Koizumi said. He cautiously added that their discussions were not directed at any specific country.
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration’s repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
“The approach we’re taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear,” Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. “Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves.”
His message is “clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China’s increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.
___
Associated Press journalists Aaron Favila in Cebu, Philippines and Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report.

Seven out of ten women in West Bengal are anaemic, according to the last figures available. The National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) showed the rate to be 71.4% among women aged 15 to 49, the highest in India’s major states, as compared with 39% among men. However, when NFHS-6 released its fact sheets this year, the section on anaemia was omitted. For the first time since the late 1990s, India has a national health survey that does not include an estimate of anaemia, so it is now impossible to tell whether the situation for women in West Bengal has improved or gotten worse.
This more than a minor omission: anaemia in India is a major public health concern, of greater significance in women, since the difference between men and women when it comes to rates of anaemia is generally attributed to biology. This, however, isn’t entirely accurate.
A burden that kept rising
From 2015 to 2016, the rate of anaemia among women of reproductive age increased nationally from 53% to 57%. In West Bengal, the figure rose by approximately 9 percentage points, and for children between 6 months and 5 years, it rose from 54% to 69%. The gap appears early on: nationally, 59.1% of adolescent girls were anaemic as compared with 31.1% of boys, and this difference becomes greater as people go through their reproductive years. Within the State, the severity of anaemia is linked to disadvantage, so that in districts like Purulia and Uttar Dinajpur almost four out of five women were anaemic.
Anaemia prevalence, NFHS-5 (2019–21)
| Anaemia prevalence NFHS-5 (2019–21) | West Bengal | India | 
| Women 15–49 | 71.4% | 57.0% | 
| Men 15–49 | ~39% | 25.0% | 
| Children 6–59 months | 69.0% | 67.1% | 
Source: IIPS & ICF, NFHS-5 (2021). NFHS-6 (2026) did not report anaemia.
Not just biology
The usual explanation given in textbooks is that women lose more iron because they menstruate, carry pregnancies, and breastfeed; this is correct, but it does not explain a 30-point gap or why this gap changes so markedly across districts, castes, and wealth levels. The answer may lie in examining gender rather than biology alone.
It takes four factors to accomplish this. The first of these is time: since women’s duties, both at home and in agriculture, are mostly unpaid, they have little time for rest, for preparing iron-containing meals, or for visiting a health centre. The second is the meal pattern: in many households, food is given to men and children before it is offered to women, so that the women end up eating last and the least of the food from the kitchens that they manage. The third is social norms: it is considered a woman’s responsibility to look after people, and their own health is of secondary importance, and anaemia is regarded as a ‘women’s ailment.’ That stigma has a double effect in that about four out of every five men in West Bengal are anaemic as well, but they are almost never checked or treated. The fourth is money: women who rely financially on others are often unable to act on what they already know about diet.
An anaemia programme that ignores the gender dimension and merely distributes free iron tablets encounters all four of these obstacles and fails to alter any of them. Fieldwork carried out in Bankura in 2025 illustrates exactly what happens in practice. Pregnant and breastfeeding women discarded the fortified (with iron) rice kernels they were given, since they ‘looked like plastic’. They skipped the iron-folic acid tablets, which they did not like, and forgot their doses because of household chores no one else took on. Husbands, who are mostly engaged as migrant labourers, played almost no role in household nutrition. An improved supply chain would not remedy any of this.
The present scenario
The government has, this year, restructured the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme. In June, the previous 6×6×6 arrangement (six target beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms) was replaced by a 7×7×7 scheme which includes testing and treatment, a digital ‘T4’ tracking system and a new national centre of excellence for anaemia. On paper, these steps are the correct ones. A digital tracking system broken down by sex could finally show the problem affecting men, a factor kept out of sight because previous messaging had focused only on women.
Yet, in this same year, the country lost its standard for measurement. The official stance is that that anaemia has been omitted from NFHS-6 since blood samples taken from finger pricks are not fully reliable and may have inflated the figures, and also because India had been following the World Health Organization’s cut-offs for anaemia, which may not be suited to the local context. Instead, venous blood sampling was recommended.
All of these are valid concerns, and there is merit in them. The government had also justified dropping the anaemia reading in the NFHS-6 by stating that it would be surveyed more scientifically in the Diet and Biomarkers Survey in India (since renamed the SAMPADA survey), spearheaded by the ICMR-National Institute on Nutrition, and launched in December 2022. Venous blood samples were collected from residents across 183 districts. The problem is, that SAMPADA has not yet released any of its results, despite the survey being completed in November 2025. Until it does, there is no up-to-date national or State figure against which to assess the new programme. It is therefore impossible to verify or alter West Bengal’s status as the most severely affected of the major States, and nobody can tell whether the new framework is having the desired effect.
At present, reform and measurement have become detached from each other, even though they should be closely linked. A programme which is not measurable cannot be held responsible for its actions.
What should follow
There are three issues. The first is that the government ought to make available SAMPADA’s findings on a specific date, breaking the findings down by sex, age and State, and it should ensure that the methods used are sufficiently similar to those employed in the NFHS so that the new figures can be compared with the old ones rather than simply replacing them. An improved measure must not cause the trend to disappear.
The second point is that the new tracking system should regularly provide data by sex, and supplementation for men should be carried out in exactly the same way as it is for women. The third is that counselling and outreach activities must treat anaemia as a problem that affects the entire household, not merely as a problem of women; it is therefore necessary to reach mothers-in-law, since they are often in a position to decide who eats what, and migrant husbands should also be targeted since they are never present in the room.
India is now carrying out a more ambitious programme than before to combat anaemia, and has no current figures with which to evaluate it. Until the data is available, we are facing a problem for which records have been discontinued, and the women who are affected most may be the last to find out whether or not any change has taken place.
(Anurag Telang is a researcher in public health. dranurag225@gmail.com; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of Economics at XLRI, Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

Since 2020, under Walz and Flanagan's leadership, the state has awarded several grants to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based charity that operates several harm reduction programs, including boofing kits. The $8 million figure cited in examples of the claim is not the amount of money Southside spent on the boofing kits — it is the total amount of money granted to Southside for all purposes. (Though Snopes calculated that figure at $9.1 million, promised through 2030.)
A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election, conservative investigative journalism outlet The Washington Free Beacon published a story saying Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz provided funding to an organization that gives drug users "booty bumping kits," allowing them to consume drugs through the rectum (a practice sometimes called "boofing").
The claim about the Democratic then-candidate for vice president spread on social media before fizzling out.
Two years later, The Washington Free Beacon published another story saying Walz and the state's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan "Steered Millions To Pay for Disgusting 'Booty Bumping' Kits." Flanagan is currently running for U.S. Senate in the 2026 midterms.
Citing the outlet's 2026 report, social media users claimed in October that Walz and Flanagan have provided roughly $8 million to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based nonprofit organization that operates several harm reduction programs and supposedly provides the kits.
Snopes readers also contacted us for more information about this story.
We found that Walz and Flanagan's administration has provided funding to Southside since 2020. While The Washington Free Beacon claimed in October 2026 that the state government has promised roughly $8 million to the organization, Snopes calculated Southside has been promised $9.1 million in grants through 2030.
Southside does provide "booty bumping kits" to drug users. However, it was not possible to find evidence that the organization spent "millions" in state funding on such paraphernalia. The actual figure is likely to be significantly lower — not a seven-figure sum.
Snopes contacted Flanagan's campaign, the Minnesota state budget office and Southside Harm Reduction Services for comment on the story. None had replied prior to publication.
What's true?
In 2023, during Walz and Flanagan's time in office, the Minnesota State Legislature passed a budget that designated $100 million in funding to organizations that assist the state's homeless population. Southside Harm Reduction Services is directly named in the news release announcing the funding.
"[The charity provides] harm reduction services via outreach to people experiencing unsheltered homelessness who use drugs, primarily in or near Minneapolis and St. Paul," according to the news release. "Services include syringe exchange, naloxone distribution, education, rapid HIV testing and referrals to social services including housing."
Snopes reviewed contracts for active and expired grants between the state and Southside, confirming they are a recipient of funding and have been since 2020.
Turning to the nonprofit's social media sites and yearly reports shows the "booty bumping kit" in question and its accompanying mini-zine containing instructions and information about the paraphernalia.
In sum, Southside Harm Reduction Services does receive funding from the state government, and it does provide boofing kits.
Clarifying the figures
The $8 million figure does not represent the amount of money the state has spent on boofing kits, as some may have incorrectly inferred from the social media posts. The Washington Free Beacon says this figure is the total amount of money the state granted to Southside. The headline of the outlet's article could, however, lead some readers to incorrectly believe the nonprofit spent "millions" on the kits.
Using Minnesota's funding transparency database, Snopes calculated that The Washington Free Beacon's $8 million figure was previously correct but is now outdated. Our calculations showed the state's Health Department and Human Services Department have promised Southside approximately $9.3 million in total between 2020 and 2030 for all operational purposes. 
The grants function as monthly reimbursements from the state (Page 4, Section 3.2) rather than an up-front lump sum payment. In other words, if Southside does not spend the $9.3 million, the state does not pay anything.
This is noteworthy because budgeting documentation from multiple grants reveals that Southside sometimes, but not always, does not spend all its allocated money (see the table on Page 7). For instance, in an amendment to a grant worth $620,400 spanning a 42-month period, the organization budgeted $22,200 from the grant for "supplies" for the 2025 fiscal year (part of which would presumably have been used to fund the boofing kits). But, according to that grant amendment, Southside spent less than $6,000 of the grant on supplies that year. 
Other grants provide a more detailed breakdown of the organization's budgeting. Southside's largest active grant for a total of $2.5 million runs between October 2025 and June 2029. The budgeting documentation provided alongside that contract breaks down Southside's yearly budget for supplies — $84,378 for the 2026 fiscal year (PDF Page 29) — into individual components, including $37,000 for "Safer-use supplies for safer injection, smoking, and all works" (PDF Page 31).
Southside also spends the grant money on things like travel, benefits and salaries for personnel — not just supplies.
Given that boofing is a rather uncommon method of drug ingestion, that Southside does not always spend all of its granted money, and that the money gets spent in other areas, we conclude Southside is spending a a small fraction of the funding it receives from the Minnesota state government on the kits. 
Why offer these kits in the first place?
As its name suggests, Southside Harm Reduction Services provides harm reduction programs for the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro area, according to its website. Though the kits may sound odd, they do qualify as harm reduction products.
According to the National Harm Reduction Coalition, harm reduction is a set of principles that aim to reduce the negative consequences that come with drug use, like HIV or hepatitis C infections. The principles are formed around the idea that humans will always choose to consume substances, both legally and illegally, and therefore it is worth minimizing the potential harm these substances can cause.
Well-known harm reduction programs are needle and syringe exchanges, which are called syringe service programs, or SSPs, in the United States. Since infections like HIV and hepatitis C can be spread through contact with blood, used needles and syringes can transmit the virus from person to person. SSPs reduce infections by approximately 50%, according to the U.S. government. These programs also help establish reliable lines of communication with drug users, which can be used to provide additional information on treatments for substance use disorders. (Boofing also requires a syringe, explaining why Southside offers the kits).
In addition to a syringe exchange, Southside's website notes it also helps give people access to both mental and physical care, including substance use programs, vaccinations, STI testing and more.

Consumer protection regulator imposes ₹1 lakh fine on Sunrise Foods over ‘100% whole wheat bread’ claim
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) directed the company to immediately discontinue the misleading advertisement across platforms.
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹1 lakh on Sunrise Foods for misleading consumers by marketing its Everyday bread as “100% Whole Wheat Bread”, despite the product containing only 64% whole wheat.
According to an order dated October 28, the regulator directed the company to immediately discontinue the misleading advertisement across print and electronic media, including social media, and submit a compliance report within 15 days.
CCPA flags ‘whole wheat’ claim
The CCPA found that the claim conveyed the impression that the bread was entirely made from whole wheat flour, while the product’s actual composition did not support the representation. It also noted that the company had not adequately disclosed the proportion of whole wheat used on the packaging.
Under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) labelling regulations, bread marketed as “Whole Wheat Bread” must meet a minimum whole wheat flour content threshold of 75% on a flour basis. The CCPA said the product’s disclosed composition of 64% whole wheat fell below this threshold, raising concerns not only over the “100%” claim but also the use of the term “Whole Wheat” itself.
“The impugned representation is consequently misleading on two distinct and independent counts,” the order said, referring to the claim of 100% whole wheat despite the lower content and the use of the nomenclature “Whole Wheat” despite the product allegedly failing to meet the prescribed threshold.
Under Section 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the CCPA can direct advertisers to discontinue or modify misleading advertisements and impose penalties of up to ₹10 lakh for a first contravention and up to ₹50 lakh for subsequent contraventions.
The inquiry
The proceedings followed a complaint by KMA Law Offices, Solicitors and Advocates, alleging systematic mislabelling of packaged bread products by several manufacturers and marketers. The CCPA initiated an inquiry into Sunrise Foods’ product and subsequently referred the matter to its investigation wing on August 6, 2026.
The investigation report, dated October 15, concluded that the claim was misleading and ambiguous. It also cited FSSAI’s observations in a similar matter that the use of “100%” on food product labels was not permissible under the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.
FSSAI issued an advisory on May 28, 2025, asking food business operators to discontinue the use of the term on food labels, packaging, and promotional materials.
The company's argument
Sunrise Foods argued that “100% Whole Wheat Bread” was intended to convey that the wheat flour used in the product was entirely whole wheat flour, or atta, rather than refined wheat flour, or maida. It maintained that the claim did not mean every ingredient in the finished product was whole wheat.
The company told the authority that whole wheat flour constituted 96.3% of its total flour-related inputs, while the revised packaging declared whole wheat flour at 64% of the finished product’s net weight. It said the two figures reflected different calculation methods and that the product met applicable food safety requirements.
The company also said it had approved revised packaging under the name “Everyday Whole Wheat Bread”, removing the “100%” claim. However, the CCPA found discrepancies in its account of when the revised packaging was implemented.
What happened in the hearing?
During a hearing on October 23, the company’s representatives said the earlier packaging had been withdrawn and removed from all quick-commerce listings. But the authority said it checked Blinkit and Zepto through live screen-sharing during the hearing and found that the disputed packaging and claim were still displayed on the platforms.
The CCPA said this contradicted the company’s assurance that the earlier packaging was no longer being offered or displayed for sale. It also rejected the argument that product listings and images on third-party platforms were maintained independently by the platforms, noting that the claim remained accessible to consumers.
The authority further held that the prominent “100%” claim on the front of the packaging could not be neutralised by ingredient information in smaller print elsewhere on the pack. It said the overall presentation had to be assessed from the perspective of an ordinary consumer, rather than on the basis of the manufacturer’s stated intention.
“ The test is not the subjective intent of the manufacturer, but the objective understanding of an average consumer of ordinary prudence,” the order said.
The CCPA also noted that the company had sold 107,754 packets of the product in 2024-25, generating ₹38.11 lakh in revenue, and 132,437 packets in 2025-26, generating ₹53.14 lakh in revenue. During the hearing, the company said it sold approximately 2,000 packets a day.
Using that figure, the authority estimated sales of around 4.1 lakh packets, worth approximately ₹2.25 crore, over 205 days of the 2026-27 financial year up to the relevant hearing date. It said the product’s market reach was a material consideration in assessing the potential impact of the misleading representation.
The CCPA concluded that the claim constituted a misleading advertisement and an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and violated consumers’ right to be informed about the quality, composition and other characteristics of goods.
The authority said the company’s internal compliance procedures did not absolve it of responsibility, particularly as its own documents showed that the product name, ingredient list and packaging artwork were subject to quality assurance and regulatory review.

Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro. Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago.
The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage.
There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM, but can go to 4TB of storage.
It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election
URDA, Spain — Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.
Spain's network of high-speed rail has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It ranks second to China in track mileage in the world. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
The collision Wednesday that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the central province of Toledo after regional authorities confirmed that more than 60 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals.
Only in January, 46 people had died when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
Sánchez pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.
"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sánchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."
Sánchez's government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday.
Both deadly crashes this year involved a train operated by the state-owned RENFE company and one from the privately owned IRYO. Spain only liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.
Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election
Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, staying in power and winning reelection after the COVID-19 pandemic and the global rise in inflation.
But polls show he faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election since 2023. The new rail disaster can't help the prospects of his Socialist party.
Sánchez and other progressive parties had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections earlier this month.
About an hour before news of Wednesday's crash spread, Sánchez had posted on X a message that "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."
Now it appears he will have to handle concerns over the state of Spain's rail service along with attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.
His transport minister, Óscar Puente, had to handle media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. His response was that he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future.
Sánchez's main rival, Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party canceled its campaign events for the day.
"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Núñez Feijóo said. "That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."
The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.
"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," Abascal said just hours after the crash.
"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.
Human error was behind the crash
Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) behind it.
But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on Wednesday after a hectic day involving hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police and soldiers all pitching in to rescue survivors and recover bodies.

Ex-West Brom & Stoke striker Berahino retires at 33
- Published
Former Premier League striker Saido Berahino has retired from football at the age of 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi's national team.
The Midlands-bred Burundi international made his name with boyhood club West Bromwich Albion, where he had one especially prolific season of 20 Premier League and cup goals in 2014-15 before joining Stoke City for £12m in January 2017.
But, having already faltered at Albion in his latter days under Tony Pulis, Berahino flopped badly for Stoke, who went on to suffer relegation from the Premier League in April 2018.
After being given a second chance by then Stoke boss Gary Rowett, he scored five times in 2018-19. But he soon fell out of favour again until he was released by mutual consent with still three years remaining on his contract.
Having left Stoke in August 2019 for Belgium, Berahino played at Waregem and Charleroi before being signed by former Baggies boss Darren Moore at Sheffield Wednesday in August 2021.
He has since played in Cyprus, India and Slovenia, as well as for his native country, having previously been capped by England at all age levels up to and including under-21.
Berahino was twice called up for England's full squad by then manager Roy Hodgson - but was not picked to play.
Berahino's 'Letter To The Game'
Berahino reserved special thanks for his first club, for whom he scored 36 goals in 121 appearances in all competition, including a hat-trick on his first start, as a 20-year-old, against Newport County in the EFL Cup in August 2013.
In a statement, entitled 'A Letter To The Game', posted on Instagram, Berahino wrote: "I want to thank West Bromwich Albion for believing in me when I was a boy.
"Those years at the club, the goals, the fans, the moments, they will always be special. There were highs and lows, mistakes and lessons. I learned that the game can lift you up and test you at the same time.
"The time has come to hang up the boots. My body and my heart are ready for the next chapter. I am proud and grateful to now serve the Burundi national team as a coach. Giving back to the country that made me, and helping the next generation, feels right.
"To my family - you have been my strength. To the fans who stayed with me through every chapter - I will never forget your support. This is not goodbye to football. It is simply the end of one story and the beginning of another.
"Football has given me everything. From the streets of Bujumbura to The Hawthorns, from the Premier League to places I never imagined I'd play - this game carried a young refugee kid through life."
