Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”
Additional reporting Aakash Hassan

Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides, saying he has used some of them himself.
Peptides are strings of amino acids, shorter than proteins, that can exert powerful effects in the body. Some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. Wellness influencers and some clinicians have promoted unproven peptides for a wide range of uses, though the evidence for their safety and effectiveness is sparse.
So even though these peptides have not been through the Food and Drug Administration's rigorous drug review and approval process, they could become easier to get. But the policy's focus on smaller producers may mean that pharmacists will have a tough time meeting demand.
In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies. However, at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
The new policy says compounding is a safer alternative to illicit "research-use-only" peptides that are available online. They're often sourced from sketchy suppliers overseas.
The peptides, and some of their unproven uses, are:
- BPC-157, ulcerative colitis
- Epitalon, insomnia
- KPV, wound healing
- MOTS-c, metabolic health
- Semax, migraine
- TB-500, wound healing 
Joshua Fritzler, the president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, says people have been asking about these peptides for years. But because they were illegal to compound, his company didn't make them.
The new policy doesn't change their legal status, but it does create a path for small compounders, called 503A compounding pharmacies. It doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs, that are outsourcing facilities producing higher volumes of medicines.
So at Fritzler's company, only its smaller compounding facility will be able to make the peptides – and only in small quantities, he says.
And that has implications for consumers.
"We won't be able to meet demand," he says, explaining that Olympia will likely only compound one of the six peptides and needs to get its facility ready first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand."
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding's CEO Scott Brunner wrote in a statement that his group is pleased with the administration's decision to allow the peptides to be compounded because it offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides.
"It also brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply," he says.
Brunner warned, however, that it may take some time for compounding pharmacies to begin dispensing these products to patients. That's because ingredient suppliers need to make sure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements — and pharmacies need to verify that, too.
Several consumer advocacy groups say the policy puts patients at risk, however. The nonprofit Public Citizen noted that Kennedy seems to have acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process.
"By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Dr. Robert Steinbrook, Health Research Group Director at Public Citizen wrote in a statement. "All peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs. The HHS Secretary should support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers."
Steinbrook advised clinicians to talk to their patients and tell them about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects.
The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations around the country, filed a citizen petition last week, urging the FDA to ignore the recommendation from its advisory committee in July to allow compounding pharmacies to make the six peptides.
"Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence," its executive director Shabbir Safda wrote in a statement.

Hungary’s effort to purge itself of all things Viktor Orban is now reverberating through the global auto industry.
Under its former leader, the country positioned itself as a European hub in the battery supply chain, courting companies from China and South Korea that went on to set up plants making components for electric vehicles. But concern about the environmental impact became a political battleground and production at some facilities has been halted under new Prime Minister Peter Magyar.
Semcorp’s separator factory in Debrecen in eastern Hungary is entering its fifth month of shutdown after tests showed toxins in nearby soil. The Chinese company makes 40% of the world’s membranes, the thin layers that keep the positive and negative poles of a battery apart.

Ireland all-rounder Orla Prendergast was signed by Gujarat Giants for Rs. 30 lakh at the Women’s Premier League (WPL) 2027 auction on Wednesday.
One of Ireland’s key all-rounders, Prendergast has enjoyed a productive year in T20Is, scoring 455 runs in 15 matches at an average of 35 and a strike rate of 128.89. She has also claimed 15 wickets in those games.
“I was lucky enough to work with her at the Welsh Fire in the Hundred this year. She’s a leading player for Ireland, she’s got good leadership qualities and really fantastic around the group,” Giants coach Michael Klinger said on the JioHotstar brodcast. “The versatility she can give us in our squad whether there’s an injury, whether we want another overseas medium-pace option, she can bat in the top six or seven. She’s a world-class allrounder so it’ll be great to have her in the squad,” he added.
Prendergast will compete for one of the four overseas slots in the Giants’ playing XI, unlike Associate Nation players, who are eligible for a fifth overseas spot under the WPL rules.
Earlier this year, Prendergast smashed 63 off 44 balls as Ireland registered its first-ever T20 World Cup win after 22 attempts across five editions, beating West Indies by six wickets.

Apple's redesigned MacBook Pro has an OLED touchscreen, weighs just three pounds
It starts at $2,899, and it could really use a more distinctive name.
What's better than a MacBook Pro? A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen. Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
The new MacBook Pro has a refined design that's noticeably thinner than the existing models, has slimmer bezels and the aforementioned touchscreen. But, similar to the recent RTX Spark Windows laptops, you'll need deep pockets if you want one: The 14-inch model starts at $2,899, making it the highest launch price we've ever seen for a MacBook Pro. The 16-inch model is even wilder, starting at $3,399.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models. And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up. As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds. That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds. The 16-inch model weighs four pounds, whereas the non-touch 16-inch MacBook Pro weighs between 4.7 and 4.8 pounds.
The ProLED XDR screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, according to Apple, and it features an "industry-leading" 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen. It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros. Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.
Beyond the new specs, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR doesn't look much different from Apple's current lineup. And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.
So what's the point of a touchscreen MacBook Pro? It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years. But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects. It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers. Apple says its own apps are optimized for the new MacBook Pro's touchscreen, and you'll be able to touch any app because macOS recognizes touch interactions as clicks. Third-party creator apps like Notion, Canva, Powerpoint and Blender will also work with the touchscreen natively.
There's no doubt Apple is late here, but there was also a certain wisdom in completely separating its touchscreen platforms (iOS, iPadOS and watchOS) from macOS, a platform that was designed entirely around traditional computer inputs. With Windows 8, Microsoft rushed to enable PC touchscreens as a way to compete with the potential rise of iPads. Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.
MacBook Pros were always expensive, especially after Apple's recent hikes, but the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR pushes cost to a new extreme. A fully-decked out 16-inch model with an M5 Max chip, 128GB of RAM and 16TB of RAM costs an eye-watering $14,549. It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer. But given the rise in demand for powerful local AI hardware, I wouldn't be surprised if there's a robust market for an over-equipped MacBook Pro OLED.

D2C nutrition and dietary supplements brand Ace Blend has raised $9.9 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a Series A2 funding round led by 3one4 Capital, with participation from existing investor Fireside Ventures. The startup will use the fresh capital for clinical trials, supply chain improvements, R&D, and new nutrition formats. “The first is clinical trials, which are going to be run by credible CROs (contract research organisations) and are intended to be published in peer-reviewed international journals. The second is cementing our moat as a business, which is our supply chain proficiency. The third is a robust testing mechanism that allows nutritional accuracy, pesticides and heavy metals to be tested batch on batch without any human intervention,” founder and CEO Shivam Hingorani told Inc42. Ace Blend also plans to conduct shelf-stability studies at launch and six months later, which Hingorani said would help build long-term safety data on its products. “Trust is not enough” in the nutritional supplements market, he said, stressing the need for scientific evidence to support product claims. Founded in 2018 by Hingorani, and later joined by Saif Mehkri as cofounder in 2022, Ace Blend offers supplements across heart health, brain health, sleep, recovery, gut health, strength and immunity. Its portfolio comprises around 14 SKUs, including plant-based protein powders, superfood mixes, and functional health supplements. Besides its website, the startup sells its products through ecommerce and quick commerce platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Zepto, and Blinkit. Its website contributes around 50% of revenue, with the remainder coming from marketplaces and other ecommerce channels, Hingorani said. Ace Blend clocked 300% growth in FY26 and has a repeat purchase rate of nearly 48%, according to Hingorani. It is targeting annual recurring revenue of ₹250-300 Cr over the next 12-18 months, with profitability also in sight, he added. The startup plans to strengthen its supply chain by sourcing raw materials from multiple countries. Hingorani said its vertically integrated model covers ingredient sourcing, formulation, and manufacturing, while automated testing will assess nutritional accuracy, pesticide residues, and heavy metals in each batch. Ace Blend is also developing new products, including a formulation created with a gut-health specialist to address leaky gut, a combination of natural nutrients intended to lower inflammation, an eye-health product, and a fibre-based format for gut health, he said. India’s dietary supplements market is growing as consumers become more aware of preventive healthcare and the role of supplements in managing chronic conditions. Investor interest in the sector is also rising. Earlier this month, D2C brand The Stack raised ₹21.5 Cr to expand its product range and invest in R&D. According to Grand View Research, India’s dietary supplements market was valued at $5.8 Bn in 2025. It is projected to reach $6.6 Bn in 2026 and $12.4 Bn by 2033, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.5% between 2026 and 2033.

Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.
In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.
South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it.
The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions.
“As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude.
Importations
In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation.

Goodbye to the everyman who gatecrashed the greats
- Published
Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.
The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never left him - even in what proved to be the final tour-level match of the 41-year-old Swiss star's glorious career.
Former world number three Wawrinka might have lost to Czech opponent Jiri Lehecka in front of passionate home support in Basel on Tuesday, but he did not wave farewell without showing the hallmarks of a stunning career that exceeded expectations.
The stylish one-handed backhand down the line. The finger pointing to the temple. The demand for more noise from the stands.
The roar of "Allez!" after winning a point he probably should not have won.
The temptation to snap his racquet over his knee after missing a shot he felt he should have made.
There were tears, too, of course.
Wawrinka, his family, and his team were dabbing their eyes once the reality of an honourable 7-5 7-6 (7-2) defeat dawned.
It meant a professional career spanning 23 years, 985 matches and three Grand Slam titles was over.
"All I wanted in my career was to give everything, have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match - out of respect for myself, the opponent, the tournament, the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP website., external
"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and the only way you can leave the sport - without any regrets."
Wawrinka is loved by millions of fans because he is relatable - an everyman personality who reached the pinnacle of his sport by pushing himself to the limit.
So many talented players of his generation lamented the presence of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, believing the 'Big Three' to be a blockade preventing them from becoming a Grand Slam champion.
It did not stop Wawrinka. With explosive shot-making, relentless endurance and indomitable spirit, he barrelled past the trio of superstars on his way to winning his trio of majors.
Wawrinka had been a player whose career was ticking along steadily, rather than spectacularly, until he lifted one of the sport's biggest prizes at the age of 28.
Seeded eighth at the 2014 Australian Open, he saw off Djokovic in the quarter-finals before completing an unforeseen triumph against top seed Nadal.
"I never expected to win a Grand Slam because, for me, I was not good enough to beat those guys," Wawrinka admitted as he clutched the trophy in Melbourne.
In fact, he was more than good enough - proving it again and again.
At the 2015 French Open, Wawrinka brushed past Swiss compatriot Federer in the quarter-finals, then demolished Djokovic in the final with a display of unrelenting power - a performance which must be ranked among the greatest of his era.
His last major title arrived at the 2016 US Open, when he escaped from match point down against Britain's Dan Evans in the third round and went on to beat Djokovic for the title.
It is little wonder that 24-time major champion Djokovic - considered by many the greatest player of all-time - described Wawrinka as a "legend".
"Stan's had an incredible career. The competitor he is on court, talent, strength, power, precision - he had it all," said the 39-year-old Serb, who practised with Wawrinka in Basel.
Wawrinka was good enough to win majors, but he wasn't as consistently good as his illustrious rivals.
The 'Big Three' is often expanded to a 'Big Four' featuring Britain's three-time major champion Andy Murray, who soared to world number one, won two Olympic singles gold medals and lifted the ATP Finals trophy.
Wawrinka recognises he was "really far" from creating a 'Big Five' - and the evidence underlines that.
Spending 267 weeks in the top 10, winning one Masters 1,000 tournament and claiming 15 other tour-level titles is well below Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Murray, but it is also more than most players can dream of achieving.
The Grand Slam triumphs are what really set Wawrinka apart from most peers - and, coupled with his commendable attitude, is why 'Stan the Man' will be remembered for emerging as a great himself in a golden generation where others came up short.

In early October, some social media posts spread the claim that an Israeli company manufactures 3D-printed salmon meat and sells it at U.S. grocery stores.
For example, a YouTube video (archived) claimed, "the first 3D-printed salmon just hit U.S. grocery shelves." It then explained the salmon was manufactured by an Israeli company called Steakholder Foods and that the product is not required to have a label indicating it was 3D-printed on its packaging. It also noted that the salmon contained a chemical used in laxatives.
Users also shared the claim on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers sent emails asking whether it was true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat and fish products, including salmon, in Northeastern U.S. retail stores under the brand name Perfecta.
Therefore, we're rating this claim true.
Snopes has already fact-checked a claim about Steakholder Foods' 3D-printed meat hitting grocery-store shelves. That claim and the claim about salmon came from the same product announcement and thus share much of the same research.
It's not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products. Snopes reached out to Steakholders Foods via a contact form on its website for more information. The company has not replied to Snopes' prior requests for information.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
The FDA told Snopes in an email:
The product you are describing sounds like it is made from plant-based ingredients using a specific manufacturing process (3D printing). It does not appear to involve cultured cells of any type. The FDA generally does not approve finished foods or manufacturing processes. Although the FDA does not approve final food products, ingredients and additives must be demonstrated to be safe before they are used in food or in materials that contact food.
The FSIS told Snopes in an email that it regulates meat, poultry and egg products, and directed us to the FDA for more information.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there doesn't seem to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meatlike texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D printing.
Methylcellulose, the chemical used in laxatives, is included on the 3D-printed salmon's ingredient list. Methylcellulose is used in plant-based meats as a binder to keep the ingredients together and to replicate the texture of real meat.
The FDA has approved this kind of use of methylcellulose in food.

'No choice left but to look to increase fares': IndiGo CEO on 'very significant' rise in fuel bill
The warning comes as IndiGo’s parent company, InterGlobe Aviation Ltd, reported a loss for the third consecutive quarter.
IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh has said the airline has “no choice left but to look to increase fares” as it faces a “very significant” rise in its fuel bill. The warning comes as IndiGo’s parent company, InterGlobe Aviation Ltd, reported a loss for the third consecutive quarter, with surging fuel expenses offsetting the gains from higher fares.
The airline’s loss narrowed in the July-September quarter compared with a year earlier, but remained substantial despite an increase in revenue, Bloomberg reported. Walsh said the airline did not expect immediate relief from elevated fuel costs.
“We are looking at a period of elevated fuel cost for sometime,” he said, adding that IndiGo would continue to explore internal measures to absorb the increase. “We will continue to look at every measure that can be taken internally to offset the very significant increase in our prices,” he said.
IndiGo raises fuel charges
Jet fuel can account for around 40% of an airline's operating costs, leaving carriers vulnerable to sharp price increases and increasing the likelihood of higher ticket prices, as per Reuters. India’s largest airline has already revised fuel charges on domestic and international routes amid a sustained increase in jet fuel prices.
The latest revision, effective October 6, came after IndiGo said the month-on-month increase in ATF prices had exceeded 14%, taking costs to among their highest levels in the past decade, HT reported earlier.
Under the revised structure, IndiGo’s fuel charges on domestic flights range from ₹375 to ₹1,300, depending on the distance travelled. The charges were raised by ₹100 to ₹350 per sector.
For international flights, the revised charges vary by destination, ranging from ₹1,000 to ₹10,000. Flights to Europe attract a fuel charge of ₹10,000, while flights to Southeast Asia, the Gulf region and parts of East Asia attract a charge of ₹5,500.
IndiGo’s loss narrows, but fuel costs surge
According to Bloomberg, InterGlobe Aviation reported a net loss of ₹1,879 crore for the quarter ended September 30, lower than the loss recorded a year earlier and below the average analyst estimate of ₹2,063 crore in a Bloomberg survey.
Revenue increased 26% to ₹23,364 crore, exceeding analyst expectations. However, total costs rose to ₹26,188 crore, while fuel expenses surged 67% from a year earlier to nearly $1 billion, Bloomberg reported.
In its earnings statement, Walsh said the airline had faced unusually high fuel costs during the seasonally weaker September quarter, alongside continued geopolitical uncertainty.
“The seasonally soft September quarter saw exceptionally elevated fuel costs and continued geopolitical turmoil,” he said. He added that the steps taken by the airline had supported revenue but could only partly offset the increase in expenses.
The July-September period typically sees relatively subdued domestic air travel in India. Demand is expected to improve during the festival season, potentially providing some support to airlines as travel picks up.
Passenger numbers fall as airline cuts capacity
IndiGo carried 27.5 million passengers during the quarter, 4.5% fewer than a year earlier. It also reduced capacity by 1% as part of efforts to manage costs.
Passenger yield -- the average revenue earned per passenger -- increased 34% year-on-year, according to Bloomberg. However, the airline’s passenger load factor, which measures how much of its available seating capacity is occupied, declined to 80.3% from 82.5% a year earlier.
The company’s debt increased 7.1% from the preceding quarter to ₹87,303 crore, Bloomberg reported. IndiGo expects capacity growth in the December quarter to be in the low single digits.
Why rising fuel costs are pushing airfares higher
Aviation turbine fuel is one of the biggest expenses for airlines, accounting for a substantial share of their operating costs. Sharp increases in fuel prices can squeeze profit margins, particularly when airlines are unable to pass on the entire increase to passengers.
Fuel prices have remained volatile amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia. The impact on airlines is compounded by fluctuations in international oil prices and currency movements. IndiGo’s latest move follows an earlier revision of fuel charges in April. The airline has said it will continue to monitor fuel prices and make adjustments as required.

In August, Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s egg-freezing journey incited a national debate about fertility and reproductive rights, with women on both sides of the aisle hailing her decision as a feminist one (amid, of course, the expected right-wing conservative backlash).
I agree that Ocasio-Cortez’s choice to freeze her eggs, and do so publicly, is certainly feminist. But the industry as a whole is not.
A few years ago, I, an internal medicine physician who works on health policy and financing, froze my eggs — and the experience was anything but empowering.
My journey began when I learned that my employer subsidized “family planning” — including egg freezing, in vitro fertilization (IVF), and adoption — by several thousand dollars per attempt for up to two attempts. As a woman in my 30s, I thought it would be harmless to at least consult a fertility specialist to make an informed decision. I always imagined that if I wanted children and could not naturally conceive, I might pursue adoption — but why not make an appointment to properly assess, with a specialist, the pros and cons of freezing my eggs?
From the moment I entered the doctor’s office, I felt reduced to nothing more than a vessel for reproduction — a severely flawed, cracked vessel, through which my eggs were rapidly escaping and deteriorating with every passing day. As the doctor reviewed my age and hormone levels, she urged me to freeze my eggs right away, lest I regret the decision down the road. At the time, I was single — what if, she posited, I met a man who wanted children? I would certainly look back on this moment and wish I had gone through with the procedure. Time is ticking, she reminded me.
Not once did she ask me about my own reproductive goals.
Instead, my doctor sent me down a path of extreme body-shaming. Explicit in her “advice” was the message that the train had already left the station: My body’s decline was well in motion since the day I was born — and something must be done right away. She had me sign up for egg freezing within a week. I felt rushed, unsure if it was right, but that thinking was overwhelmed by the immense fear, anxiety, and shame that every single day I waited was another day my ovarian function would further depreciate.
It took an immense amount of self-reflection to pull myself out of the mental spiral she triggered: that my body was failing me. To the contrary, I reminded myself, my body has accomplished incredible feats. In 2020, when I fell ill while on the front lines of the Covid-19 pandemic, I had difficulty breathing while walking around my apartment. When the symptoms did not resolve for months, I seriously worried my body would never return to normal. Now, a few years later, I was back to hiking mountains. My body was fine. My body was healthy. Just because my future fertility was in question — as it is with all people as we age, to varying degrees — did not mean that my body itself was failing. My body’s sole function, and my life’s sole purpose, was not biological reproduction. What business did any hypothetical future partner have to guilt me over it?
But the damage had already been done, the seed of shame planted, and I signed the paper and handed over the money to get started.
It should have been entirely unsurprising that my doctor pushed this narrative. After all, the fertility industry is exactly that — an industry. Indeed, a study published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in February showed that the number of patients undergoing egg freezing in the U.S. has increased exponentially, from 4,153 patients in 2014 to 16,436 in 2021. Over that same period, the average age decreased from 36.0 years to 34.9 years.
Some of this trend may certainly reflect positive drivers — for example, increased awareness and access, as in my case, facilitated by employer subsidies. But much of this increased demand is undoubtedly also driven by the financialization of fertility.
The global egg and embryo banking industry was valued at $4.49 billion in 2024 — and based on current trends, projected to increase to $11.26 billion by 2030. Fertility startups have proliferated and expanded across the country, undergirded by colossal private equity and venture capital investments seeking returns. These investments go hand-in-hand with efforts to consolidate the market. In 2023, private equity backed more than 32% of all fertility clinics, which performed an estimated 54% of all IVF cycles across the U.S.
These trends are more stark in certain geographies: A 2025 JAMA study found that in 14 states and Washington, D.C., more than half of fertility clinics were private equity affiliated, and were estimated to perform somewhere between 60%-100% of all IVF cycles. At least as of a few years ago, fertility was thought to be the medical specialty with the greatest private equity owned market share, with expectations that consolidation would continue, decreasing provider competition, restricting patient choice, and increasing high-volume facilities that patients often characterize as impersonal “fertility factories,” with limited face time with their doctors.
Directly marketing toward younger and younger clientele, fertility clinics compel women to shell out tens of thousands of dollars to proactively preserve their fertility. But their often simplistic messaging around “fertility preservation” masks the reality that egg freezing neither guarantees future use nor future success. The same February American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology study showed that only 5.7% of all patients who had frozen their eggs returned to utilize them within 5-7 years, and only 28.9% of their attempts resulted in live births. Not to mention the health risks that both mother and fetus face with increased maternal age, whether the pregnancy is spontaneous or through IVF — with marginalized patients facing worse outcomes, likely due to the structural discrimination they face before, during, and after pregnancy.
Certainly, there have been scientific advances in fertility treatment, but overall women’s health research has been vastly underfunded. National Institutes of Health funding has disproportionately favored research into conditions primarily impacting men over those primarily impacting women. And while the absolute amount of research dollars for women’s health has increased over time, the share of NIH funds decreased from 9.7% in 2013 to 7.9% in 2023. Particularly under-resourced are common (and likely significantly underdiagnosed) conditions like polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, endometriosis, autoimmune conditions, and menopause — all of which substantially impact fertility.
These trends are worse when we look at marginalized communities. Though infertility among Black women is twice as high as for white women, research into the causes is scant. And while funding for research on sexual and gender minoritized population health has grown over time, the overall amount remains woefully inadequate, particularly for fertility.
One can assume that if these conditions were better understood, our clinical guidance regarding overall reproductive health including fertility would be better. The Trump administration’s cuts to research funding, and the increasing influence of private equity over reproductive endocrinology and infertility training, may further threaten future progress.
As I began my egg freezing cycle, my doctor reminded me that much of the medication and dosing is “guess and check.” We cannot really predict what regimens will work best for each person. This is why patients are extensively monitored while undergoing egg freezing — to assess how their bodies are responding to the medications, and make adjustments based on more “guessing and checking.”
This “guess and check” approach has meaningful financial (and emotional) repercussions. You may over-order the medications you need, which can result in thousands of dollars’ worth of waste. You may need to order more medications midcycle, which is quite common and manageable — except in the event of shipping delays, which I had the misfortune of experiencing. My replenishment, expected to arrive the day before my last remaining dose, was delayed by at least two days in transit. My options were limited: I could drive hours to a specialized pharmacy in the snow (though they might close by the time I arrived); use a friend’s leftover medications (not advised); or cancel the cycle altogether (though I was halfway through, and had already spent thousands on the first round of medications).
The stress of feeling somewhat coerced into having the procedure was compounded by having to navigate these unexpected hiccups and the finances — without any support from my providers themselves. On top of the physical and emotional toll of deciding and then pursuing egg freezing, patients are advised to spend hours shopping around to find which specialty pharmacy might supply their medications at the lowest price.
I also found that I had to maintain constant vigilance over the fees from my fertility provider. Surprise charges regularly appeared on my account — duplicate charges for services already bundled in my upfront self-pay package (e.g., extra laboratory fees, extra charges to my insurance and co-payments for clinic visits) — which took hours on the phone and in person to have canceled or reduced. This included my Natera testing — a blood test that screens for risk of passing on genetic conditions, strongly advised by my doctor — which was advertised as $250, but resulted in a bill exceeding $700. (In September, Natera settled a class action suit alleging deceptive billing practices. It did not admit to any wrongdoing.) I had to make yet another hours-long phone call to sort this out.
The “surprise bills” did not end there. As I was arranging for a friend to help with my “trigger shot,” my nurse advised me that I could instead have a nurse administer it at the clinic at my precise trigger time — a preferable option, I thought, best not to take any chances.
When I arrived, I was shocked at the nurse’s greeting: “You can Venmo me $150.” Had I been informed of the extra charge, I would have made alternate arrangements in advance. But five minutes before my precisely timed trigger shot was to be given, I had no other option. I transferred the money to her personal account. There would be no official record or billing of the service in my chart.
Having studied “informal payments” — extra under-the-table payments for health care services, common in other countries but not in the U.S. — I was concerned that this exchange at the health facility could be considered illegal. When I asked my doctor and the billing department about this practice, they simply shrugged their shoulders. Upon discussing with other people who had frozen their eggs, I found that several had the same experience.
Like all health care in the United States, fertility care is mired by fragmentation and inadequate transparency on cost, price, and billing. What makes it perhaps worse than general health care is that its billing architecture can be even more complex — with clinics, specialty pharmacies, laboratories, and anesthesia providers individually charging fertility benefit administrators, health insurers, and patients through a variety of mechanisms including bundled cycle packages and fee-for-service. This results in errors costing patients hundreds to thousands of dollars, whether intentional or not, as I experienced: failure to submit insurance claims, incorrect coding, duplicate billing to patients and insurance. Though I knew that my employer benefits would not cover the full costs of elective egg freezing, I did not realize that I would end up paying over half the costs out-of-pocket until all was said and done. There is considerable variability in how much of the total cost fertility benefits cover, even in the case of IVF for medically documented infertility.
As a physician who had the privilege of an employer-subsidy, I should have found the journey relatively easy to navigate — yet I found it entirely disempowering.
To the contrary of right-wing pronatalist and anti-IVF arguments, the solutions are not to abandon IVF altogether, but rather improve innovation, quality, access, and informed decision-making. If fertility “preservation” were truly a feminist enterprise, we would have significantly more research to increase its precision beyond “guess and check.” We would teach and empower primary care providers and others to properly counsel patients on their fertility, eliciting their goals, carefully advising on their options, and making referrals to fertility specialists accordingly. And, as Ocasio-Cortez suggested in one of her follow-up videos, we would make it affordable for all people, not only those rich enough to access it, and not only those already medically defined as having or being at high risk of infertility.
But most of all, we would strengthen regulation of the industry. It is likely that the high costs of fertility treatment in the U.S. compared to European countries like France and Spain, and the frustrating patient experiences, stem from several factors: self-pay or fragmented payment models, growing private equity investments, market concentration, less government regulation, and higher labor costs. Expanding insurance coverage for elective egg freezing, as New York state is exploring, as opposed to relying on employer subsidies which perpetuate inequities and the administrative burden on self-paying patients, is a critical step.
Simultaneously, we need to strengthen regulation of the industry — the service providers, labs, and pharmaceuticals — toward greater transparency, competition, and safeguarding of patient safety and interest.
Years on, I do not regret freezing my eggs. I have largely put my experience behind me, out of mind (except for the over $100 monthly storage fee, of course). I have since regained my sense of self-worth both within and outside the context of fertility. And in truth, I do not know whether I will ever attempt to use my frozen eggs. Regardless, I am keenly aware that I was privileged to access the services, no matter how flawed, out of reach for many who seek them.
So, while I cannot know if I would have made a different decision under different circumstances, I can at least try to contribute to an honest conversation about fertility care.
If we are serious about the “fertility industry” being feminist and inclusive, we must ensure that “reproductive choice” is truly at the heart of the care provided — that all people are empowered to make the decisions and access the care that are right for them.
Pooja Yerramilli, M.D., is a clinical assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. She has previously worked at the World Bank, World Health Organization, and various nongovernmental organizations on improving affordable access to high-quality health care and public health. Her views represent her own and not those of her current and former employers.

New Delhi: Union petroleum and natural gas minister Hardeep Singh Puri was on Wednesday nominated by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for the Rajya Sabha by-election from Madhya Pradesh, paving the way for him to return to the Upper House as his current term from Uttar Pradesh nears end. The nomination comes weeks after the party left him out of its list of eight candidates for the Rajya Sabha elections from Uttar Pradesh. Puri, 74, is currently a Rajya Sabha member from Uttar Pradesh, with his term set to end on 25 November. The by-election was necessitated by the resignation of Union minister of state L. Murugan, who stepped down from the Rajya Sabha on 14 October to focus on strengthening the BJP in Tamil Nadu. His term was due to end on 2 April 2030. Murugan was re-elected on 2 April 2024, with his second term beginning the following day. Polling for the Madhya Pradesh seat is scheduled for 12 November, with counting on the same day. The last date for filing nominations is 2 November. If elected, Puri will serve the remainder of Murugan’s term until 2 April 2030, giving him about three years and five months in the Upper House. His tenure would extend roughly a year beyond the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. The BJP holds a majority in the Madhya Pradesh assembly, whose elected members vote to choose Rajya Sabha representatives, giving its candidate an advantage in the by-election. Puri is a former diplomat and his nomination helps him in retaining his parliamentary membership beyond the end of his current Rajya Sabha term. Rajya Sabha members serve six-year terms, compared with the Lok Sabha’s five-year term, unless the lower house is dissolved earlier. Dhirendra Kumar is a seasoned policy reporter with about 20 years of experience in deep, on-ground reporting across key economic and governance sectors. His work spans finance, public expenditure, disinvestment, public sector enterprises, textiles, trade, consumer affairs, and agriculture, with a strong focus on uncovering structural policy shifts and their real-world impact.

Kumar has been awarded the Chaudhary Charan Singh Award for Excellence in Journalism in Agricultural Research and Development, recognising his contribution to reporting on critical issues in the farm sector. He has also been a recipient of a fellowship in international trade from the National Press Foundation, which has further strengthened his coverage of global trade dynamics and their implications for India.

Kumar is known for breaking complex policy developments into clear, accessible stories. His reporting focuses on uncovering under-reported trends, explaining policy shifts, and helping readers stay informed about developments that shape India’s economic landscape. Oops! Bihar MLC election results: BJP wins 2, leads on 1; JDU, RJD, JSP win 1 seat each, Independents 2
Tension prevailed at the counting centre during the counting of votes for the Darbhanga graduate constituency in the evening.
The Bihar Legislative Council elections for eight seats boosted the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which won two seats on Wednesday – Tirhut Teachers’ and Kosi Graduates’ and was leading in Darbhanga Graduates’ – even as it lost its 30-year stronghold in the Patna Teachers’ constituency out of the four seats it contested.
Counting was still on in Darbhanga Graduates’ constituency, with Sarvesh Kumar of the BJP securing 16,115 votes, leading over Anil Kumar Jha (14,615 votes) of the RJD till the filing of this report at 9:45 pm on Wednesday. RJD candidate Anil Kumar Jha was in second place, followed by Mohammad Imtiyaz of the Jan Suraaj party, with 10,227 votes. Tension prevailed at the counting centre during the counting of votes for the Darbhanga graduate constituency in the evening after a dispute broke out between counting agents of the NDA and RJD candidates
Darbhanga district magistrate-cum-assistant returning officer Kaushal Kumar directed the detention of five people following the uproar. "Those detained included 3 counting agents of the BJP candidate and 2 counting agents of RJD candidate", said a DSP rank official. The result was expected to be declared around midnight.
Deep Dive
Follow live updates on the MLC election results 2026 here.
The Janata Dal-United [JD(U)], an NDA ally, retained the high-voltage Patna Graduates’ seat despite stiff internal dissension. It, however, lost the other three – Tirhut Graduates’ and the Saran and Darbhanga Teachers’ seats, thus winning a seat less than in 2020.
Dr Sanjeev Kumar of the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), Suresh Prasad Rai of the Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) and Independent candidates Rahul Raj and Banshidhar Brijvasi won the Patna, Darbhanga and Saran Teachers’ and the Tirhut Graduates’ seats, respectively. The Congress, which contested five seats, failed to open its tally, dealing a blow to the grand old party.
The Graduates’ results offered the NDA a counterweight to its mixed performance among teachers, as the NDA won the Patna and Kosi Graduates’ seats and led in Darbhanga.
BJP’s Narendra Kumar Yadav, who polled over 10,000 votes, won by a margin of over 2,000 votes, recording a hat-trick of victories in the Kosi Graduates constituency.
The Patna Graduates’ contest remained a major political flashpoint for the JD(U), with Neeraj Kumar, a senior party leader, former minister and sitting MLC, registering a hat-trick of victories. He defeated RJD candidate Dilip Kumar, with JSP’s Dr Anuj Singh trailing in third place.
The Patna Graduates’ contest was marked by open dissent within the JD(U), with Mokama MLA Anant Kumar Singh campaigning against Neeraj Kumar and backing JSP’s Anuj Singh. The party suspended Anant Singh for six years over alleged anti-party activities. The result was seen as a test of the JD(U)’s ability to contain internal dissent and consolidate support behind its official nominee.
Also Read | Decoding MLC polls: Who votes, how seats are filled
What the leaders said
Calling the result a victory for the party, Neeraj Kumar said, “Dhanbal aur bahubal hara hai. Karyakartabal aur janbal ki jeet hui hai” (Money power and muscle power have lost; the strength of party workers and public support has won). He also credited Nishant’s leadership, saying the result had established him as a leader.
Anant Singh accepted Neeraj’s victory but said he had no regrets about backing the JSP candidate. He maintained that he had differences with Neeraj, rather than the JD(U) itself. On his possible return to the JD(U), Anant Singh said, “The party will know that better.”
The result of the Patna Graduates’ seat strengthens the JD(U)’s position behind its official nominee, though the public disagreement has exposed tensions within its ranks.
Bihar MLC election results
The Teachers’ results were otherwise fragmented. Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) candidate Suresh Prasad Rai defeated sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha in Darbhanga, while BJP rebel Rahul Raj won Saran Teachers’ as an Independent, defeating JD(U)’s Anand Pushkar and JSP’s Afaque Ahmad, who won as an Independent in the April 2023 by-election. Raj secured 3,300 votes against Pushkar’s 2,727, while Ahmad finished third with 2,454.
The most significant setback for the BJP was the defeat of veteran MLC Nawal Kishore Yadav in Patna Teachers’. Yadav, who had won the seat for five consecutive terms, lost to the RJD’s Dr Sanjeev Kumar, handing the opposition a key victory in a constituency the BJP had long held.
The result highlights the limits of the BJP’s organisational strength in a specialised electorate of teachers, even as its candidate Narendra Prasad Singh won the Tirhut Teachers’ seat. Singh defeated Independent candidate Bhushan Jha with 2,945 votes against 2,351. The win also marked a reversal from the 2020 election, when CPI’s Sanjay Kumar Singh defeated Narendra Prasad Singh. The CPI candidate ended third this time.
For political strategist-turned-politician Prashant Kishor, Rai’s victory offers a boost in Darbhanga and expands the JSP’s presence in Bihar’s legislature. It is the party’s second electoral victory after Kishor won the Bankipore Assembly by-election on August 3. However, Afaque Ahmad’s third-place finish in Saran, after winning the constituency’s 2023 by-election as a JSP-backed Independent, tempered the gains.
With the BJP and JD(U) contesting four seats each this year, the saffron party had a better strike rate, winning two seats - the Tirhut Teachers’ and the Kosi Graduates’. It led in the Darbhanga Graduates’ seats, while the JD(U) won the Patna Graduates’ contest.
Also Read | 'DK, it's done bro': BJP mocks Shivakumar after party sweeps Karnataka MLC
The NDA won four seats in the MLC polls in 2020, with the BJP winning the Kosi Graduates' (Narendra Kumar Yadav) and Patna Teachers’ (Nawal Kishore Yadav) seats, and the JD(U) pocketing the Patna Graduates’ (Neeraj Kumar) and Tirhut Graduates’ (Devesh Chandra Thakur, who subsequently won the Lok Sabha polls in June 2024. Independent candidate Banshidhar Brajvasi won the December 2024 byelection).
Meanwhile, there was still tension in the counting hall for Darbhanga graduates constituency after the scuffle between RJD and NDA poll agents of the nominees. Agents associated with RJD candidate Anil Kumar Jha alleged that the government and district administration were attempting to defeat the RJD candidate through alleged electoral manipulation. There was no official comment on it.
The Bihar Legislative Council has 75 seats, of which 63 are elected members and 12 are nominated.
(With inputs from Bishnu K Jha)

The early years of a child’s life are critical for lifelong health, learning, emotional well-being, and social development. Inclusive early childhood development (iECD) seeks to ensure that every child, including those with developmental delays, disabilities, autism and other forms of neurodivergence, has equitable access to healthcare, nutrition, nurturing care, early learning, protection, and early intervention, Deepa Bhaskaran, Director, Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, said.
Speaking at a media workshop on inclusive early childhood development and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for effective storytelling, organised by UNICEF India in association with the Press Information Bureau, Dr. Bhaskaran said early identification and interventions were vital to ensure that children with disabilities and developmental delays were included at home, in learning environments, and in their communities.
“We train and support medical staff and caregivers, improve early identification and intervention, and provide advanced disability inclusive services,” she said.
Amar Fettle, State Nodal Officer for Adolescent Health, speaking at the workshop, added that while medical infrastructure and personnel were geared towards clinical care, research, teaching, and community outreach, it was equally important to shape public understanding of children’s issues and government programmes.
“Families and the public should understand the services available and help reduce the stigma surrounding disability and developmental delays. The idea is to ensure that children are included in society,” Dr. Fettle said.
The workshop aimed to strengthen understanding of inclusive early childhood development, child rights and disability inclusion, promote ethical, child-sensitive and non-stigmatising reporting, and raise awareness of AI-related risks, including misinformation, deepfakes, bias, privacy violations, and fabricated content.
While reporting, subject matter expertise is essential, Muralikrishna Chinnadurai, trainer with the Google News Initiative India Network, said. Relying on a single AI prompt could produce unreliable information, Mr. Chinnadurai said.
“Humans must be in the loop. AI tools should be used ethically and in an environmentally responsible manner,” he said.

Theni jailbreak: All 17 escaped prisoners back in custody after arrest of remaining 4
Brothers K Thirupathy and K Meenakshi Sundaram surrendered at the Cumbum police station in the district.
The four convicts out of the total 17 prisoners who were on the run after making an escape from the Theni jail were arrested on Wednesday, police said.
While two prisoners, P Ponmuthuselvam and R Rejin, were traced by one of the 17 special teams formed to nab the convicts, brothers K Thirupathy and K Meenakshi Sundaram surrendered at the Cumbum police station in the district, officials said.
Drones used to trace two prisoners in forest area
P Ponmuthuselvam and R Regin were nabbed using drones at the Kottaipatti foothills located behind the jail in a dense forest area. They were nabbed by a team led by the Superintendent of Police K S Praveen Gowtham, officials said.
Also read | Theni jailbreak: 13 of 17 recaptured after drones track inmates hiding in jungle; 9 prison staff suspended
When HT reached out to DGP Prisons Sandeep Rai Rathore on Wednesday, he confirmed that Thirupathy and Meenakshi Sundaram, who were on the run, surrendered later this afternoon at the Cumbum police station and they were taken into custody.
With this, all 17 inmates were taken back into custody.
17 prisoners recaptured after two-day manhunt
Based on the instructions of Rathore, an intensive operation was launched on Wednesday to secure four of the 17 convicts. On Tuesday, 13 of them were recaptured by the police.
DGP Tamil Nadu Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal spoke to his DGP Keralam R A Chandrasekhar and requested him to maintain alertness in districts bordering Keralam and Tamil Nadu to nab the prisoners.
Also read | 13 captured, hunt for four others underway after Tamil Nadu jailbreak
The special teams formed undertook combing operations in various locations, including vehicle checks. The services of Armed Reserve, Tamil Nadu Special Police and Special Task Force were utilised as part of the manhunt.
According to the police, the 17 prisoners allegedly overpowered guards and escaped after one of them feigned an epileptic seizure in the prison’s third block, said officers. The accused were involved in various cases including offences for murder, robbery, drug-related offences and offences under the Arms Act.
The 13 prisoners who were recaptured on Tuesday are -- P Sabarinathan, M Muthu Elangovan, N Karthickraja, C Dharunkumar, N Solaimugileswaran, S Pandiselvam, M Karuppusamy, G Nishanth,J Lingaprasath, K Rajkumar, A Raja Sikkandhar, S Silambarasan, T Praveen Kumar.
DGP Tamil Nadu Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal, DGP (prisons and correctional services) Sandeep Rai Rathore, IG (prisons) R Kanagaraj and others visited the jail on October 27 and reviewed the situation.
Nine prison personnel, including two jail wardens, were suspended, according to an investigating officer.
The Theni district jail has been functioning since January 10, 2019. It has a capacity to accommodate 200 prisoners.
Following the jailbreak incident, multiple cases were filed at the Gandamanur Police Station under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including 121 (1) (causing hurt to a public servant from performing their official duties), BNS 296 (b) engaging in obscene acts, BNS 115 (2) (causing hurt by using a weapon), among others.
The jail escape drew criticism from the opposition in Tamil Nadu, with DMK President M K Stalin and AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami slamming the government over the issue.
The mass jailbreak comes a week after two inmates who escaped from the highly secured central prison in Puzhal near Chennai on October 13. As many as 14 special teams were formed to nab the convicts. The police launched a manhunt and two days later, nabbed the two escaped prisoners in Chennai.

Cledith Arthur was never tried on the rape charge because he and Donna Arthur fled the state, and Cledith Arthur never returned to face the charges before his death in 2004. Without a conviction, Snopes cannot definitively confirm he raped Acton.
In October, less than a month before the U.S. 2026 midterm elections, Ohio's Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released an advertisement featuring Donna Arthur, the mother of his opponent Dr. Amy Acton. In the advertisement, Arthur claimed that Acton "lies about her past." 
In response, Acton's campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, noting that the two had been estranged from their mother for decades. Her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, raped Acton when she was 12, and both she and her brother were removed from Donna and Cledith Arthur's custody after his arrest, according to the statement. Stearns' statement further claimed that Donna Arthur "stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died" in 2004. 
Acton, the former state health department director, has been open when talking about her difficult childhood for years. A 2019 piece about Acton for Youngstown, Ohio's local newspaper The Vindicator described her as "abused, abandoned, neglected," and claimed she lived in "18 or so homes in her first 12 years," including a winter spent living in a tent at a Youngstown campground. That article also mentioned the sexual abuse she suffered at the hands of her stepfather.
Donna Arthur disputed the "living in a tent" claim directly in the pro-Ramaswamy advertisement, but did not mention the abuse allegations. (PolitiFact found she did claim Acton lied about being raped in a 2020 interview with Operation Rescue, an anti-abortion group.)
Ramaswamy has stood by the ad, and President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have said they support running it. Vance told Republicans to "stop whining" about the ad at a rally.
But the insinuation Acton was lying about her abusive childhood struck many as insensitive, including some Republicans. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (who is running for reelection this year) said he would not have run the ad, and incumbent Gov. Mike DeWine (who is not running because he is term-limited) called for Ramaswamy to take it down.
Snopes received several requests from readers asking us to get to the truth of the matter — was Acton actually lying about her childhood, as her mother claimed?
We vetted the story. Court records show Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her, as she claimed. We also found evidence that Donna and Cledith Arthur remained married and lived together until Cledith Arthur's death in 2004.
In a response to Snopes' request for comment, the Acton campaign provided a comprehensive timeline of events and images of court documents documenting the rape charge filed against Cledith Arthur, Acton's stepfather, alongside several interviews in which she discussed her childhood. The Acton campaign also noted that Donna Arthur was found guilty of felony theft in 1996 and of animal neglect in 2021, and that Cledith Arthur was also indicted on an incest charge in 1974, before he and Donna married. (A note in The Youngstown Vindicator on March 22, 1974 — Page 25, at the bottom of the article titled "Trumbull Indicts 2 Mahoning Men for Shooting Deaths, clear third" — lists Arthur as both indicted and not indicted for incest. While this suggests he faced two separate charges and was only indicted for one, we were unable to definitively verify that was the case.)
We then requested the files for the rape charge against Arthur from the County Clerk in Mahoning County, Ohio (which can be viewed here), in order to confirm the legitimacy of the documents the Acton campaign provided.
Next, we searched the archives of local newspapers for Cledith Arthur's name, and found two brief articles in The Vindicator reporting on the rape charge in 1978.
To verify that Cledith and Donna Arthur remained married, we ran a background check on both, and found that both were using the same mailing address as late as 2003, suggesting they continued living together. We also searched the courts for divorce records and found none.
In sum, all of the information matched Acton's claims.
It's worth noting that because she was a minor at the time, Acton's name was redacted on the set of documents Snopes obtained via public records request.
The documents we received from the Acton campaign, meanwhile, were not redacted. In order to obtain those, someone personally involved with the case (likely Acton or her brother, Philip) would have needed to make the request.
It's also worth noting that while a grand jury indicted Arthur on rape charges (he pleaded not guilty, according to the court records viewed by Snopes), he was never tried because he and Donna Arthur moved out of state before the hearing. Cledith Arthur died in Pennsylvania in 2004, according to FindAGrave and the Acton campaign.
The timeline
According to the 2019 Vindicator profile, Acton's biological mother, Donna, and father divorced when she was 3, and her mother retained custody of the children. In 1975, according to the statement from Acton's campaign, Donna remarried Cledith Arthur. 
On July 13, 1978, Acton's biological father filed a formal complaint against Arthur, alleging he raped Acton between December 1976 and April 1978, when she was between the ages of 10 and 12.
The court documents viewed by Snopes listed Arthur's address as "Terrace Lake Park" on State Route 7 in Rogers, Ohio. Snopes found the property is now called Terrace Lakes Camp Ground.
Arthur was arrested the day after the complaint was filed, and he pleaded not guilty to the rape charge five days later. This fact was reported in The Vindicator on July 17. Acton and several police officers were subsequently subpoenaed as witnesses, according to court documents.
On Aug. 11, The Vindicator reported that Arthur would face a grand jury for the rape charge. The court documents showed Arthur testified before the grand jury in late September 1978, where he was indicted.
"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away," Acton said of her mother while speaking to The Vindicator in 2019. "That was the last time I ever saw her."
Cledith and Donna Arthur seemingly skipped town before Arthur's Oct. 13 hearing, and a judge issued a warrant for Arthur's arrest on Oct. 26. "It appears the Defendant has willfully vacated his last known address and has failed to provide any forwarding address and his present whereabouts are unknown," the order read.
The court issued an additional warrant against Arthur on Dec. 9, 1981, but, as previously stated, he was never found.
There was exactly one sticking point in the files — it was unclear exactly when the court officially transferred custody of Acton and her brother to their biological father. 
Snopes requested those files from both the Mahoning County Clerk and the Acton campaign. The Acton campaign did not have them available and the Mahoning County Clerk did not provide them alongside the file on Arthur's court case. The files are likely unavailable to third parties under Ohio law, but Snopes is awaiting confirmation from the County Clerk on this fact.

'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
- Published
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.
Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.
Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.
In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.
"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".
The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.
Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".
Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.
It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.
