Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.
Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.
One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.
Mapping the risks
The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.
Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims, and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

Rugby League World Cup: England's Brian McDermott admits side face 'unique task' to progress and can't get distracted
England head coach Brian McDermott speaks to the media on Thursday, as his side seek to avoid historic Rugby League World Cup pool stage exit; England face Papua New Guinea in their final pool fixture on Friday (9.05am kick-off), knowing they need a big win to keep semi-final hopes alive
Thursday 29 October 2026 11:13, UK
Brian McDermott has warned his England side not to chase the points as they look to keep their slim Rugby League World Cup hopes alive with a big win against Papua New Guinea.
England are up against it in their bid to make it through to the semi-finals after they lost 30-12 to Tonga in their opening game.
They must beat Papua New Guinea in their final pool game in Woollongong on Friday and then wait until Sunday, when they need Tonga to beat Samoa, upon whom England must also make up a 68-point deficit.
That means tries will be the order of the day against Papua New Guinea but McDermott, who saw his side beat France 82-0 in their second game, has called for patience.
"We've got a specific task this weekend. I think it'll be a stiffer test than it was against France," McDermott said at his Thursday press conference.
"We once again find ourselves in another similar situation, very unique as well, that we don't just need to beat them, we need to be beat them convincingly.
"If we're going to go through, we need to score the points, but we can't get to the points first.
"We've got to get to the physicality first and we're going to manage a very physical team, a very dominant team.
"There's a discipline in that we don't start looking for things or searching for things outside of how we want to play.
"That was really impressive against France because we knew we had points in us and they weren't coming in that first 20 [minutes]. We didn't try to do anything different.
"Every team, and I've been involved in so many teams, where you're winning by a large margin and you either take your foot off the gas because we think it's job done or you start to overplay.
"But against France we stuck to the game model and just put it on rinse and repeat."
While England made hay against the French in Perth, McDermott knows Papua New Guinea represent a tougher task.
"They're well coached by Jason Demetriou, who's got a chunk of players who are playing in the British game as well," he said.
"So I think they are going to be really well co-ordinated."
What do England need to avoid historic early World Cup exit?
Quite simply, before Tonga face Samoa, England must beat Papua New Guinea and do it by a considerable margin.
Samoa's thumping 78-4 win over France in their tournament opener and a 64-6 victory over Papua New Guinea on Saturday leaves them with an impressive +132 point difference.
England beating France takes them to a +64 points difference, 68 points behind Samoa heading into the final round of fixtures. Another win Friday would lift them to four points and level with both Samoa and Tonga.
McDermott's side would then be left to wait 48 hours for the outcome of Tonga vs Samoa in Sydney. A Samoa win would guarantee England's elimination, while a Tonga victory would see the points difference decide second spot.
England don't necessarily need to beat Papua New Guinea by 68 points or more, but a victory by that margin would mean any loss for Samoa would be enough to progress.
A smaller England win would see them need Samoa to lose by a bigger score, depending on England's final points difference.
The winner of the combined Groups B+C table would progress to the semi-finals to face the runner-up of Group A, a four-team league consisting of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and the Cook Islands.

Madih Talal has been a man on the move since he set foot in India three seasons ago. After impressing with Punjab FC in its debut ISL season, he journeyed across the Eastern belt, spending a campaign each with East Bengal and Jamshedpur FC.
And now, as the Indian Super League enters a new era, the French attacking midfielder has found a new home in the South of the country with Chennaiyin FC.
“I feel comfortable (in India). You know, in my country sometimes we say the grass is not greener somewhere else. (But) I feel happy, I like the league and the football is good,” Talal told Sportstar during an exclusive chat.
But it has not exactly been smooth sailing for the 29-year-old, who suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury (ACL) while with East Bengal. The blow left him off the pitch for several months, and he was eventually released by the club at the end of the 2024-25 season.
“It was not easy. You feel alone, like the world has stopped because we only play football. So, when you remove football, it’s like nothing is there,” Talal recalled about that period in his life.
ALSO READ | Tough times never last, only tough people do: Edmund aims to take next leap in Indian football
When he recovered and signed for Jamshedpur, the league was in financial crisis that ended up postponing his return to the pitch.
“I came back from injury, and I was ready to play even during the summer. So, after that, it was difficult because we didn’t know if the league would start or not,” he said, adding, “That was not easy not only for me but for everyone. I hope this will never happen again.”
Then another setback followed, with Tata Steel deciding to withdraw Jamshedpur from the league ahead of this season, news that Talal admitted left him “totally shocked.”
But when one door closed, several others opened, and Chennaiyin was the one that Talal eventually decided to walk through.
“I had a great introduction to the club. Owen Coyle (his coach at Jamshedpur and former Chennaiyin head coach) told me a bit about it, and so far it has been good,” he said.
Pulling the strings in attack
His time in the ISL will be especially valuable to the two-time champion, considering it recruited 15 new players over the summer after a poor last season, where it finished 13th out of 14 teams.
Meanwhile, Chennaiyin has had a challenging start to its campaign, drawing 1-1 with FC Goa in the opener before facing defeats against Bengaluru FC (0-2) and Mohun Bagan Super Giant (0-1).
The shortage of goals will be particularly concerning as Chennaiyin was the only side, apart from the relegated Mohammedan SC, to not hit double figures in goals scored last season. And Talal knows that he will have to get his gears running as soon as possible, especially considering the three words he used to describe his playing style were: offensive, creative and technical.
In the last edition, Talal created 39 chances in nine appearances – the third-highest in the league – and led the charts for chances created per 90 with 4.33. His progression across the three games this season, although, has been encouraging.
After coming off the bench against FC Goa, Talal started the next two games, largely running Chennaiyin’s attack, especially against Mohun Bagan. He often linked up with Serbian Nikola Stojanovic to find space in the final third and then release the forward players. A couple of those releases could have resulted in a goal if not for some sloppy finishing and timely saves from Vishal Kaith.
And while Chennaiyin has gathered just one point so far, Talal is cautiously optimistic about what’s coming up.
“Now we have a new team, and we don’t need to compare with last season. The club is building a new project with the young and experienced players. So, it takes time. If you compare the first game and the last game, it’s completely different. We are getting better. I think we just need to continue to work like that and be more clinical in front,” Talal noted.
And while time will tell if Talal can end Chennaiyin’s scoring woes, his understanding of the Indian football landscape has drawn him into other conversations: Would he be interested in following Ryan Williams’ footsteps and hypothetically representing India in the future?
“I think if I’m not wrong, Ryan has maybe someone in his family history who is Indian. So it’s easier for him. But for me, if they want, they can call me and let’s talk,” Talal concluded with a laugh.

Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.
The promise of fortification
That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.
Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).
At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.
What the barriers are
What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.
Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Potential to be a global model
India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

Ranbir Kapoor, director Nitesh Tiwari, actor Ravie Dubey and producer Namit Malhotra have come together for a conversation with students about the values and characters of the Ramayana. Titled Har Yug Mein Ram: A Conversation with Young Leaders, the special episode will stream exclusively on JioHotstar from November 1.
Ranbir Kapoor, Nitesh Tiwari, and others discuss Ramayana’s values with students from 500 schools; special episode to stream on JioHotstar
Organised by JioHotstar in partnership with the makers of Ramayana and the International Institute of Management and Entrepreneurship (I.I.M.U.N.), the initiative brought together nearly 20,000 students from more than 500 schools across 18 cities. The event aimed to explore how the epic’s themes of duty, courage, friendship, love, forgiveness and sacrifice continue to resonate with younger audiences.
Ranbir Kapoor reflects on playing Lord Rama
Ranbir Kapoor, who plays Lord Rama in the upcoming film Ramayana: Part One, said interacting with students gave him an opportunity to hear how a new generation interprets the character. “Rama’s story has been part of our lives for generations, and stepping into his shoes has been an incredibly humbling experience. What made this interaction special was hearing young minds engage with his story in their own way,” Ranbir said.
He added that the conversation reminded him how different generations can find their own meaning in Rama’s journey while continuing to connect with its familiar themes.
View this post on Instagram
Students explore the Ramayana’s characters and choices
The event took place at I.I.M.U.N.’s headquarters in Mumbai, with around 150 student leaders attending in person and others participating virtually from classrooms across the country. Students asked the guests questions about the epic’s central characters and their decisions. The discussion included who they considered the true hero of the Ramayana, what they would ask Lord Rama, which character they would choose as a friend and whose journey among Rama, Sita and Lakshman they found most challenging.
Producer Namit Malhotra said the conversation was an opportunity to help young people develop their own understanding of the epic. “Ramayana has given us generations of stories, values and lessons that continue to guide us even today. As we bring this epic to the big screen, it’s equally important that young people discover these values and find their own connection with them,” he said.
Malhotra added that the students’ curiosity and perspectives demonstrated how the story continues to connect with new generations.
Nitesh Tiwari and Ravie Dubey on the epic’s enduring relevance
Director Nitesh Tiwari said the Ramayana’s appeal lies not only in its larger-than-life events but also in the personal choices and emotions of its characters. “The richness of Ramayana lies in the fact that alongside its larger-than-life moments, its characters face deeply human choices and emotions. As filmmakers, our responsibility was to preserve that emotional truth while bringing the story to the screen for a new generation,” Tiwari said.
Ravie Dubey, who portrays Lakshman in the film, reflected on the relationship between Lakshman and Rama, which is shaped by loyalty, love and duty. “Playing Lakshman gave me the opportunity to explore a relationship built on loyalty, love and an unwavering sense of duty. What I found interesting during this interaction was how young people viewed these relationships and choices from their own experiences,” Dubey said.
He added that hearing the students’ interpretations gave him new perspectives on his character.
The special episode arrives ahead of the theatrical release of Ramayana: Part One, which is directed by Nitesh Tiwari and produced by Prime Focus Studios in association with DNEG and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. The film is adapted by Shridhar Raghavan from Valmiki’s Ramayana.
The cast includes Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana, Sunny Deol as Hanuman and Ravie Dubey as Lakshman.
Ramayana: Part One is scheduled to release worldwide in cinemas on November 5, 2026, in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and English, including IMAX 3D. Following its exclusive theatrical window, the film will be available on JioHotstar through an on-demand purchase offering.
Meanwhile, Har Yug Mein Ram: A Conversation with Young Leaders will premiere on JioHotstar on November 1, bringing the discussion about the epic’s values and relevance to a wider audience.

It’s a bright day in Cupertino. Apple’s new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company’s otherworldly ring-shaped headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn’t mind at all.
Nearly two months into his tenure, he’s been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus’ leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited foldable iPhone, a household device that can control digital appliances, new Mac Minis, and AirPods. Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”
We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.
This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”
Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”
Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.
The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rug rats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.
In 2015, while doing a story about a new iMac, I pressed Phil Schiller, then the senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, on this very question. Usually, top Apple executives field such queries with cryptic remarks. In this case, Schiller began a filibuster. “I’m going to get a little bit philosophical,” he said, then launched into what I later described as the Grand Unified Theory of Apple Hardware.
He explained that every Apple hardware product—the Watch, iPad, iMac, MacBook—is basically a computer and a piece of glass. Each one has a specific function. And each one has an interface appropriate to the hardware. Multitouch is fine for products like the iPhone, he said—but not the Macintosh. He provided two reasons: ergonomics and the software interface.
“From the ergonomic standpoint, we have studied this pretty extensively, and we believe that on a desktop scenario, where you have a fixed keyboard, having to reach up to do touch interfaces is uncomfortable,” he told me.
As for the interface, Schiller argued that Apple’s two main operating systems were built on different design principles. The iPhone and iPad’s iOS was multitouch from the get-go, and didn’t use macOS conventions that require precision, such as cursors and tiny boxes to close windows. “These two worlds are different on purpose, and that’s a good thing—we can optimize around the best experience for each of those and not try to mesh them together into a least-common-denominator experience,” he told me.
A year later, when Apple introduced a MacBook Pro with the ill-fated “touch bar”—a dynamic strip of virtual function keys above the keyboard’s top row—Schiller doubled down on the view that touch should never find its way into a Mac display. He said that such a move would mean totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers, and that would clash with the experience of pointer devices like a touchpad or mouse. “You can’t optimize for both,” he said.
To double-check this assumption, Apple conducted user tests with touchscreens on Mac. “What the heck, we could be wrong,” Schiller told me then. “We’ve absolutely come away with the belief that it isn’t the right thing to do. Our instincts were correct.”
When I met with Apple executives Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak this week to discuss the touchscreen MacBook Pro, you bet I invoked Schiller’s list of concerns. (Apple’s reps chose not to make Schiller, who now holds the title of “Apple Fellow,” available for an interview. In fact, they laughed when I asked.) It wasn’t only Schiller drawing a red line. In 2021, Ternus told journalist Joanna Stern, “The Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”
“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it's the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.
Joswiak, who holds Schiller’s old title of SVP of worldwide marketing, concedes that touch was overdue, at least for users with sophisticated needs. Its pro customers—engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators—were impatient with Apple for its failure to let them interact directly with the screen. “Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”
Between the lines, Srouji and Joswiak seem to consider their competitors’ touchscreen implementations shabby and lazy. The Apple ethos, as every one of its executives will happily explain to anyone who asks, is an expectation of quality that’s sky-high. “If you’re working on something easy, you’re wasting your time,” says Srouji, who has been at Apple since 2008 and has pretty much driven its innovation by spearheading the company’s charge to custom-build silicon.
“The easy things, I want to outsource,” he continues. “So the custom silicon is hard. The touch is hard. The display is hard. Everything we build is hard.” This swaggering philosophy dates from the Steve Jobs days and, in 2026, stands in contrast to the endgame of the ascendant AI industry, which hopes to turn over the toughest parts of industrial production to superintelligent entities.
Srouji presents Mac touch as a suite of innovations, starting with that screen that Ternus described as the Mac’s best ever. It also involves custom silicon and a rearchitected thermal system to prevent the display from feeling hot when people pinch, stretch, and swipe on it. Srouji contends that current touchscreen laptops suffer from “wobble” when fingers make contact with the display; to minimize this effect, Apple has redesigned the hinge on the MacBook Pro screen to stabilize it.
When I get a demo of the 16-inch version (as with previous Pros, it’s also available in a 14-inch version), I see what they mean about the display. It’s noticeably dense and bright, and the obsidian blacks are the deepest I’ve seen on a computer screen. In part because the OLED screen doesn’t require backlighting, this MacBook weighs less than its predecessor.
As a pair of Apple managers take the MacBook through its paces, I see how Apple has addressed some of Schiller’s decade-old concerns, like having to redesign the menu bar for fingers. While it looks the same, when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to allow you to select your choice with precision. Some of the objects on the screen, like the traffic-light buttons that close or hide windows, also get bigger when you touch them.
They show me how the touch tech can handle precision tasks, like color grading in the video editing software DaVinci Resolve, or tweaking a soundtrack on Logic Pro, Apple’s high-end audio workstation. One innovation, not just for pros, is a new gesture to pull down the “Dynamic Island,” that black oval hosting ongoing tasks that has made its way to Mac from iPhone. An expanded version floats on the screen like a widget, enabling easy access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.
But what about greasy fingers messing up the screen? I was told that the new display has an anti-reflective outer coating that will require no more cleaning than your normal non-interactive screen.
Apple clearly hopes that the MacBook Pro launch puts an exclamation point on the burst of product announcements that Apple customers are still absorbing. For the foldable Duo, some customers are impatiently waiting for delivery dates that stretch into January. (Lines were long at Apple stores last Friday, when the device went on sale, and Joswiak personally greeted those who queued up at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York City.)
I ask Srouji whether Apple is making a statement with its armada of new products, maybe as a way to say that in a year dominated by AI obsession, Apple is still here. He responds much as his new boss did, contending that Apple is simply sticking to its game plan. “We’re here to build the most amazing products in the world, and we want to ship them when we believe it’s ready and complete,” says Srouji. “That’s the statement we’re making. I think everyone knows we’re here.”
While longtime users will be happy to hear that a Macintosh now has a touchscreen, those with limited budgets will be disappointed. Apple’s current stance—that touch-on-a-Mac display is most appropriate to the “pro” crowd—rationalizes an astronomical price tag: The new MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Financial analyst Neil Cybart, who got an early MacBook Pro briefing, thinks that serious professionals will pay up. “People are in search of value, and that means going for products that leverage technology to improve what they’re doing,” he says.
When I ask Ternus about the timeline, or even the possibility, of seeing touch displays on less exorbitantly priced MacBook Airs and iMacs, he shakes his head. “You’ve been doing this a long time,” he says. “You know I will never tell you anything about our future.”
I don’t know why I bothered to ask. If Ternus said that touch would never happen on a MacBook Air, who would believe him? I’d be back at The Ring a year later, hearing that Apple had finally figured out a way to do it right.

A recent review of international clinical practice guidelines published in The Lancet Rheumatology highlights a shift in the management of non-specific low back pain towards clinical assessment, patient education, physical activity, and exercise, while discouraging routine imaging when there is no suspicion of serious disease.
Examining guidelines issued between 1994 and 2026, the review underscores the importance of assessing symptoms and identifying warning signs before deciding on investigations or treatment. Bengaluru-based specialists said the approach reflected a growing emphasis on restoring function and avoiding unnecessary investigations and interventions.
Ravikumar Mukartihal, senior consultant orthopaedic and robotic joint replacement surgeon at SPARSH Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the approach had moved from investigation-driven care to one focused on clinical assessment and restoring function.
“Most cases of non-specific low back pain do not indicate a serious structural problem and can be managed without extensive investigations or invasive procedures,” he said.
Treatment should focus on understanding symptoms, reassuring patients, maintaining normal activities, prescribing appropriate exercises and physiotherapy, and using medication judiciously, he said.
Treat the patient, not the scan
Karuna Kabadi, neurosurgeon at Apollo Speciality Hospital, Jayanagar, said a disc bulge or prolapse described in an MRI report was an observation about the disc, not necessarily a diagnosis explaining the pain. “Many of us may be having disc bulges but do not have symptoms and feel perfectly fit,” she said.
Back pain can arise from muscles, ligaments, and joints, and may also be associated with systemic diseases. A disc bulge may cause symptoms when it irritates or compresses a nerve, resulting in shooting pain in the buttock or leg, commonly known as sciatica. A detailed history and clinical examination help doctors assess the likely cause, with imaging supporting the diagnosis where necessary, she said.
Ravikumar T., Head and Consultant of the Department of Orthopaedics at Ramaiah Memorial Hospital, said incidental findings on scans could cause unnecessary anxiety if patients interpreted them as proof that their spine was damaged.
“Treat the patient and not the scan,” he said, noting that disc bulges and mild degenerative changes were also seen in people without back pain.
Non-specific back pain can involve several factors, including muscle strain, weak core muscles, poor movement patterns, sedentary habits, stress and inadequate sleep. Clinical examination helps assess pain, movement limitations and neurological signs before treatment is decided, he said.
Movement over prolonged rest
The review found that most guidelines recommended taking a patient’s history, conducting a physical examination and assessing psychological factors, including risk-stratification tools where appropriate. Routine imaging was generally discouraged without indications of serious pathology.
For acute low back pain, recommendations commonly included self-management, heat therapy, spinal manipulation and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For chronic pain, they included exercise therapy, psychological interventions and multidisciplinary care, with acupuncture and spinal manipulation recommended in some guidelines as part of broader treatment programmes.
Dr. Ravikumar T. said treatment had moved away from prolonged bed rest and early reliance on strong painkillers towards reassurance, education, continued activity and structured physical therapy.
“Movement is medicine,” he said, warning that avoiding activity out of fear of scan findings could cause muscle deconditioning and prolonged disability.
Dr. Kabadi said sitting for long hours and reduced daily movement contributed to mechanical back pain. Staying active, avoiding prolonged sitting and following guided physiotherapy and muscle-strengthening exercises could help, although consistency was essential.
When is a scan necessary?
Doctors stressed that discouraging routine imaging did not mean scans were unnecessary. Imaging remains important when there are warning signs of serious disease, progressive neurological deficits or persistent symptoms for which the findings could change treatment.
Surgery also has a role in selected patients, but decisions should be based on clear clinical indications rather than an MRI finding alone, Dr. Mukartihal said.
The specialists said the focus should be on appropriate clinical assessment and treatment tailored to each patient, with the aim of restoring movement and function while avoiding unnecessary investigations and procedures without overlooking serious underlying conditions.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

Myanmar official breaks down at UN as he urges world to ‘end our suffering’ under junta
Myanmar’s representative to the United Nations made an emotional appeal for the international community to end its silence over the country’s suffering on Wednesday (28 October).
Kyar Moe Tun, who was appointed by the previous democratically-elected government prior to the country’s 2021 coup, said the world had “failed the people of Myanmar again and again” and urged member states to stand in solidarity with its people.
During his speech, the ambassador held up a scarf created by revolutionary community Theatre 21, bearing the names and ages of those killed in the struggle for freedom against the junta that now rules the country.
He said reading the names of the “fallen heroes and innocent civilians” broke his heart, highlighting the human cost of the ongoing crisis.

Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressured
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.
Under the change, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.
Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.
But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of a new set of guidelines governing donation following circulatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.
The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.
Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?
"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.
The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have included patients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organs when they were still alive.
"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.
A balance of safety and speed
In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.
"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.
The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.
When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.
More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Does the change cross an ethical line?
Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.
"It's a very important bright line," says Dr. Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."
She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."
Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."
Others also see problems with the change.
"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."
Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.
"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," says Lois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."
But the change was endorsed by the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations (AOPO), a trade group.
"Families/agents who are considering [withdrawing life support] must be informed about donation and how the donor evaluation process may affect the timing of the [withdrawal of life support]," the group said in its public comments. "Many families have expressed frustration with learning about this timing impact after planning for other family members to be present at the time of [withdrawing life support]. Waiting until the family has made the decision is too late."
The AOPO declined to make someone available for an interview with NPR. But AOPO President Allison Erickson said in a written statement: "Donation depends on public trust, and it is our responsibility to respect and maintain it. Any time there is confusion or concern, [organ procurement organizations] clarify and improve the process. Donor families deserve to fully understand each stage of the end-of-life and donation processes, as well as that their loved ones are cared for by all involved."

(Bloomberg) -- New World screwworm was found in Arizona for the first time, detected in a dog, as cases of the deadly parasite accelerate.
The US Department of Agriculture confirmed the infection late Wednesday in a dog in Cochise County, Arizona. 
The spread of the parasitic fly, whose larvae burrow into the wounds of animals, had remained relatively contained since the pest was first detected in the US in June. Most of the early cases were limited to Texas. However, the pace of infections has increased this month, particularly in New Mexico. 
There have been a total of 71 cases of screwworm in the US since the outbreak began, according to the USDA. Eighteen are still active, with 10 located in New Mexico. 
The increase in October comes after screwworm, which can be deadly to livestock if left untreated, was discovered for the first time in wildlife last week. Spread among wildlife has been a key concern for cattle ranchers since the animals travel through the same terrain that their herds graze on. 
The spread also comes as the USDA has reopened ports in Arizona and New Mexico to shipments of cattle from Mexico. The US had halted livestock shipments from the country, and largely maintained that ban until late August when it began a phased reopening of the ports. 
The US had previously eradicated screwworm, pushing the pest south of Panama. But the fly began spreading north again after the pandemic, reaching Mexico in late 2024. 
While screwworm is a major threat to the US cattle herd, the parasite has also infected animals from goats to horses. The most recent five cases involved four dogs and one cat.

Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.
American automakers are reporting their third quarter earnings, and they're saying revenues are up, but they're also facing some serious headwinds.
Or as Mike Wall, an analyst at the automotive data company Mobility Global, put it: If this year was a book about the auto industry, "It would be a mix of suspense and thrills and maybe a little bit of comedy and a little bit of horror."
For the thrills: Auto companies are doing well when it comes to selling big cars and light-duty trucks. General Motors reported its sales of light-duty trucks rose 9% in the past year. Ford's F-Series trucks continue to be a company bestseller. Stellantis' pickup sales in the U.S. rose 34%.
And revenues overall are up: General Motors reported its revenue was up 2.9% in the past year; for Ford it was a 2% rise and Stellantis was up 1%.
To analysts, all of this signals that consumers are still buying vehicles — despite concerns about affordability. The average new vehicle transaction price was just over $50,000 in September, close to a record high, according to the Kelley Blue Book. Broadly speaking, customers are paying more for high-end trims and for bigger vehicles, which tend to be more profitable for the auto companies.
"Customers have been resilient amid higher fuel prices, interest rates and inflation," said Sherry Ann House, Ford's chief financial officer, on a call with investors.
But now for the suspense: The Detroit Three automakers are also cautioning investors that it's getting more expensive to make cars. Key materials like steel, copper and computer chips have all gotten pricier.
"Should we see prices at this level, it makes that more challenging heading into next year," Paul Jacobson, the chief financial officer of General Motors, said on the company's earnings call.
On the call for Stellantis, which owns Chrysler and Jeep, CEO Antonio Filosa noted that higher prices for memory chips and other raw materials "will be an industry-wide phenomenon to work with."
Tariffs, fuel and rising chip prices
Since 2025, the Trump administration has put additional tariffs on imported materials like steel, aluminum and copper. Much of a car's frame — and weight — is steel. So are nuts and bolts.
Copper, critical for a car's wiring and for electric vehicle batteries, has also grown more expensive — both because of tariffs and because there's more global demand for it, especially as the need for EV batteries grows. Plus, copper wire is also in high demand for data centers.
Then there are the costs of computer memory chips, which are used in a car's electronics, and are more expensive due to a tight supply chain and demand from many industries, including from AI.
Plus, there are other logistics costs. To bring vehicles from factory floors to dealerships, they get shipped on trucks, many of which run on diesel. The average price for a gallon has been hovering around $6.35, just short of its September all-time high, according to AAA.
High diesel prices play out in other ways too. The U.S. and Canada have closely intertwined auto supply chains and parts often cross the border several times as they get shaped into a car. That movement becomes more expensive when fuel is pricier — and when the U.S. tariffs Canadian goods.
"Higher fuel prices are impacting our freight and energy costs. But notably, we are not seeing it impact customer demand for trucks and fleet vehicles at this point," said House, the CFO of Ford.
In a report to investors, General Motors forecast that the cost of materials including computer chips and diesel would run the company as much as $2 billion this year. GM is also still paying about $2.5 billion in tariff costs, Jacobson said — which was lower than the company's earlier forecasts, partially offset thanks to tariff refunds.
In Ford's earnings call, CEO Jim Farley noted a similar figure: "We currently expect commodities, memory and logistics costs to represent a year-over-year headwind of about $2 billion at Ford."
Farley and House both said growth in other parts of Ford's business, as well as software services and parts, are helping offset these costs.
On their call, Stellantis executives said they would provide more information about these costs in the fourth quarter.
All of this is disruptive for an industry that is not built for high-speed changes. It takes time and money for carmakers to plan which vehicles to build, how many, and to line up supply chains.
" This is an industry that moves at a glacial pace between generations, between vehicles, between plants," said Sam Fiorani, a vice president for Auto Forecast Solutions. "And so when you throw in tariffs and you throw in all kinds of disruptions between countries, it throws off the supply chain and the calculation for profit and loss."
The electric transition
This quarter marked a full year since the demise of the $7,500 federal tax credit, which incentivized car buyers to purchase electric vehicles. Congress nixed it as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the credit ended on Sept. 30, 2025.
Data from the car analytics platforms Edmunds and Cox Automotive shows that after the credit went away, EV sales dropped nationally.
Tesla, which only makes EVs, reported that their global sales fell during the quarter, compared with the same period last year.
General Motors reported that its third quarter sales were down 6% overall compared to the previous year, partly because of the "smaller EV market."
On GM's call, Jacobson singled out the end of the tax credit as a reason for lower EV sales. He said the company plans to keep making electric vehicles, and that it's "right-sizing" its capacity and aligning its production with demand. "We think with these oil prices and these fuel prices that EV penetration may continue to go up, and we want to make sure we're ready for that," he said.
On Ford's call, executives didn't address EV sales, but they were enthusiastic about the Fathom, an electric truck the company plans to make available as a pre-order in early 2027, priced under $30,000.
But there are two bright spots for automakers when it comes to EVs. First, after last autumn's drop, EV sales have leveled out. As of September, they now make up about 6% of new car sales in the U.S., according to Edmunds.
American shoppers have also taken a greater interest in hybrids, especially given high fuel prices. Sales of hybrids are up 27% in the past year, according to Edmunds.
American automakers have noticed this trend, said Wall. "We have seen more inclination and more movement towards hybrids, and some automakers are adjusting their product plans accordingly," he said. But he added, gas-powered cars are still driving the profits of the big companies.
When it comes to electric vehicles, the companies are stuck in a kind of Catch-22. On the one hand, they're international companies — and EV demand is growing globally. Over 30 percent of new cars sold in Europe last year were electric. In China, more than half were, according to the International Energy Agency.
But EV demand in the U.S. just isn't the same. American drivers have long expressed concerns about limited range, charging infrastructure, or the cost of replacing an enormous lithium-ion battery.
"The thinking 10 years ago was we're going to skip hybrids and go right to electric vehicles. So we saw a lot of investment in factories, in battery plants, in new platforms to build fully electric vehicles," Fiorani said. But "when that volume didn't show up, they had to backtrack and develop new internal combustion vehicles going forward."
Fiorani expects to see the Detroit Three automakers offer more hybrid vehicles in the coming years, he said, "because this transition towards fully electric vehicles is going to take a lot longer than they anticipated."
Tesla's regaining ground
The Detroit Three's pullback in electric vehicles has given Tesla a leading edge — again. The company's third quarter revenue is about the same as it was this time last year, but its market share has grown.
Tesla used to sell the majority of EVs in the U.S. In 2024 and 2025, Tesla lost that lead. This year, it's winning the majority back: almost 52% of new EV sales in the U.S. have been Teslas, according to Edmunds.
"It makes sense that Tesla is clawing back market share," Ivan Drury, the director of industry insights at Edmunds, wrote in an email to NPR. Between other automakers peeling back some of their investments, plus the cancellation of the credit, Drury said, many buyers are probably going with what they know.
"Tesla is like the Kleenex of EVs," he continued. "Many people just default to them regardless of other offerings."
Still, on Tesla's earnings call, CEO Elon Musk did not spend much time talking about cars. He said they're focused on building new technologies, like robotaxis and humanoid robots, and they're investing a ton in these endeavors. Their capital expenditures this year are almost double from this time last year.
And on an earnings call for his rocket company SpaceX, Musk hinted at the possibility of a merger between the two companies, saying that special committees at each were discussing it. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," he told investors. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders would have to be supportive of this."
While analysts say there is some technological overlap between the two companies, a merger could be a hard sell for some Tesla shareholders, who would need to embrace adding SpaceX's business portfolio — Starlink satellites, the Grok AI chatbot, the X.com social media site — to Tesla's automotive business.

New Delhi, Oct 29: Noel N. Tata will retire as chairman and director of Trent Ltd on November 11, after nearly three decades with the Tata Group retailer, with the company's board appointing Bahram Vakil as his successor effective November 12.
Tata, who has been associated with Trent since 1997, will become chairman emeritus from November 12 in recognition of his contribution to the company, Trent said in a regulatory filing.
The leadership transition is in accordance with the Tata Group Governance Guidelines, which prescribe requirements relating to board composition, committees and the retirement of directors.
Board Approves New Director Appointments
The board also approved the appointment of Rajiv Dube as an additional non-executive, non-independent director from October 30, subject to shareholder approval. Kalpana Merchant has been appointed an additional director and an independent director for a three-year term from October 30, 2026, also subject to shareholder approval.
Trent said Tata, who is also the chairman of Tata Trusts – the majority shareholder in Tata Group holding company – had provided strategic direction and leadership during his tenure, helping the company strengthen its market position and deliver growth for stakeholders.
The board placed on record its appreciation for his contributions over the past 29 years.

Trent Expands Retail Operations Amid Growth
The changes come as Trent expands its fashion retail operations through brands, including Westside and Zudio, while developing its Star food and grocery business. The company reported a 25 per cent year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 468 crore for the September quarter, with revenue increasing 22 per cent to Rs 5,873 crore.
Vakil's appointment marks a change in board leadership as Trent continues to scale its retail footprint and pursue growth across fashion, lifestyle and grocery markets.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday fumed over rising digital arrest cases and expressed shock over how educated people were getting "arrested on mobile phones" despite public awareness campaigns, news reports and court orders.While hearing a suo motu case on digital arrests, CJI Surya Kant reportedly made an oral observation: "What is wrong with these victims? How are these victims being trapped like this? They can't understand this basic thing? What's the fear of arrest on mobile?""Hit the mobile on the wall and arrest goes. Something is wrong with people. God knows what is there. What kind of person are you in a democratic country if you think you are getting arrested on mobile?" a PTI report quoted the CJI.This comes after the amicus curiae in the case, NS Nappinai, said that she keeps receiving repeated inputs that while much was being done to stop digital arrests, the problem continues unabated.She told the court that a woman lost Rs 2.5 crore last week in such an incident."Something is wrong with people. God knows what is there. You are victimising yourself," the CJI retorted."We feel frustrated that all educated people are getting duped.
What will you pass on to the next generation if you get digitally arrested at this age? People can go to the court's website to find if there's an order," the CJI added.'Banks must act as a protective umbrella'During the hearing, the apex court also said that banks must be held accountable for compensating victims of digital arrest scams, stressing that they should act as a “protective umbrella” for customers vulnerable to such fraud.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana questioned why unusually large withdrawals from a retired person's bank account could not trigger timely intervention to prevent the loss.The top court said it was considering directions requiring banks to compensate victims and face prosecution where digital arrest fraud occurred due to their failure to exercise due diligence.
"We are proposing to direct that wherever such fraud takes place, the bank will compensate the victim and suffer prosecution. It has to be done," the CJI said.Observing that banks must be made accountable to indemnify losses of victims of digital fraud, the bench said that victims of offences like digital arrests should receive compensation of at least the amount lost if the fraud is found to have resulted from a failure of due diligence by the financial institution.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

The recent protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and helmed by Opposition parties, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have exposed a chink in journalists’ armour. The crackdown on journalists, especially freelancers and independent journalists, during the October 10 protests, has rekindled the debate on who has the right to be recognised as a journalist and about who decides who is a journalist.
One has seen how during the CJP protests, both in July over the NEET paper leak and in October over the demand for the CEC’s removal, freelancers and independent journalists, and content creators descended in hordes at the protest venue already bulging at the seams with reporters from registered media houses. However, during the second round of protests on October 10, phalanxes of riot police removed them from the protest site and sent them to detention centres. Only journalists with the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP) accreditation were allowed to cover the protests.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, while hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) which seeks the protection of the right to freedom of expression by freelance journalists and content creators, wondered whether the right to freedom of expression empowered every citizen of this country to be a journalist. “If everyone starts becoming a journalist, it will create problems for every other person,” the CJI said. During the hearing, senior advocate Indira Jaisingh said that there must be a national protocol for police not to obstruct the professional work of any journalist who has an identity card from the employer. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said that in the present era, any person with a mobile phone could claim to be an independent or freelance journalist when he/she would, in fact, be making reels only to garner popularity on social media to earn money by either presenting one-sided stories or sensationalising events.
Recognising journalists
These developments have put the focus back on the question of who recognises journalists. As per the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, a working journalist is a person whose principal avocation is journalism and who is employed in a newspaper, electronic media or digital media. This definition excludes people employed in a managerial or administrative capacity. Further, Central and State governments provide accreditation to working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Accreditation recognises working journalists and others and gives them access to designated official sources of information. For journalists in Delhi-NCR, accreditation is provided by the PIB for covering the Central government while the DIP accreditation gives them the right to cover the Delhi State government. Media accreditation guidelines of the PIB and DIP define the eligibility criteria for all those seeking accreditation. However, one of the major issues with government accreditation is that it has a quota depending upon circulation (for newspapers, periodicals and magazines), subscribers (for news agencies), licence under uplinking and downlinking guidelines (for private satellite TV channels), and unique visitors (for digital news publishers). Therefore, all journalists in recognised media organisations don’t get accreditation. This leads us to the question on how all working journalists can be recognised.
One solution could be a national media council or commission. Just like there is the Bar Council of India for lawyers and an Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for chartered accountants, the media council can recognise all working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Just like you need a law degree to practise law, a medical degree to become a doctor, the media council may mandate a degree or diploma in journalism and mass communication while applying for a licence.
A few years ago, the Press Club of India drafted a Media Transparency (and Accountability) Bill, which mandated the formation of a national media council, among other things. Recently, some other journalists’ bodies have also submitted a memorandum to the government with the same demand. As more and more people with a camera claim to be freelance journalists, it may be high time for the government to give some serious thought to the idea of such a council.
Rakesh Goswami is Professor of Journalism at Indian Institute of Mass Communication, New Delhi
