‘Delhi's air will be very bad after Diwali’: SC judge on request to defer a hearing
The issue of pollution in Delhi is being monitored by the Supreme Court in a suo motu proceeding arising from a petition filed by advocate MC Mehta.
Delhi’s air will be much worse after Diwali, commented Supreme Court judge Vikram Nath on Wednesday while entertaining a request to accommodate hearing of a matter for November 17.
The light-hearted comment by a bench headed by justice Vikram Nath exposed a sad reality of Capital’s deteriorating air quality. The issue of whether firecrackers will be allowed on Diwali this year is to be heard and decided by another bench of the Supreme Court on Thursday.
Also Read | Supreme Court: Firecracker ban needs a ‘pragmatic, practical’ approach
SC to hear plea on Diwali firecrackers on Thursday
Justice Nath said, “Post Diwali, the air in Delhi will be very bad.” He was responding to a request made by senior advocate Indira Jaising who appeared in a matter with a request to adjourn it to November 17.
The judge was willing to grant a date for the matter on November 3 as justice Nath, who is presently the senior most puisne judge in the Supreme Court, continued the light banter, “You come before Diwali, the environment would be cleaner. After Diwali, it will be worse.”
But the senior counsel remarked that before Diwali too, it will be no better. “Diwali is an extremely polluted time in Delhi. Please have the matter on November 17.” Continuing the light-hearted conversation with the bench, Jaising remarked, “Your lordships already have to suffer the bad air.”
As Jaising was appearing virtually before the court through the videoconferencing facility, justice Nath quipped, “You have the privilege of sitting at home and saving yourselves from the pollution. But we can’t sit at home.”
The issue of pollution in Delhi is being monitored by the Supreme Court in a suo motu proceeding arising from a petition filed by advocate MC Mehta. Along with this, in 2015, a petition was filed by three toddlers seeking a complete ban on firecrackers owing to the detrimental effect on children, aged and sick persons who face breathing and other health related complications.
Incidentally, both these matters are listed before a bench headed by justice MM Sundresh on Thursday. Under orders passed in the MC Mehta petition, there is a ban on bursting, sale and distribution of firecrackers in Delhi, extending further to the national capital region. Last year, a window was provided by the court for sale and bursting of crackers during Diwali in order to strike a balance between the right to health of citizens and the celebrations surrounding the right to observe festivals and religious beliefs.
This year too, the fireworks retailers have requested the court for a similar arrangement demanding that under monitoring of the court, specified dates could be allotted for sale of crackers and its bursting be regulated during specified times. This issue will be decided on Thursday.
Also Read | Supreme Court rules out blanket cracker ban ahead of Diwali: 'It will hurt sentiments'
SC calls for ‘practical and pragmatic’ approach
Early this month, the court indicated that banning firecrackers needs a “practical and pragmatic” approach. It emphasised that religious sentiments cannot be hurt and at the same time, the health of citizens must be taken into consideration by promoting the use of green crackers that are less harmful to public health.
While striking this middle path, the Centre has submitted formulations of improved crackers having less emission by involving experts including CSIR-NEERI, PESO and CPCB. The experts have presented formulations for next generation joined crackers, which are less polluting than conventional joined crackers (lari). They are presently undertaking studies on the reduced use of barium in firecrackers, for which open ground testing is being conducted across multiple places in the country.

Airlines seek more time to shift international flights to Navi Mumbai airport
MIAL presented its redevelopment plans and proposed temporarily shifting international traffic accounting for five million passengers per annum (MPPA) to NMIA.
Mumbai airport operator Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) has asked airlines to submit plans by November 3 for temporarily shifting international flights to Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA) ahead of the redevelopment of Terminal 1 (T1). Airlines have sought more time, people aware of the development said.
"At a meeting with the Airport Airline Operators Committee (AOC) on Wednesday, airlines indicated that the transition should not take place before the winter 2027 schedule, citing the need for advance planning," one person said.
"The airlines opposed any unilateral reduction in flight slots from the summer 2027 schedule and called on the airport operator to begin discussions on the winter schedule at the earliest, in line with the civil aviation ministry’s slot-allocation guidelines," they added.
The meeting lasted around 90 minutes and was attended by about 50 officials representing 35 airlines.
MIAL proposes shifting 5 million passengers to NMIA
During the meeting, MIAL presented its redevelopment plans and proposed temporarily shifting international traffic accounting for five million passengers per annum (MPPA) to NMIA.
IndiGo, the Air India group and Akasa Air have already finalised plans to shift international flights accounting for around 3 MPPA to the new airport. However, international airlines have yet to agree to the airport operator’s proposal.
MIAL has proposed shifting the remaining traffic from Terminal 2 (T2) at Mumbai airport during the summer 2027 schedule to meet its target, another person said.
The proposed relocation is part of MIAL’s plan to redevelop the ageing T1, which was commissioned in 1964.
Terminal 1 redevelopment to begin in April 2027
A spokesperson for Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA) said structural audits conducted by Structwel in 2017 and IIT Bombay in 2024 highlighted safety and structural concerns. According to the airport operator, these findings make replacing the terminal necessary.
The spokesperson said the airport shared artistic impressions of the proposed terminal with the AOC on Wednesday. The images represent the intended design and passenger experience rather than a definitive preview of the final structure.
The redevelopment is expected to increase T1’s annual passenger-handling capacity from 15 MPPA to 20 MPPA. Demolition is scheduled to begin in April 2027, with completion targeted for December 2030.
To manage domestic traffic during the redevelopment, an expansion of the north-west pier of T2 is planned. The expanded section is expected to become operational by March 2029.
Mumbai airport capacity to rise to 65 MPPA
CSMIA currently handles around 55 million passengers annually. Its capacity is expected to increase to 65 MPPA after the redevelopment of T1 and the expansion of T2.
MIAL has said the temporary relocation of five million passengers would leave around 91% of the airport’s current traffic unaffected. The shifted international traffic is expected to return after the T2 expansion.
NMIA currently has a passenger-handling capacity of 20 MPPA and is eventually planned to handle 90 million passengers annually.

As the U.S. midterm elections approached in late October, comments President Donald Trump made about peoples' bodies during his speeches at GOP campaign rallies gained widespread attention.
Trump's fixation on the physical attributes of the men and the women around him appeared to reflect his party's focus on gender roles and masculinity more broadly. "I examined his a** and then I looked at his shoulders," Trump said of Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, on Oct. 17, eliciting a roar of applause. "I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I'm still recovering."
By late October, another remark attributed to Trump, 80, circulated about rapper Nicki Minaj, who he told rallygoers had "one hell of a beautiful a**." The quote spread across multiple social media sites and prompted derisive comments from late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel.
The quote was correctly attributed to the president. Trump extolled the beauty of Minaj's body while stumping for Republican candidates in Michigan on Oct. 25. Videos of the event are widely available, including on C-SPAN (Trump's full comments beginning at 52:49).
"By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful a** before — Nicki Minaj," he said (at 0:20 below), pointing to a Gucci-clad Minaj in the audience, who covered her mouth and laughed. "That's hard to miss. That — stand up Nicki. That's hard to miss." The crowd laughed and whistled as she stood and waved.
Though Minaj has yet to openly address Trump's comments as of this writing, she did later join him on stage and pledged her allegiance to him, all the way through a theoretical third term (at 1:44:01). "I will continue to support you forever and ever," she said. "If you run again, I will support you again."
Minaj, an outspoken supporter of Trump and the GOP in recent years, emerged from Air Force One with the president on Oct. 25 and posted a video from inside the aircraft, where she sat down with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung to answer questions about Trump's role in the leadup to the midterms.
When asked about "these fake news polls," Minaj told Cheung: "We don't pay those polls any mind, obviously they are there to deter our voters from going out and casting their vote."
As of this writing, the majority of polls show voters favoring Democrats. The party out of power typically gains ground in midterm elections, according to New York Times polling researcher Caroline Soler.

- The claim that the U.S. Postal Service hired a private security company to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices in "blue" states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections is unproven.
- The rumor stems from reporting by the independent newsroom RawStory. The outlet reported in early October that Prosegur, an international security company, had deployed "nearly 1,000" armed security officers to at least 55 post offices ahead of the 2026 elections as part of a contract with the Postal Service.
- A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in a statement that it had deployed "a mix of unarmed and armed contract security officers to key USPS facilities" but that this deployment started in 2025 and had "absolutely nothing to do with elections." According to Postal Service policy, the deployment of security officers to mail facilities is based on the number of employees, not political leanings in any given location.
- Neither the Postal Inspection Service nor Prosegur confirmed how many officers had been contracted or where. The president of the union that represents postal police officers said RawStory's "nearly 1,000" estimate was based on the union's tally of approved work hours for contracted guards rather than the number of contracts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We asked Prosegur to confirm its contract with the Postal Service and to respond to RawStory's allegations that it had "a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." We await replies to our queries.
In October, a claim circulated that the U.S. Postal Service hired a private security company to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices in Democratic-leaning states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
For example, one X user wrote (archived): "USPS has hired security company Prosegur to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices primarily in blue states. Prosegur has a history of human rights violations in Brazil."
Similar claims also circulated elsewhere on X (archived) and Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us asking about the claim.
The claim stemmed from investigative reporting by the independent newsroom RawStory. The outlet reported in early October that Prosegur, an international security company, had deployed "nearly 1,000" armed security officers to at least 55 post office locations ahead of the 2026 midterm elections as part of a contract with the Postal Service.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, which is the federal law enforcement arm of the Postal Service, said in a statement on Oct. 28:
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service's deployment of a mix of unarmed and armed contract security officers to key USPS facilities has absolutely nothing to do with elections. These deployments have been ongoing since last year, under supervision, and represent a supplemental staffing to our career employee Postal Police Officer complement.
The statement said the Postal Service could not confirm where it stationed armed or unarmed guards in order to "maintain operational security." For that reason, we could not confirm the claim that the service stationed additional security in Democrat-led areas. The service's own policy on security staffing said deployments were based on staff numbers at a given facility.
Because the claim is unproven, we leave it without a rating.
The Postal Inspection Service's statement did not confirm that the Postal Service contracted specifically with Prosegur or how many armed security officers the company had deployed. We asked Prosegur to confirm its contract with the service and to respond to RawStory's allegations that it had "a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." We await replies to our queries.
Speaking to RawStory, a spokesperson for Prosegur reportedly said that the company had a "USPS account" that they were not able to discuss the details of.
USPS contracted guards since 2025, not connected to elections
Cathy K. Purcell, a senior public relations representative for the Postal Service, reportedly told The New Republic in October that the service had deployed armed security officers "since last year."
The Postal Inspection Service told Snopes in a written statement that the deployment of armed and unarmed officers was "part of our overall security plan" and repeated Purcell's reported timeline for the deployment, which it also said had "absolutely nothing to do with elections."
Frank Albergo, executive director of the Postal Police Officers Association, which represents officers who are part of the service's uniformed force, also told Snopes that wider deployment of armed security officers within the Postal Service began after October 2025. He added that "claims that the guards were brought in to meddle with the election are not supported by the information we have."
The Postal Service security staffing policy (Page 3) shared by Albergo in September showed the service allocated security officers — contracted or non-contracted, armed or unarmed — to locations based on how many employees were at a facility, not the political leaning of the state in which it was located. RawStory reported that the service had deployed armed security officials to seven cities in the U.S., all of which were in or near Postal Inspection Service divisions.
USPIS hired security through Prosegur from 2019
According to a 2022 report (Page 3) by the Postal Inspection Service Office of the Inspector General, which audits the service, the Postal Inspection Service has contracted security officers through Prosegur since at least 2019, when Prosegur took over another company that the Postal Inspection Service had contracted with since 2014.
Albergo said Prosegur was the only company that provided security officers to the Postal Inspection Service in 2026.
The inspector general's report said the Postal Service contracted additional security officers to provide "perimeter and building security at assigned postal facilities" alongside the service's own postal police officers. According to the Postal Inspection Service, this was still the case in 2026, as a spokesperson described the deployment of armed and unarmed guards as "supplemental staffing" to existing postal police officers.
There were several key differences between postal police officers and contracted security officers. Most importantly, the inspector general's report said (Page 3), postal police officers could "conduct investigations, and make arrests" while contracted security officers could not. Both types of security officers could carry firearms, though Alebergo told Snopes that the security officers Prosegur and its predecessor supplied before October 2025 generally were not armed.
Albergo said the Postal Inspection Service employed 440 postal police officers in October 2026. By comparison, he said the Postal Service had approved 39,587 contract guard-hours per week — the approximate equivalent of 990 full-time positions. Though neither Albergo, the Postal Inspection Service nor Prosegur had confirmed exactly how many contracted security officers it hired using the approved hours, Albergo's comparison suggested that contracted security officers far outnumbered postal police officers.
Reporting questioned Prosegur's labor and human rights record
Though the Postal Service had contracted with Prosegur for several years by 2026, it didn't appear the cooperation had always been easy. The 2022 inspector general's report (Page 4) found that 35 of the 115 security officers reviewed by inspectors during fiscal year 2021 — around one in three — worked on the contract without proper security clearance. Inspectors were also unable to verify the duration and nature of any training the Prosegur security officials had undertaken before working on post office sites.
According to the report, the service did not adequately track the quantity or quality of the Prosegur security officials' work, meaning Prosegur could have overbilled the service for work carried out under its contract. According to the inspector general's report, the estimated total cost of the potentially 10-year contract with Prosegur was $250 million (Page 3). The report did not present any evidence that Prosegur actually overbilled the Postal Service during the contract in question.
Snopes could not independently confirm the value of any newer contracts between the Postal Service and Prosegur because the former does not report (Page 6) its spending to the federal USAspending.gov database.
RawStory's reports on the service's contracts with Prosegur raised additional labor and human rights issues relating to Prosegur's work in the U.S. and abroad.
For example, the Charlotte, North Carolina-area branch of the American Postal Workers Union reportedly requested that the Postal Service replace contracted security officers with postal police officers at one site after a contracted security officer allegedly punched a postal worker and pushed her to the ground in April 2024. The Postal Service reportedly denied the request.
Miriam Bell, the general president of the Charlotte-area branch of the union, reportedly told RawStory that the Postal Service hired contracted security officials in an attempt at "union busting," which is when a company's management attempts to stop employees from unionizing.
Bell told RawStory that two post office employees in the Charlotte area had been fired or attempted fired as a result of speaking up against contracted security officers. Snopes has not independently verified the details of Bell's accounts to RawStory.
RawStory's reporting described Prosegur as "a multinational private contractor with a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." In particular, the reporting highlighted a 2024 recommendation by the Norwegian Council on Ethics to exclude Prosegur from investment by the country's government pension fund due to "an unacceptable risk that the company is contributing to serious human rights abuses."
The Norwegian Council on Ethics research found that Prosegur's subsidiary in Brazil had been involved in "severe acts of violence and abuse of tribal people's rights." It added that Prosegur continued to operate in "numerous countries in which there are land disputes and serious antagonism between commercial companies and local populations."
Prosegur said in a joint account of "labor controversies" from 2013 to 2020 that it believed at least one union that had accused it of human rights abuses had "misused" the concept (Page 8).
The company had not returned a request for comment on RawStory's allegations at the time of this writing.

Aga banned for fake prescription from family member
- Published
Ethiopian marathon runner Ruti Aga has been handed a six-year ban after she attempted to explain a positive test for a banned substance using a prescription from a non-existent clinic, issued by a doctor who turned out to be a family member.
Aga, who won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon, tested positive for methylprednisolone after winning a half marathon in China in March.
She received a two-year ban for testing positive for the prohibited steroid - used to reduce inflammation and classed as performance enhancing by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada).
The 32-year-old was given a further four-year ban for tampering with evidence and misleading investigators during an interview.
"Aga attributed her positive test to treatment for a knee injury, submitting a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a 'doctor' who turned out to be a family member with no medical registration with the relevant authority," the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday.
"When questioned, the family member claimed to have used an old prescription pad from a former workplace. But that clinic confirmed the individual had never worked there and the prescription was not theirs."
Aga, who has finished second three times at World Marathon Majors, has been provisionally suspended since 10 September and the ban will run from that date.

Reddit is adding a 'for you' feed for recommendations
The app will have a "following" tab to surface content from subreddits you've joined.
Reddit is changing up its main feed as it looks to emphasize more recommended content. The platform is splitting its feed into "for you," which will surface algorithmic recommendations, and "following" which shows posts from subreddits you've joined.
The change makes Reddit's central feed more like other mainstream social platforms. Up until now, the company has had one main feed that mixes in recommended posts alongside updates from subreddits you've joined. The new "for you" section will be more focused on allowing users to "discover relevant communities and conversations you might not otherwise come across," the company said in an update. With the change, Reddit will initially open to the new "for you" feed, but it will default to whichever feed you were last using the next time you launch the app.
The company is likely hoping the move will boost users' engagement with the platform. CEO Steve Huffman has said he wants to make it easier for casual users to come back to the service and that Reddit should find more ways to surface relevant posts, even if they are older. The company is also experimenting with video and audio versions of popular posts, some of which are from threads that are several years old.
So far, the company hasn't put those posts into a full-screen scrollable TikTok-like feed. But in its blog post announcing the change, Reddit said that it would "continue experimenting with ways people can more intentionally explore Reddit," including "new ways to navigate" the app. The company also said it's working on ways for users to offer feedback on recommended content to make it easier to fine tune its suggestions.

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.
“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.
Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.
“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”
Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.
The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.
Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.
The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.
“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.
With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.
In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.
“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”
Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.
Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

TBS Holdings executives outlined the strategy behind the Japanese broadcaster’s tie-ups with Legendary Entertainment and Korea’s CJ ENM in a TIFFCOM presentation today.
In January 2026, TBS acquired a $150M minority stake in Legendary and entered into a non-exclusive agreement with the Dune and Godzilla franchise producer to source and develop Japanese IP.
Katsuaki Setoguchi, TBS Holdings Executive Officer, Global Business Division, opened the presentation by explaining why the Japanese broadcaster made this move: “Why did we partner with Legendary? Our needs matched each other perfectly.”
He continued that Legendary has been “keeping a close eye on Japanese IP” and as the Godzilla franchise and other projects have proved, are willing to invest in big-budget live-action adaptations. In addition to Godzilla, the company is producing several theatrical and episodic projects based on Japanese IP, including Street Fighter, Gundam and Drops Of God Season 2.
Watch on Deadline
“They needed upfront investment and to tie up with Japanese IP holders, but also had to understand the soul of the original work,” Setoguchi said. “Finding partners you can develop a deep relationship with is difficult. But TBS has long-standing relationships with many creators for live-action works, so working together with us, they could deliver Japanese IP to the rest of the world.”
Setoguchi also said TBS has “neutral” relationships with all the major publishers in Japan, so isn’t limited to working with specific rights holders.
He added that, starting this month, TBS employees will be setting up desks in the Legendary offices in Los Angeles to ensure a close working relationship. TBS already has its own offices in LA, and an outpost of its international production outfit The Seven, which has produced shows including three seasons of Alice In Borderland and Did Someone Happen To Mention Me, starring Koji Yakusho, both of which are streaming on Netflix, and Prime Original Rock Paper Landmine.
Meanwhile, back in Asia, TBS has been forming similar tie-ups, launching a production joint venture Studio Monowa with Korea’s CJ ENM and Japanese streamer UNEXT, with announcements on the first projects expected soon.
The aim for TBS is to propel Japanese drama to the same level of global recognition as Korean dramas. He observed that while K-drama is widely distributed to international markets, Japanese live-action content is not as well known, although anime and manga are hugely popular nearly everywhere in the world.
Setoguchi recalled that one of the first shows co-produced by Japan and Korea was 2002 drama Friends – produced by TBS and Korea’s MBC – which was created to commemorate the 2002 FIFA World Cup co-hosted by South Korea and Japan. He described the show as “the first time Japanese was spoken on Korean TV since the war”.
He added that, back then, Japan’s TV drama industry was much stronger than Korea’s and that Korean production staff were “enthusiastic to absorb every aspect of Japanese production expertise”.
“We thought that since there’s a huge gap in production capabilities, it would be difficult for Korean teams to create global hits. More than 20 years have passed and we all know how that has turned out. Japan pursued domestic viewer ratings, while Korea looked at global markets, and those decisions have shaped today’s reality. We feel our mission now is to create a new global genre of J-Content.”
On the unscripted side, TBS has built a global industry around the Ninja Warrior format, working with partners including Banijay, RTL and ITV Studio, who all appeared via video clips during the TIFFCOM presentation to talk about the strengths of the format. Banijay is selling the Israeli version of the show, which is returning after a three-year hiatus, while Australia is bringing it back after five years.
Noting that sports-related programming is having a resurgence, Banijay Chief Content Officer James Townley said: “With the Olypmics coming up, Ninja Warrior can capitalize on the strength of that and will be a major focus for us across Europe next year.”
TIFFCOM is running for three days (October 28-30) at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center in Hamamatsucho.

Dictionary.com has named “maxxing” its Word of the Year for 2026, recognising its growing popularity. Announced on October 26, the choice reflects a desire to get more from everyday life. The word also captures how people joke about constantly trying to improve themselves. Short for “maximizing”, maxxing means doing something fully or making it as effective as possible. It can stand alone or join the end of almost any word. This flexibility has helped it spread across many different subjects online. “Sleepmaxxing” describes efforts to get the best sleep while “proteinmaxxing” means eating more protein. “Cozymaxxing” turns a quiet evening at home into the cosiest experience possible. Other examples include “gymmaxxing”, “healthmaxxing” and “fibermaxxing”. Dictionary.com also connects maxxing with “min-maxing”, a gaming strategy that strengthens a character’s best abilities. Steve Johnson, Dictionary Media Group’s director of lexicography, said the word appeared across many subjects. Its reach extended through different articles and areas of life. That widespread use helped it stand out as this year’s choice. Johnson said usage increased more than 1,000% since the year. This figure came from media analysed by Dictionary.com. Another reported estimate compared August 2026 usage with the average monthly rate during 2025. August’s figure was almost 19 times that earlier average. These figures measure different comparisons and should be understood separately. According to Johnson, maxxing reflects a culture seeking the most from everything. Dictionary.com highlighted both personal improvement and humour surrounding the pressure to improve constantly. The word has also moved beyond fitness and daily routines. “Tokenmaxxing” describes making the most of AI tools. Political messaging has also used “homelandmaxxing”. Its roots, however, go back several years. Dictionary.com’s archived records trace “looksmaxxing” to 2015. The term developed in online incel and manosphere forums. Men used these spaces to discuss becoming more attractive. “Moneymaxxing” and “statusmaxxing” appeared by 2021. The spelling with two Xs spread through online forums before reaching mainstream social media. According to CBS Minnesota, Gen Z and Gen Alpha helped popularise it. Its journey brought an older online expression into much wider use. Maxxing beat four finalists: “affordability”, “data center”, “odyssey” and “unc”. Affordability reflected discussions about housing, health care, gas and groceries. Data center highlighted AI growth while odyssey gained attention after Christopher Nolan’s film. Unc describes someone considered out of touch. Last year’s winner was “6-7”, a Gen Alpha expression without a clear meaning. Maxxing offers a contrast through its clear meaning and widespread use. Chennai-based stroke medicine expert Sivarajan Thandeswaran has called for certification of Indian hospitals to distinguish them as ‘stroke-ready’ so that people do not waste time in seeking treatment.
“Hospitals in India have to apply for and obtain NABH or JCI certification; instead, a proper government legislation making it mandatory for patients to be taken to and treated at comprehensive stroke centres, as done in the West, will improve stroke care,” said a senior consultant in Stroke Medicine, General Internal Medicine and Gerontology, at Kauvery Hospital in Alwarpet on Wednesday.
He was speaking at a webinar on ‘The Golden Hour: Every Minute Matters, Every Life Counts’, presented by Kauvery Hospital in association with The Hindu to mark World Stroke Day, observed annually on October 29.
He was joined by Harish R. Kamath, consultant neurologist, Kauvery Hosur. The experts stressed on the need for timely access to care as time is the most crucial factor to salvage the brain. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and, therefore, treatment in the window period of 4.5 hours is critical.
Treatment of stroke has transformed tremendously, and families need to be aware, Dr. Thandeswaran added.
In his presentation, Dr. Kamath explained the symptoms of stroke, including loss of balance, blurring vision, facial asymmetry, weakness in arms, and slurring speech. He said 1.8 million new stroke cases are added every year and 7.25 million deaths due to stroke occur every year.
Dr. Thandeswaran said that while big city hospitals have facilities for scanning, imaging, and treatment, including thrombolysis (dissolving blood clots with medicine) and thrombectomy (removing clot through surgery), in remote areas, telemedicine and video calls were being used in identifying stroke patients and transferring them to Comprehensive Stroke Centres, where advanced services and specialist teams are available.
The doctors discussed lifestyle-related risks, including poor dietary habits, physical inactivity, and inadequate sleep.
“People should take ownership of their health through routine check-ups for better treatment outcomes,” Dr. Thandeswaran suggested.

Went to Russia for $1,200 job, Indian man's family alleges he was tortured to join Ukraine war
Vinit Kumar Dubey's sister said she had not heard from him since October 7 and had received neither calls nor messages.
A 21-year-old man from Chhattisgarh was allegedly detained and tortured in Russia to force him to join the war in Ukraine, his 17-year-old sister has claimed. She has approached the local police in Bilaspur, seeking help to bring her brother back to India.Vinit Kumar Dubey, a resident of Bilha in Bilaspur district, travelled to Russia on October 1 after receiving a job offer through a Telegram group, his sister said.
Bilaspur senior superintendent of police (SSP) Rajnesh Singh told news agency PTI that the authorities were waiting for a response from the Indian embassy in Moscow. Bilaspur collector Sanjay Agrawal said the district administration had also contacted the ministry of external affairs (MEA).
The Indian embassy and the MEA have not issued statements on the case so far.
Man detained in Russia, forced to join war: Sister
Dubey’s teen sister reportedly submitted a letter to the district administration, urging them to intervene and help bring her brother home.
Speaking to news agency ANI, she said her brother had been offered a job at a food storage facility with a monthly salary of around $1,200. “However, once he arrived, his job description was changed; he was told he would be doing delivery work instead. He was placed in a hotel alongside a young man from Jordan.”
She said that she had not heard from Vinit since October 7 and had received neither calls nor messages.
The girl said someone called the family from a Russian phone number on the night of October 10 and told them that Vinit had been implicated in a narcotics-related case and was being forced to join the war.
The family initially believed the call was part of a scam and stopped communicating with the caller. She alleged that the same person told the family that Vinit was being tortured to make him join the war.
The teenager said she had emailed the Indian embassy on October 8 to report her brother missing. "The embassy replied that it would look into the matter and try to trace his whereabouts," she was quoted as saying by PTI.
She has urged the district administration to work with the Indian embassy to locate her brother and ensure his safe return to India.
Local administration approaches embassy, MEA
Bilaspur SSP Rajnesh Singh confirmed that the police had received the girl's complaint alleging that her brother was being held in Russia. "We have written to the Indian embassy about a week ago, but have not received a response so far. Further action will be initiated as soon as we receive a reply," he said.
Bilaspur collector Sanjay Agrawal said he had discussed the matter with the SSP, who had contacted the Indian embassy. The district administration has also approached the MEA, he said, expressing hope that the matter would be resolved.

Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks has acquired Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev for an undisclosed amount to strengthen its IT service management platform Freshservice. The acquisition will add AI-powered capabilities to investigate technology outages, identify their underlying causes, and recommend corrective actions. Freshworks plans to integrate these capabilities into Freshservice and deepen their interoperability with incident response platforms such as FireHydrant. Founded by Natan Yellin and Arik Alon, Robusta uses AI agents to analyse monitoring data, information from IT infrastructure, and recent code or configuration changes to determine what caused an outage. It also identifies how disruptions affect connected services and recommends steps to resolve them. According to Freshworks, the technology is designed to reduce manual investigations, consolidate alerts, and help engineering teams resolve incidents faster. Engineers can review and approve recommended actions before changes are made to production systems. “Our technology lets AI Agents do that effectively in large enterprise environments, where there are so many raw events that investigating each one individually would be exorbitant from a token cost perspective. We're incredibly excited to join Freshworks, which gives us the scale and platform to bring that experience to engineering teams everywhere, while keeping humans firmly in control of decisions that touch production,” said Robusta founder Yellin. Freshworks said the integration would connect incident diagnosis, response, and prevention workflows, helping businesses use findings from earlier outages to reduce recurring disruptions. The deal expands Freshworks’ AI-powered service operations offerings, which focus on automating IT workflows and helping enterprises manage technology incidents. Founded in 2010 by Girish Mathrubootham and Shanmugam Krishnasamy, Freshworks offers cloud-based software for customer engagement, sales, and IT service management. The Robusta deal follows Freshworks’ agreement to acquire Torii, announced earlier this month. The SaaS management platform helps enterprises track software usage and govern AI spending. The company also acquired US-based incident management startup FireHydrant in Demember last year. While FireHydrant helps enterprises coordinate responses to software outages, Robusta adds AI-powered root-cause analysis and remediation recommendations. On the financial front, Freshworks reported a $4.8 Mn net loss for Q1 2026, even as revenue grew 16% YoY to $228.6 Mn. It also announced plans to cut around 11% of its workforce, or approximately 500 employees, as it sought to increase the use of AI in product development and automate routine work.

New RSS group registers with justice dept to lobby in America
RSS Friends’ Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) filing came just days before RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat held a major rally at Madison Square Garden in New York
A new organisation, RSS Friends registered with the US Department of Justice (DoJ) on August 27 as a foreign agent representing the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), despite the RSS’ previous assertions that it does not lobby in the US.
In its filings with the DoJ, RSS Friends explicitly listed the RSS as its “foreign principal” along with the address of the organisation’s new headquarters in Delhi’s Keshav Kunj. The newly registered group also disclosed that its work will remain primarily informational, but that it does not have a written employment or lobbying contract with the RSS with specified compensation and deliverables. RSS spokesperson Sunil Ambekar didn’t respond to queries seeking comment despite multiple reminders.
RSS Friends’ Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) filing came just days before RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat held a major rally at Madison Square Garden in New York. The RSS, celebrating its centenary this year, is the ideological fount of the Bharatiya Janata Party.
“RSS Friends’ proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations, and community-engagement activities. Consistent with its governing documents and applicable law, it may communicate with members of the public, journalists, media organisations, researchers, academic and policy institutions, community leaders, civil-society organisations, and, where appropriate, government agencies or officials,” the filing reads.
It added: “The absence of a written contract should not be understood as a representation that no relationship, request, understanding, coordination, authorisation, direction, or other relevant factual connection exists. RSS Friends will disclose the actual facts relevant to its activities.”
RSS Friends’ website provides more detail about its objectives, which tend to revolve around correcting “misconceptions about the RSS” pushed by “politically motivated actors” that have created “negative repercussions for the Indian diaspora, particularly Hindu Americans.” It is not clear how old the organisation is, but the rssfriends.org websie was first registered in 2017. It is also not clear when the current version of the website was launched.
Three individuals linked with RSS Friends are mentioned in the DoJ filings: Rajendra Sonarikar, Pratikkumar Suthar and Jayant Pant. Suthar’s Linkedin profile says he “coordinates global outreach in the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS)” and has served in his position since March 2024. Suthar is based in New Delhi while it is presently unclear where Sonarikar and Pant reside. RSS Friends did not respond to a request for comment from HT.
The new registration follows a prolonged controversy over the RSS’ lobbying in the United States. In November 2025, news outlet Prism reported that elite lobbying firm Squire Patton Boggs was hired to “introduce the RSS to US officials” through State Street Strategies, another lobbying outfit. Subsequent disclosures filed with the US DoJ showed that Squire Patton Boggs had been paid $330,000 for its work on behalf of the RSS in 2025. To be sure, the RSS categorically denied reports that it hired lobbyists in America. Squire Patton Boggs subsequently disclosed its contract was terminated on September 30, 2025.
The matter caused a significant political controversy in India in late 2025.
“This is hardly the first time that the RSS has betrayed national interest,” Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said in response to the matter at the time.
The registration of RSS Friends coincides with a systematic effort by the RSS to enhance its outreach to the United States. Prior to Mohan Bhagwat’s visit in August this year, the organisation’s second-in-command Dattatreya Hosabale undertook a multi-day tour of America in April. This was explained by Hosabale as an effort to interact with “influential opinion makers” in Western nations to communicate the RSS’ mission and objectives.

Man stabbed to death by food vendor after he asked for extra chhole in Delhi's Nihal Vihar
The deceased, identified as Sandeep, worked as a driver and was allegedly attacked during an argument with a food vendor who was selling chhole bhature.
A 35-year-old man died after he was allegedly stabbed by a food vendor after he asked for "extra chhole" in his meal in outer Delhi's Nihal Vihar area, police said Thursday.
The deceased, identified as Sandeep, worked as a driver and was allegedly attacked during an argument with a food vendor who was selling chhole bhature near Jwalapuri Nala on Sunday. The man died during treatment on Tuesday.
The deceased is survived by his parents, wife and children aged around 4 and 10, all of whom live in the Nihal Vihar area.
The Delhi Police said they have arrested the accused, identified as Chintu Gupta, and he has been sent to judicial custody.
What happened
According to the police, Sandeep visited the food cart on Sunday night and ordered a plate of chhole bhature.
“He took his plate and, after some time, asked for some extra chhole, but the accused refused. The two then got into a heated argument during which the accused picked up a knife from his cart and stabbed the victim three to four times in the abdomen,” a senior police officer said.
After the stabbing, Sandeep was initially admitted to Sanjay Gandhi Memorial Hospital on the night of October 25 and was later shifted to Maharaja Agrasen Hospital in Punjabi Bagh, where he died during treatment.
Police said he was stabbed multiple times on his abdomen and hand.
A senior police officer said his family had filed a complaint and had found eyewitnesses who gave statements against the shop vendor.
"During the preliminary inquiry, it came to light that an argument had taken place between the injured and the chole-bhature seller near Jwalapuri Nala. An FIR was registered at Paschim Vihar West police station on the same day under Section 109(1) (attempt to murder) of the BNS. Gupta, the food vendor, was arrested and subsequently remanded to judicial custody. Following his death, BNS Section 103(1) (murder) was added to the case," he said.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.

A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared.
On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents “remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.”
Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance.
Over three years, the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s Flock contract ballooned from $22,000 to $470,000 in 2025, the year before the county mandated removals on county roads. However, Erick Gill, a St. Lucie County spokesperson, told the Post that despite ending that nearly half-million-dollar contract, the county lacks resources to investigate who owned the seven other unpermitted cameras found.
“It sounds like when you do something wrong, and you don’t want to get caught, and you kind of just want to sweep it under the rug,” Galindo told the Post.
According to Gill, the county’s goal was to remove the cameras, not to identify owners, which is why the county gave owners 30 days to take the cameras down without facing any questions.
“Our goal was to get the cameras out of the right-of-way within 30 days,” Gill said. “We accomplished that goal.”
Asked for comment, Gill did not address the cameras of unknown origin, only reiterating that the directive was to remove the cameras.
The Post reported that Flock “did not respond to emailed questions about who operated and removed the cameras or the apparent confusion over permitting requirements.” However, a Flock spokesperson told Ars that Flock knows who owned them and simply won’t disclose it to St. Lucie County residents.
“The cameras have been removed and belonged to several different customers,” Flock’s spokesperson said. “Flock does not share specifics regarding individual agency contracts, camera counts, locations, or deployments.”
Flock CEO said protests aren’t “real”
In St. Lucie County, Galindo’s petition makes it clear that some residents were already concerned about the lack of transparency around Flock cameras, and that was before they learned several unpermitted cameras were also collecting their data.
“These high-tech surveillance devices have been installed without clear, publicized consent or adequate discussion with the people they affect—us, the citizens who cherish their privacy and value transparency,” the petition said. Most concerning, the petition emphasized, studies have shown that Flock’s cameras “often lead to invasions of privacy, data misuse, and can even disproportionately affect marginalized communities.”
But Flock has downplayed the mass backlash, as its camera network continues to grow. On Monday, 404 Media shared leaked audio from a private police conference in which Flock CEO Garrett Langley claimed nationwide anti-Flock protests like Galindo’s “are not real” and repeated a disproven conspiracy theory that Russian bots supposedly fueled viral anti-Flock social media posts.
“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley reportedly said. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like, ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things.’”
Seemingly hoping to reassure police facing protests in their own communities, Langley insisted that “it’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real. Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.”
Flock’s line to police ignores that the ACLU has created a toolkit to help communities “DeFlock,” citing genuine concerns that “creepy cameras make it possible to track everyone’s movements” without a warrant. On the day 404 Media leaked Langley’s statements, the ACLU updated its resource providing instructions on how to “Get the Flock out,” while warning about lack of oversight for Flock’s huge camera database.
Flock fights to obscure 100,000 cameras
For Flock protesters, cases like the one in Florida are disturbing, since Flock appears to take great pains to obscure who owns cameras where and how large its camera network is. Talking to the Texas Tribune in August, Flock estimated there are about 120,000 cameras used by law enforcement nationwide, but cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael recently discovered that the network is nearly twice as large and has since faced legal threats from Flock for sharing his findings publicly.
In a research paper this September, Michael explained how he found a Flock access token that let him retrieve device locations without logging in. He notified Flock of the vulnerability, but he also created a map tracking all the devices. Analyzing that map, Matt Busel, founder of a software studio called Tensorust, noted that Michael exposed a network of 214,073 devices, not 120,000. Most likely, the nearly 100,000 difference represents Flock’s private camera network, which Busel warned is operated without regulatory oversight.
“It is bigger than anything Flock says out loud,” Busel wrote.
Busel told Ars that “it’s concerning” that St. Lucie County isn’t investigating ownership, since Michael’s map and his analysis show how many holes there are in the public’s understanding of how much their movements are tracked by Flock. The company’s statements do not appear to sympathize with residents who fear their data may have been misused by unknown Flock owners.
“Flock’s lack of transparency is a recurring pattern; they seem to prioritize obscuring the network’s footprint over public accountability,” Busel said. “My analysis suggests this isn’t just about localized camera placement but a broader effort to limit visibility into their total operating capacity.”
Instead of increasing transparency as public criticism swells, Flock has moved to protect private camera owners, including seemingly the ones in St. Lucie County. After Michael published the map, Flock sent a cease-and-desist letter, accusing Michael of violating laws by openly encouraging others to download its confidential data.
“An inadvertently exposed credential is not an invitation to access private systems or data,” Flock said.
Flock has demanded that Michael pull down the map, the data file, and his research paper. They’ve also asked Michael to name anyone who received the data. Otherwise, Flock has threatened to sue for injunctive relief, as well as statutory and punitive damages, since they said Michael knew the data was confidential and proprietary.
Michael has no plans to yank the data. On his site, he posted an update noting that “Flock Safety has responded to my research with a cease-and-desist letter threatening litigation. In an email to its customers, the company branded me a malicious actor, announcing it had notified law enforcement. That same email concedes Flock found no indication of unauthorized access to its data when it closed the issue in December, which is precisely the monitoring failure my research warns about. I’m not backing down.”
Asked for comment, Michael sent a statement to Ars, arguing that his research has national security implications. He confirmed that he is currently self-funding his legal defense and accepting donations from supporters on his website.
“Our nation is not protected by ignorance of a risk,” Michael said, adding:
My research on FlockSurveillance.orgdocuments cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences. There is an extremely deep irony in slandering me as a malicious actor, and confirming my thesis in the same email. My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people. Flock Safety has threatened me with litigation, notified law enforcement, and promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline. These actions against my good faith cybersecurity research covering national security should be considered a betrayal to our nation and sovereignty.
“I will not put Flock’s quarterly profits ahead of the security of the United States,” Michael continued. “Today I fund my legal defense myself and I am grateful beyond imagination that Proton is taking a stand to host a mirror of my research map. This is not a problem that will just disappear and the people of our country are rightfully concerned.”
This story was updated on Wednesday to include Michael’s statement.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Chiellini guidance to Leeds 'rock' - could Muharemovic be signing of season?
- Published
"He did a tackle right in front of the South Stand and the whole place erupted. I was thinking, 'you're going to go down well with this club'."
Former Leeds United boss Simon Grayson is reflecting on the moment new signing Tarik Muharemovic endeared himself to fans on his debut in a friendly against RB Leipzig at Elland Road in July.
The 23-year-old defender had just become Leeds' most expensive defender following a £34.1m move from Italian side Sassuolo, replacing the long-serving Pascal Struijk, who joined Brighton for £20m.
At the time, some supporters questioned the fee for a player with only one season under his belt in Europe's top leagues.
"He's the right profile but the price is a bit steep," wrote one after the signing of the 6ft 4in left-footed centre-back.
Another added: "Seems like another sensible addition although the fee is eye-watering."
Three months into a five-year contract and talk has quickly turned to how long Leeds can keep Muharemovic, such has been his impact since arriving from an impressive World Cup with Bosnia-Herzegovina.
"Muharemovic has done that well that there will already be clubs looking at him, trying to nick him over the next few months," former Leeds United striker Lucy Ward told BBC Sport.
Jonny Buchan, presenter of the BBC's Don't Go To Bed Just Yet Leeds United podcast, added: "There could be a fear he is a one-year wonder with Leeds in that he does that well in the Premier League, raises his profile that much, that clubs will come for him."
There is already reported interest from Barcelona,, external Liverpool, Bayern Munich and Inter Milan in Muharemovic, who has earned praise for his no-nonsense approach to defending as well as his aerial presence at both ends of the pitch.
Grayson, who managed Leeds from 2008 to 2012, said he has proved a "rock-like" presence and a prolonged spell at Elland Road will benefit the player in the long run.
"I'm not daft enough to think he doesn't have aspirations to one day play for some of the biggest clubs in the world," Grayson told BBC Sport.
"But right now? Sometimes a player is at home with a certain club and I get that feeling with Muharemovic. I get the impression he loves Leeds, he loves the city and he loves the supporters."
The supporters have fallen for him too - and not just because of his passionate performances on the pitch.
After Leeds hammered Newcastle 4-1 in September, Muharemovic shouted into the TV cameras "United are back, United are back".
Dubbed 'The Bosnian Brick Wall' by fans, he has helped Leeds boast the second meanest defence in the Premier League behind defending champions Arsenal.
Muharemovic may not be the finished article, but will his name be in the conversation when the time comes to discuss the Premier League signing of the season?

  - Published23 July

Caught in a World Cup storm
Muharemovic was born in Slovenia, brought up in Austria, announced himself in Italy and is now showcasing his talent in Yorkshire, having unwittingly found himself in the eye of a World Cup storm.
During Bosnia-Herzegovina's 2-0 defeat to co-hosts the United States in the last 32 on 2 July, he was fouled by Folarin Balogun, which resulted in the American forward receiving a red card after a video review by the referee.
That would normally have ruled Balogun out of the subsequent game against Belgium. However, United States President Donald Trump contacted Fifa president Gianni Infantino requesting the decision be reviewed.
A disciplinary committee then decided to suspend Balogun's ban and he played in the last-16 game, with Belgium the 4-1 victors.
"After this tackle, the media was exploding," Muharemovic told the Athletic about one of the most controversial moments in World Cup history.
"I was everywhere. Every media site. I just thank God that I came out of it without an injury."
Muharemovic's parents left Bosnia-Herzegovina during the Bosnian War, which took place between 1992 and 1995, to live in Slovenia and later moved the family to Austria.
It was there where he spent most of his childhood, but his family roots remained closely connected to Bosnian identity and language.
His professional debut came at the age of 18 for Wolfsberger in the Austrian Bundesliga in 2021.
After just six senior appearances he was snapped up by Italian giants Juventus, with Muharemovic going on to feature 57 times for their Next Gen side in Serie C, where Dean Huijsen, now at Real Madrid, was a team-mate.
Although he did not play a senior game for Juventus, he trained with the first team and learned from veteran Italy defenders Leonardo Bonucci and Giorgio Chiellini, who formed one of the most iconic defensive partnerships for over a decade, winning eight Serie A titles together for the 'Old Lady'.
"It's hard to become a first-team player at Juventus," said Muharemovic about his time in Turin.
"But when you train with them [Bonucci and Chiellini], they're the first ones who come to you, they're the first to tell you how to defend."
While at Juventus, Muharemovic made his senior Bosnia-Herzegovina debut at the age of 21 in a 3-0 friendly defeat by England at St James' Park shortly before Euro 2024.
After Juventus came Sassuolo, first on loan in 2024 and then permanently, with Muharemovic helping the team to a fine 11th place on their return to Serie A.
His talents extend beyond the pitch.
Muharemovic speaks Bosnian, German, English, Italian and Slovenian, while he frequently mentions his parents when he talks about his progress and the support he has received.
This season his father, Rasim, has been spotted standing with Leeds fans at home and away games.
"My dad loves it," said Muharemovic. "He comes to every game, every away game.
"In Italy he also went to all the home games and some of the away games, but I think this year he said he can't miss any of the Premier League games."

Leeds head to Bournemouth on Saturday (15:00 GMT) with one of the best defensive records in the Premier League after conceding six goals and registering three clean sheets in their opening eight games.
Their new number five has made more headed clearances in the top-flight this season than anyone else, and three goal contributions (one goal, two assists) in 10 league and cup appearances.
Muharemovic is aerially dominant in both boxes, while there is a finesse to his technical skills, too, as shown by a backheeled assist to Dominic Calvert-Lewin for a goal against Newcastle.

"There were a lot of eyebrows raised when Leeds sold Struijk," former Leeds and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Sport.
"The biggest compliment you can pay Muharemovic is that nobody is talking about Struijk leaving.
"Muharemovic is an example of the manager being allowed to sign players that fit into his system. He plays in a back three on the left-hand side and is left-footed.

Grayson, who led third-tier Leeds to a famous FA Cup win at fierce rivals Manchester United in 2010, added: "From the very first minute against Leipzig he looked so comfortable on the ball.
"I saw enough in the first 20 minutes of that game to think he is going to be an exceptional talent - and since then he has gone from strength to strength.
"He has a cultured left foot and hits short passes, long-range passes. Playing in a back three really suits him. He also gets what it means to be a Leeds player and what the supporters want.

It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon, Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon. This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.
Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena, now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts. Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon. The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it. Its new model also beats GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1 in almost every test. Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests. The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.

The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.
A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.
Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.
Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.
The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.
"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.
Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.
Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

A mother’s knowledge, attitude and feeding practices can significantly influence a child’s willingness to try new foods, which highlights the need for stronger nutrition counselling for caregivers during early childhood, according to a new study by researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).
Reluctance to try unfamiliar or diverse foods studied
The study, published in the Journal of Nutritional Science, examined food neophobia, a condition in which children are reluctant to try unfamiliar or diverse foods. Such behaviour can limit dietary variety and potentially affect nutritional health during crucial years of growth.
Researchers assessed 150 mother-child pairs from Addagutta in Hyderabad between August and October 2025 focusing on children aged two- seven years and explored how maternal feeding practices were associated with food neophobia and children’s nutritional status.
Findings
The findings revealed that nearly 77% of children showed moderate levels of food neophobia, while 11.3% displayed high levels and 12% had low levels. Boys recorded slightly higher food neophobia scores than girls, although the differences were not statistically significant.
Nutritional status-food acceptance link
The study also found a link between nutritional status and food acceptance. Children suffering from wasting were more likely to exhibit higher food neophobia scores than those with normal nutritional status, suggesting that reluctance to try new foods may be associated with poorer dietary outcomes.
Nutrition knowledge an important factor
Researchers observed that maternal knowledge, attitudes and practices played an important role. Children whose mothers demonstrated moderate levels of nutrition-related knowledge and positive feeding practices had lower food neophobia scores than those whose mothers had lower scores.
Karthikeyan Ramanujam, Scientist-C at ICMR-NIN and lead author of the study, said the findings underscore the importance of everyday feeding behaviours. He suggested that caregivers should repeatedly offer a variety of foods without pressure, create positive mealtime experiences and respond supportively when children reject unfamiliar foods.
ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings offer an opportunity to strengthen behavioural feeding counselling through existing government programmes such as the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and POSHAN Abhiyaan.
Researchers cautioned that the study was limited to a single urban low-income community and a relatively small sample size. They noted that, as a cross-sectional study, it identifies associations but cannot establish direct cause-and-effect relationships, as per a press release.
