How unbeaten Chelsea are getting back to their best
- Published
Chelsea's 2-0 victory over Roma in the Women's Champions League was yet another demonstration they can win in different ways.
Sonia Bompastor's side disappointed last season when they lost their Women's Super League and FA Cup crowns, while rivals Arsenal handed them an exit from Europe at the quarter-final stage.
That followed a dream unbeaten season in which the Blues wrapped up a domestic treble in Bompastor's first year in charge.
Having previously won six successive WSL titles, a blip was inevitable and their transition period highlighted flaws in the new era under their French boss.
There was still optimism in this campaign and, while Bompastor expected it would take more time, Chelsea have started impressively.
They are unbeaten in all competitions, top of the Women's Super League with Manchester City after seven games, and have won two and drawn one of their opening three Champions League phase matches.
"I'm really pleased with the results for sure, but not only the results, I think the different performances," said Bompastor earlier this week.
"Right now, the way we are performing gives us a really good advantage and a big chance to win games."
Are Blues more adaptable?
Their 2-0 victory over Roma on Wednesday was well deserved.
A flurry of chances were squandered in a dominant first half before substitute Ellie Carpenter broke the deadlock after 51 minutes.
Chelsea made sure of victory when defender Kadeisha Buchanan nodded in their second just before the end.
"I'm really pleased with the solid performances in terms of the defensive aspects. We have played three games and we haven't conceded," added Bompastor.
"When you want to go far in competitions, it's good to have this solid base. With the quality we have in the team, I'm confident we will always create opportunities."
She admitted the Champions League was "a different level" to what they had already overcome in the WSL and Bompastor has rotated her squad effectively to cope in both competitions.
They seem to have sorted out their defensive leaks that were so evident last season and look more clinical going forward.
Full-back Carpenter has four goals in all competitions, England forward Lauren James is in scintillating form and young midfielder Lexi Potter is developing a flourishing partnership with Lionesses star Keira Walsh.
They look unpredictable, being able to adapt shape in a back three or a back four, and can go direct with the aid of goalkeeper Hannah Hampton's distribution.
They had to grind out their win over Roma in a way that former boss Emma Hayes' sides used to do - proof in itself they have learned from the previous campaign.
"Even when we opened the competition against Austria Vienna, it was a tough game because they were brave and exposed us to some challenges," said Bompastor.
"We found a way to win, but obviously we want to control every game as much as we can, no matter what competition it is.
"Tonight and on Sunday we rotated the team a little bit. We find different ways to impose ourselves in the game and to score goals. That's good."
'The team's gone up another level'
Manchester City won the WSL title impressively last season but externally, there was an expectation Chelsea would bounce back.
Bompastor was more cautious, insisting they were still transitioning after the departures of big-name players including Sam Kerr, Millie Bright and Guro Reiten.
She said: "You need to consider the fact that Chelsea had the same coach for 12 years. It takes a while for players to adjust to a new coach, a new way of playing and a philosophy.
"Even if you have really good players, it doesn't just go like this. There are a lot of things we are doing behind the scenes for us to stay successful.
"I was lucky enough to come in when [Hayes] left the team in a really good place. But last season we had a year where a lot of important players left."
But captain Erin Cuthbert said she was "not really" surprised at how good their level has been so far.
"We had a good time to build in pre-season and a good trip away. The quality was always there, we just weren't clicking," she added.
"Manchester City ran away with the league in the end, but we were there or thereabouts. I feel this time the team's just gone up another level."
As well as adapting more to Bompastor's ways, and adding defensive solidity to a creative frontline, work has gone into improving the club's culture.
Cuthbert said before Wednesday's win there was "really good momentum and a good feeling" in the squad - so can they kick on now?
"For me, the mental aspects and cultural aspects are just as important," admitted Bompastor.
"We probably needed to rebuild a little bit of that going into this new season. We reflected a lot on how we wanted to set up the process for that.
"Right now, we are in a good place. When you are able to get good results, it's not only about the tactical aspects. It also has to be about mentality, culture and values.
"I think we have clarity on where we want to go as a team and how we want to get there, and that's just as important."

Cannes Marché du Film and Tokyo International Film Festival Content Market (TIFFCOM) have announced that they will co-organize the Japan IP Market in Cannes for a second consecutive year, from May 14-15.
The announcement was made at TIFFCOM during the seminar ‘Beyond Country of Honour: Building the Next Global Partnerships with Japan’, featuring Alexandra Zakharchenko, Head of Industry Programs at the Marché du Film, among the speakers.
Launched in May 2026 as part of Japan’s Country of Honour activities at the Marché du Film, the Japan IP Market brought leading Japanese rights holders together with international industry professionals through pitch sessions, targeted one-to-one meetings and industry discussions.
Participating companies included Kadokawa, Shochiku and Toei Company, while guest speakers included Filosophia Inc CEO Tetsu Fujimura, who was an executive producer on One Piece.
Watch on Deadline
Japan had a big presence at both the Cannes film festival and market this year. In addition to being selected as Country of Honor in the Marché, three Japanese films were selected for Cannes Competition and several others played in other sections of the festival. Japanese actress Tao Okamoto was a joint winner of the festival’s Best Actress award, along with Virginie Efira, for their roles in Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudden.
“The success of Japan, Country of Honour showed what can happen when a focused national presence creates lasting opportunities for the industry. The Japan IP Market is one of those outcomes: a collaboration that extends beyond a single edition and gives Japanese intellectual properties greater access to international partners,” said Guillaume Esmiol, Executive Director of the Marché du Film.
“I’m delighted that we are continuing this work with TIFFCOM to create more opportunities for rights holders to connect with international producers and partners, develop new adaptations and bring their stories to global audiences.”
Zakharchenko said: “The Japan IP Market is about creating the right conditions for business opportunities between Japanese rights holders and international companies,” says Alexandra, Head of Industry Programs at the Marché du Film. “By bringing them together in Cannes, we can help turn growing interest in Japanese content into concrete adaptation deals and acquisitions, while fostering new collaboration opportunities.”
TIFFCOM CEO Yasushi Shiina said: “Our partnership with the Marché du Film, the world’s largest film festival market, plays a significant role for Japan’s audiovisual industry. Meeting the international professionals who gather there and creating together with them is the key to nurturing Japanese IP into global content. I am grateful to the Marché du Film for its focus on Japanese IP and for co-organizing the Japan IP Market with us once again next year.”
Kaori Ikeda, TIFFCOM Managing Director, said: “At the inaugural Japan IP Market, we experienced the enthusiasm of producers and partners worldwide for Japanese IP,” adds “Through the continued partnership linking Cannes in May with the Tokyo IP Market in October, we are pleased to offer more professionals the opportunity to meet Japanese rights holders directly and discover the rich diversity of Japanese IP.”
Further details on participating companies and the 2027 program will be announced in coming months.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

For years, scientists have struggled to elucidate key biological differences between early onset colorectal cancer, typically in patients under the age of 50, and older patients. They’ve long believed that these cancers must be biologically distinct, since younger patients tend to be far more difficult to treat. They’re often diagnosed at later stages with tumors with more aggressive features.
“Their survival, especially for the very youngest patients under the age of 35, may actually not be as good as somebody in their 40s or someone in their 60s, despite receiving more aggressive treatment and being at baseline healthier,” said Kimmie Ng, a colorectal cancer researcher and director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center. “So we have always believed tumors may be biologically different.”
On Thursday, Ng published a new study in Nature Medicine that may help illuminate critical differences between older and younger colorectal cancer patients. With 189 tumors, it’s the largest biological database — what researchers call a single cell atlas — of colorectal cancer tumors in patients ranging from their 20s to their 90s. The atlas, along with the technology Ng and her colleagues used, should help researchers control for variables that confounded studies in the past.

Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia?
- Published
Second Test, Gqeberha (day three of five)
South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81
Australia 3-1: Boland 2*; Rabada 1-0
Australia trail by 422 runs
Captain Temba Bavuma dragged South Africa back into their Test series against Australia with a masterful 179 on day three in Gqeberha.
Bavuma, who emerged in the gloom at 12-2 on day one, batted for 552 minutes across three days in making his highest Test score, allowing the Proteas to declare on 425-9 with half an hour to play having been 110-6 earlier on day three.
Kagiso Rabada nicked off Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of Australia's reply to further boost the hosts' cause.
Bavuma's knock was every bit as impressive as Matthew Renshaw's 190 for Australia in their first Test win - arguably more so given the momentum that had built behind Australia since South Africa's batting struggles and the quality of the tourists' attack.
He remained composed in sharing partnerships of 132 with Marco Jansen and 183 with number nine Simon Harmer - the best eighth-wicket partnership in South Africa's Test history.
The century was Bavuma's fifth in Tests - 10 years after his first made him the first Black African to score a Test hundred for the Proteas.
He said it was "definitely" one of his best innings.
"That bowling attack, at least three are in the top 10 of the bowling rankings," he added. "There is a reason why."
More relevant for this series and England's tour to come over Christmas, it was Bavuma's fourth century in 14 Tests as South Africa captain.
He now averages 54.36 as Test skipper, compared with 34.53 across 93 innings before taking the reins. Few can match that improvement.
Should South Africa have declared earlier?
It was Bavuma's dismissal - caught behind off Mitchell Starc - which triggered South Africa's decision to declare with half an hour to go in the day.
They had resisted doing so earlier in the session and when Harmer was bowled by Marnus Labuschagne a ball before the Bavuma wicket.
With the floodlights on and skies dark, conditions were perfect for seam bowling when Australia's reply began. Maddinson was only able to resist four deliveries before nicking to third slip.
The umpires then deemed the light too poor for seam bowling to continue, however, and after three overs of spin with the new ball the players left the field.
Had South Africa declared earlier, Jansen could have bowled in tandem with Rabada in the gloom.
"There was thought of that," Bavuma said. "I was a little hesitant because of the weather.
"If we [had declared] a bit early we would have got one or two more overs. Saying that we got the one we wanted.
"Right now I hope things go our way and we set ourselves to be on the field for the majority of those two days."
After only 42 overs were possible across the first two days, South Africa now have an outside shot at victory over days four and five, ideally by dismissing Australia cheaply and enforcing the follow-on.
"We have given ourselves a chance," Bavuma said.
"There is the other side of the draw but going into [the third Test in] Cape Town whatever the confidence we can get here, being able to put their bowlers on their feet for a considerable amount of time, hopefully that can pay off in the long run."

The Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO. In picture: WHO Director-General Dr Tedros and Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers. ©WHO
The Netherlands strengthened its longstanding engagement with WHO on Monday with the renewal of the multiannual contribution of the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to WHO for €13.34 million for 2024–2028 and for €6 million to the technical partnership with Dutch WHO collaborating centres.
With the new contribution, the Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO.
"Amid increasingly complex and connected threats, from pandemics and climate change to conflicts, the Netherlands remains an essential supporter of WHO and global public health," said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus during the agreement signing.
"The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's new contribution reflects the Netherland's commitment to its long partnership with WHO, and its support of the sustainable financing for WHO that Member States have agreed. This will enable WHO to respond quickly to global health challenges, and strengthen public health worldwide, including in the Netherlands."
Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers added that “the Netherlands values our strong and long-standing relationship with WHO. Given the global challenges we collectively face, and the added value the Netherlands can deliver, we believe this renewed arrangement with long-term flexible funds well represents our commitment to advancing health worldwide. These funds will be used to achieve our shared priorities in the WHO’s General Programme of Work, facilitate the secondment of Dutch experts, and to support the Dutch WHO collaborating centres.”
The Netherlands recently recommitted to its role as a leading voice for global health through its Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030. The strategy aims to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has provided for many years critical financial and technical support to WHO’s efforts to strengthen health security, improve the capacities of countries to address health emergencies, fight antimicrobial resistance, promote access to medicines, and support food safety, tobacco control and mental health.
The renewed partnership expands the joint work of the Netherlands and WHO into new global health challenges, such as those posed by climate change.
The interconnection between the health of the Earth and human health makes climate change a fundamental threat to decades of progress on health. The joint work of the Netherlands and WHO aims to make healthcare more climate resilient and sustainable while mainstreaming health into internal climate policies.

US-based Innodata has become the latest company to lay off a big chunk of its staff in India. The AI services company reportedly axed nearly 550 jobs in the country, nearly 5% of its global workforce. According to a termination email reviewed by India Today, the company cited a “ramp-down of the (a) business assignment” as the reason for the layoffs. It also noted that the decision was not linked to individual performance. Simply put, a major client likely pulled the plug on a massive project and Innodata responded by slashing the costs associated with that project. The extent of the layoffs, the teams involved and the status of the affected client assignments remain unclear. Inc42 has reached out to the company seeking more clarity on this. The story will be updated on receiving a response. As per the report, the impacted employees lost access to official IDs and internal systems in the middle of the workday on Monday (October 26), followed by termination emails sent to their personal email accounts. Many employees had, as usual, reportedly logged in and marked their attendance before reports of layoffs started circulating around lunchtime. As workers sought clarity from their managers and HR teams, access to company systems was gradually withdrawn, the report said. The email also noted the impacted employee's full and final settlement had been prepared through a demand draft, which would be handed over once company-assigned assets are returned. Separately, the AI services company has also reportedly laid off an undisclosed number of employees in the Philippines. Founded in 1988, US-based Innodata provides data engineering and AI services, including data labelling, model training, evaluation and safety testing. The company lists Google, Microsoft and Amazon among its clients. Innodata had 10,107 employees globally at the end of December 2025. The development comes amid a broader wave of workforce adjustments across the tech sector as companies reassess their operations and staffing requirements due to AI-led automation. Earlier this month, ecommerce giant Amazon reportedly laid off at least 100 employees in India as part of its latest global job cuts. Before that, it was also reported that Oracle was preparing to lay off thousands of employees globally, with India expected to be among the markets affected by the planned cuts.

Charging points in trains to remain off 11 pm-5 am
The Railway Board has reiterated its instructions to switch off electricity supply to power sockets in train between 11pm and 5am after a passenger’s power bank exploded while charging aboard the Mumbai-Howrah Mail in Odisha on October 24, disrupting train operations.
The incident occurred around 3.38am in an AC coach when a passenger’s power bank exploded, caught fire and released smoke. The12809 Mumbai-Howrah Mail was halted for around 15 minutes near Bandamunda station before resuming its journey at 3.53am.
In a letter dated October 26, the Railway Board directed all zonal railways to ensure strict compliance with existing instructions on switching off mobile charging points during night hours.
The letter, addressed to the principal chief mechanical engineers of all zonal railways, stated, “Recently, an instance has occurred in SER wherein onboard staff has not switched off the mobile charging points during the aforesaid period. Subsequently during charging a passenger’s power bank exploded with smoke.”
It further read, “In view of the above, all Zonal Railways are advised to issue necessary Instructions to all concerned staff to ensure strict compliance for mobile charging points to invariably remain switched off from 11.00 PM to 05.00 AM. No exception should be permitted on this account”
On June 19, 2014, the Board had introduced instructions for railway staff to switch off charging points between 11 pm and 5 am after the Commissioner of Railway Safety (CRS)’s recommendation that followed a 2013 fire incident in an AC 3-tier coach of the Hazur Sahib Nanded- KSR Bengaluru Express in the Bengaluru division of the South Western Railway zone.
To be sure, the South East Central Railway issued similar instructions to all its divisions in March this year too.
“No exception should be permitted on this account,” the letter stated, directing zonal railways to issue necessary instructions to all concerned staff to ensure that charging points invariably remain switched off during the specified hours.
The Board also called for staff to be counselled, instructed and trained to ensure effective implementation of the directions. It also asked railway officials and supervisors to conduct surprise inspections to ensure strict compliance with these instructions.
Besides the SER incident, a passenger’s power bank exploded in a Mumbai AC local last week.
A similar fire incident occurred in a sleeper-class coach of the New Delhi-Darbhanga Humsafar Clone Special in the North Central Railway area in November 2023 when the fire spread throughout the coach and engulfed the adjoining coaches.

A hacker stole a trove of personal information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The breach exposes the names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, including those in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), according to TechCrunch and Wired. The data also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools.
A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records
The names, job titles, phone numbers, and emails of thousands of ICE, CBP, and other DHS employees were compromised in a massive hack.
As reported by TechCrunch, a hacker known as “Department of Peace” gained access to the data through Okta, an identity and access management service used by the DHS. Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE. The data also includes records from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
The DHS has worked to conceal the identities of CBP and ICE agents, who have carried out anti-immigration raids around the US, while also tracking down online critics. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the “Department of Peace” hacker said, according to TechCrunch. This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants.
The leaked DHS information was reportedly given to cybersecurity researcher maia arson crimew, who shared it with Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit organization that’s now hosting the leaked “Icepick” dataset. The leak also reportedly includes information about DHS groups that have access to tools that can be used for surveillance, such as the facial recognition app Mobile Fortify and PenLink, which can collect and analyze data from phones and online services.
The DHS didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

FCC chair wants to let prisons jam illegal cellphones
The agency will vote next month on relaxing its long-standing opposition to jammers.
The US Federal Communications Commission announced today that it will vote on a new rule that would allow state prisons and jails to use cellphone jammers. The goal of the change would be to block use of illegal cellphones by inmates, since having outside contact could allow them to continue engaging in criminal activity.
The planned vote during the agency's open meeting on November 19 would consider allowing state and local incarceration facilities to opt in to using jammers; use of the tech would not be required. Any tech that interferes with communications signals is illegal for non-federal parties to use. In 2018, the Federal Bureau of Prisons began testing "micro-jamming" in federal prisons as a way to block unauthorized cellphone use by inmates. This move would potentially open up similar tools at the state and local levels, and provide a formal pathway for federal facilities to jam signals as well.
It's a reversal from previous policies where the FCC has not allowed implementing jammers as a method of reducing illegal cellphone use in prisons. Previous concerns about jammers suggested the tech could interfere with emergency and public safety communications, as well as creating new security risks by putting more jamming tools into the wild where they could be exploited by bad actors. The bulletin today notes that if the new rules are adopted, correctional facilities would need to meet some standards, including proving "that the jamming solution does not cause harmful interference outside of the designated geographic areas."
Today's move isn't the first time the FCC has changed its approach toward prisons under the current administration. In July 2025, the department said it would delay implementing a cap on the rates charged for prison phone calls.

The recent conversation over the merchant discount rate on select UPI transactions raised the question of who pays for the digital convenience that millions of people enjoy. Hospitals may soon face a similar problem for strengthening their privacy even if no separate “privacy charge” appears on a patient’s bill.
Protecting digital patient information will require secure systems, trained personnel, and continuous compliance. Parliament enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 in response to this need. The Act consists of 44 sections in nine chapters plus one Schedule. The government notified its Rules on November 13, 2025, with the Sections pertaining to provisions for consent managers set to kick in from November 13, 2026. The rest of the substantive obligations will start to apply from May 13, 2027.
Unusually difficult places
The Act is a general framework to protect digital personal data across sectors, including healthcare. In healthcare, the Act recognises that clinical consent and data consent are different. For example, a person agreeing to undergo a medical scan does not automatically mean they have agreed to every later use of the same scan, no matter how useful the hospital or doctors deem the scan data to be. While facilitating this distinction, the Act also makes room for data-processing during emergencies and specific medico-legal and public health situations.
Under the DPDP Act, the patient is the data principal (or owner) and the hospital — which usually decides why and how some information will be used — is the data fiduciary. Some external software, cloud, and/or data-processing company will serve as the data processor.
That said, hospitals are unusually difficult places in which to ensure compliance with a general data-protection law. Unlike banks or regional transport offices, hospitals continuously create information of an intimate nature. For example, healthcare workers record a patient’s clinical notes, nursing observations, diagnostics and laboratory results, ventilator readings, and prescriptions — all within hours.
At the same time, several professionals will need to access different parts of that record at different times. If access is too tightly controlled, patient care may suffer; on the other hand, unrestricted access can result in significant breaches of privacy. So the Act needs to facilitate the lawful processing of consent with reasonable security safeguards, grievance handling processes, and of course the correction or erasure of data where permissible.
Failure to take reasonable safeguards can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore.
Compliance costs
In the same vein, compliance requires hospital information systems with role-based access, facility to encrypt or mask data as necessary, systems to generate and preserve audit logs, backups, vendor contracts, breach response protocols, staff training, and a clearly identified person who is responsible for data governance.
Entities designated data fiduciaries must also appoint a statutory data protection officer, and smaller hospitals will need a privacy or data management lead in practice.
Further, information rarely stays within the hospital, since a cashless claim can send diagnoses and reports to an insurer or a third party administrator. Laboratories, radiology platforms, cloud vendors, and telemedicine services will create additional routes for the same record. Even low-cost WhatsApp-based workflows that became popular because they were convenient will have to be examined for compliance and security.
Healthcare may therefore need specific DPDP provisions, either explicitly or eventually as a separate Act, to cover sector-specific uniqueness, such as small hospitals and large hospitals separately, as clinical care is more than a commercial transaction.
Lesson from Chandigarh
U.S. estimates show the cost of complying with the famed Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, to be around $5 per patient a year in 2008. Estimates for 2025 suggest the cost of $498 per affected record.
In a 2023 study, researchers from India and Norway estimated that adding an integrated information and communications system to an urban primary health centre (PHC) would expand the centre’s annual economic budget by 17.7%. But when the researchers applied the same model across 400 PHCs, the incremental cost fell to about 6% per PHC. The reason: common development and infrastructure costs were shared.
The finding offers an important policy clue: the government should not expect every small hospital, diagnostic centre, and/or PHC to independently purchase the same privacy tools, legal templates, and so on.
That said, the harder problem is that India has legislated faster than it has trained the people who must make the law work. Medical education teaches confidentiality and ethics, but there is no uniform DPDP-oriented National Medical Commission curriculum or standard course materials that span medicine, nursing, allied health, hospital administration, and healthcare IT training.
The vendor side faces the same problem: behind every software workflow is a human being who configures access, checks claims, handles support or views data. And an untrained person handling data in a hospital can pave the way for a major breach due so little as to one leaked password. So data literacy has to become a core healthcare competency.
Building an ecosystem
The National Health Accounts 2022-23 released this year estimated the out-of-pocket expenses on healthcare to be 43.4% of total health expenditure. There is a nontrivial chance that the new costs of complying with the DPDP Act will be passed on to patients as well.
Ahead of the November 13 date, the Indian government should step in by enabling a shared infrastructure through the Unified Health Interface of the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. It could provide model consent and vendor agreements with affordable cybersecurity support, and healthcare-specific implementation standards.
User data is routinely commoditised today, and passing a law assuming compliance and waiting for complaints or litigation will not suffice. As the DPDP Act comes into effect, the government must finance, build, and sustain an ecosystem that allows every health worker to comply and patients to be able to better access care.
Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. Views expressed here are personal.

Hackers leaked details of more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel
They include email addresses and phone numbers of ICE agents and border police.
A hacktivist group stole records for more than 41,000 Homeland Security personnel and got help to release it on the web, according to Wired, the Washington Post and NPR. The leaked records contain email addresses, phone numbers and office addresses of the personnel, but they also include sensitive information about the agency's undercover and surveillance programs.
Of the records that were leaked, 21,000 identify people working with the US Customs and Border Protection, while 10,000 records belong to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel. A third of those records is related to the Homeland Security Investigations unit, the criminal investigative arm of ICE. Overall, the leaks expose the details of a seventh of Homeland Security's workforce.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace said in a statement. They're talking about the DHS' Secretary's words during a press conference, wherein he said that the agency is "turning up the heat on the streets" when asked how it would hold the agents who violated its use of force policy accountable. The agency held the press conference following the fatal shootings of Joan Sebastian Duran Guerrero from Maine and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo from Houston, neither of whom were subject to ICE's enforcement activities.
The group apparently stole the data via Okta, the single sign-on service used by the DHS. With Okta, users just have to sign on once with their credentials to get full access to a system's backend, cloud service and/or mobile apps. Okta told Wired that it has found no evidence that its "data or systems were compromised." The hackers shared the data with transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and a Swiss cybersecurity researcher called maia arson crimew. They created a searchable online database using the information the Department of Peace had provided.
"They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," the hackers wrote in a note with the stolen records. The Distributed Denial of Secrets is calling the database "Icepick." Its founder, Emma Best, said the records contain links between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations ...along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."
Meanwhile, a Homeland Security spokesperson said it is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." They added: "We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available."

While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).
In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.
Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.
The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu. “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”
The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.
The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu. Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.
The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.
The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.
Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.
Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.
The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff says it is "extremely satisfying" to see Kimi Antonelli's turnaround from last year as the Italian looks to secure the 2026 Formula 1 world title this weekend in Mexico.

Wolff recalls the 2025 Belgian Grand Prix as a particular low moment when Antonelli was in tears after being eliminated in Q1.

"I think maybe it was to his benefit that the regulations were all new. When last year he came in and those cars existed, those cars existed for four years. The other drivers were used to it," he said.

Antonelli admits his success has been a "good surprise" but Mercedes have played a pivotal role in his quick development over the last 18 months.

Engadget is hiring writers!

'He knows his role' - Rulli provides heroics but no worries for Donnarumma
- Published
Geronimo Rulli's penalty shootout heroics against Brighton in the Carabao Cup may have some questioning Gianluigi Donnarumma's spot at Manchester City, but manager Enzo Maresca has no doubt about his number one.
Rulli returned to the club in the summer from Marseille for a modest £1.7m to feature as a back-up to the Italy captain, but seemed to press his claims to challenge the jersey with an impressive display.
The 34-year-old dived full stretch to his left to save the last two penalties from Brighton's Yasin Ayari and Lewis Dunk to allow holders City to progress to the quarter-finals of the competition.
The match had ended 2-2 in normal time and would not have gone all the way had Rulli not made a sensational fingertip save to deny Georginio Rutter in the second half.
Veteran Rulli will be back on the bench though for this weekend's Premier League game against the same opposition - despite Donnarumma's form being questioned by many in recent weeks.
When asked if Rulli had put pressure on Donnarumma's spot, Maresca told BBC Sport: "No, absolutely not from my point of view.
"He is working well but Rulli knows exactly his role, there is no doubt about that. Saturday it will be Gigio plus 10."
'Overall he was good'
Rulli is no stranger to being the hero in a penalty shootout.
In the 2021 Europa League final, he famously scored a penalty for Villarreal against Manchester United, before denying opposite number David de Gea to decide the marathon shootout and the destiny of the trophy.
If Rulli had not already ingratiated himself to City supporters with that moment against their rivals, then he will have rubberstamped the affection on Wednesday night.
The goalkeeper had spent the 2016-17 season at City without making a first-team appearance and returned to the club to replace James Trafford after the England international moved to Leeds for £45m.
It looks to be a canny piece of business from City.
In the pre-match news conference, Maresca said Rulli was "doing well" and "knows exactly his role" as understudy to Donnarumma, and that message was re-iterated after the game.
Along with Erling Haaland, Ruben Dias, Elliot Anderson and Josko Gvardiol, Italian Donnarumma has been given three days off to "recover the energy" and Maresca will be hoping he returns to training this week rejuvenated.
Donnarumma was at fault for Aston Villa's second goal last weekend and Maresca acknowledged he has been "making some mistakes".
"Apart from penalties, overall he was good especially in the build-up," Maresca said of Rulli. "It was not easy because they are a team that go man to man and are aggressive.
"In the first half, we tried some long solutions with Floyd [Samba] and then in the second half we tried on the floor with Phil [Foden]. He made one good save and was good."
Big chance for City to go all the way again
Maresca shook up his starting line-up by making nine changes to the side that were beaten at Aston Villa on Saturday and it almost backfired.
City had twice fallen behind to goals from Malick Yalcouye and Georginio Rutter, but the hosts showed their battling spirit to draw level through Mateo Kovavic and Vitor Reis.
But the result continues Maresca's impressive start as manager, losing only against Villa and Paris St-Germain, as well as Arsenal in the Community Shield.
The Gunners were knocked out of the League Cup and so were Chelsea which means City will continue their quest to retain their trophy, coming up against Bradford in the quarter-finals.
Asked if it a big opportunity to go all the way again, Maresca said: "Absolutely.
"It's a different competition but the ambition has to be the same: this is a new project, new players, a new manager who started three months ago and we need to do our business and that is winning games.
"At the moment we are doing that."

- The claim that rapper Nicki Minaj is not a United States citizen is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from X and TikTok posts claiming that even though Minaj is expressing her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and encouraging voters to support Republicans in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote.
- In January, Minaj — who was born in Trinidad and Tobago — stated that she was not a citizen, but was "finalizing" her citizenship application. In the same post, she suggested she was instead a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green-card holder, writing "Residency?" She has not given any more updates on her status since then. Noncitizens, including permanent legal residents, cannot vote in federal or state elections and most local elections.
- Since a person's immigration record is not publicly available, we were unable to confirm Minaj's immigration status using primary evidence as of this writing.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Minaj's record label, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, and await responses.
As rapper Nicki Minaj expressed her support for U.S. President Donald Trump and joined him at a Republican campaign rally in late October, many people questioned (archived) her own citizenship status.
Numerous posts (archived) claimed that while Minaj called on voters to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections, she herself cannot vote because she isn't a citizen.
One X user wrote, "The GOP is telling people to 'vote red' with Nicki Minaj as the messenger. Problem is, she can't even vote. She's not a U.S. citizen."
Minaj wrote in a Jan. 28 X post that she was "finalizing" her citizenship paperwork. In the same post, she suggested she was a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green-card holder. Noncitizens, including permanent legal residents, cannot vote in federal or state elections and most local elections.
Since a person's immigration record is not publicly available, we were unable to confirm Minaj's immigration status using primary evidence as of this writing.
We also reached out to her record label, the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to learn more, and will update this story if we receive responses. Until then, we leave this claim unrated.
On Jan. 28, Minaj wrote on X:
Residency? Residency? The cope is coping. 😅
Finalizing that citizenship paperwork as we speak as per MY wonderful, gracious, charming President. 
Thanks to the petition. 📋 
I wouldn't have done it without you. 
Oh CitizenNIKA you are thee moment
Gold Trump card free of charge
Minaj was referring to the Trump administration's "gold card" visa, which guarantees foreigners U.S. residency for a $1 million fee. In January, The New York Times reported that, per a Department of Homeland Security official, Minaj has been a legal permanent resident in the U.S. for over two decades, meaning she likely would not need to apply for a gold card.
In a 2024 TikTok livestream, Minaj said she was "not a citizen" despite paying "millions of dollars" in taxes.
In 2018, while posting about children in immigration detention centers, Minaj said on Facebook that she "came to this country as an illegal immigrant @ 5 years old." She was born in Trinidad and Tobago. In the same post, she wrote, "Please stop this. Can you try to imagine the terror & panic these kids feel right now?" 
Citizenship applications can take around 12 months to process and timing varies based on the applicant's primary city of residence. Assuming Minaj uses Los Angeles as her primary residence, where she has a home, the process could take more than a year, according to processing times on USCIS website. Given that she has a close relationship with Trump, it is possible her application could be expedited.
On Oct. 25, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted a video of Minaj in Air Force One, pretending to be the new White House press secretary and praising Trump.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on the unsupported rumor that Minaj was the only "Trump gold card" visa recipient, and the claim that her husband is a registered sex offender.

China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
- Published
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
What is a plenum?
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
What is on the agenda this year?
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Ecommerce major Meesho reported a 68% decline in its consolidated net loss to ₹132.5 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹411.4 Cr in the year-ago period as its revenue growth outpaced increase in expenses.However, net loss remained largely unchanged from ₹132.8 Cr in the June quarter.
Operating revenue rose 34% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹4,131.6 Cr. Including other income of ₹127.4 Cr, Meesho’s total income stood at ₹4,259 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 31% from ₹3,254.9 Cr a year ago.
Meesho incurred exceptional expenses in the last year quarter which it didn’t incur this year, leading to the sharp annual reduction in loss. In Q2 FY26, Meesho incurred exceptional expenses of ₹45 Cr towards a business combination and a vendor dispute settlement, besides a ₹64.4 Cr tax charge related to the business combination. Neither charge recurred in the quarter under review.
Before exceptional items and tax, its loss narrowed by 57% to ₹123.3 Cr from ₹285.5 Cr a year earlier.
Meanwhile, Meesho’s total expenses increased 24% to ₹4,382.3 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹3,540.4 Cr. (The story will be updated soon)

Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.
The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.
A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.
“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.
They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.
Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.
The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
Former CIA deputy director’s call to repeal Obama-era ban on economic espionage comes as Beijing rushes to protect trade secrets
A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China.
“The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month.
“By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.”

Mumbai Indians has announced that Lasith Malinga, Paras Mhambrey and Carl Hopkinson will leave their respective roles in the men’s team coaching setup.

North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
South Korea says North Korea has launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the sea
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters Thursday, South Korea’s military said, days after the North threatened to resume front-line propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy new weapons along the rivals’ tense border.
The launches also followed leader Kim Jong Un’s surprise weekend visit to China, the North's main ally and economic pipeline, to push for greater cooperation.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected about 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the North's eastern costal town of Wonsan and that they each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles). It said South Korea's military maintained its readiness to repel any provocations by North Korea under a solid alliance with the United States.
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected ballistic missile launch by North Korea.
Animosity between the Koreas have deepened since last month’s land mine blasts at the border that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of planting mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded it apologize. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea said it would restart propaganda broadcasts and place new weapons systems on alert along the border in protest of what it called repeated warning shots by South Korean troops at border areas. South Korea later proposed talks on clarifying the border to prevent accidental clashes, but North Korea hasn't responded.
During a visit to a South Korean border town earlier this week, Associated Press journalists saw North Korean artillery guns located on the other side of the border, which weren't previously visible.
In recent years, North Korea has been placing more mines, barbed-wire fences and other defense structures along the border in line with Kim's policy of severing ties with South Korea. Seoul has said North Korean troops have repeatedly violated the border during the work and that South Korea's military has responded with firing warning shots. North Korea has denied the alleged border breaches.
Thursday's launches were the latest in a series of weapons tests by North Korea in recent weeks, which included submarine-launched cruise missiles and hypersonic missiles. Experts say North Korea likely aimed to pressure the U.S. into making bigger concessions as President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim.
On Saturday, Kim visited the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly inaugurated bridge to pay respect at a memorial marking China’s support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War. It was his sixth visit to China since succeeding his father as North Korean leader in late 2011.
At the memorial, Kim said North Korea will firmly carry forward “the invincible" friendship with China. Later he met top Chinese Communist Party official Wang Huning and reaffirmed his resolve to develop bilateral cooperation.
Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China after years of prioritizing ties with Russia by sending troops and ammunitions to support its war against Ukraine.

My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people.
 
John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999.
 
Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008).
 
Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023), with effect from October 17. The move has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
The MSMER-2023 was withdrawn with immediate effect through a notification dated October 14, published in the Gazette on October 17. There is no single new regulation replacing MSMER 2023. Instead, the requirement for medical colleges to submit Annual Disclosure Reports (ADRs) will continue under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other applicable regulations, the NMC said.
Rules on penalties, enforcement removed
The withdrawal comes close on the heels of a nationwide agitation for greater accountability in the undergraduate medical entrance examination.
Healthcare activists and medical education experts have raised concerns about three key areas that may fall through the gaps with the withdrawal of these regulations: the alleged removal of specific penalties under MSMER-2023, including fines of up to ₹1 crore for specified violations and personal fines of up to ₹5 lakh for faculty and administrators submitting false records; the verification of colleges’ annual disclosures on faculty, infrastructure, clinical facilities, and patient load; and the removal of the specific procedures and timelines for enforcement and appeals laid out in the MSMER-2023.
‘Patients at risk’
Bejon Kumar Misra, consumer rights activist and founder-director of the Patient Safety and Access Initiative of India Foundation (PSAIIF), said the withdrawal raised concerns about transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education.
While the NMC Act, 2019, provides statutory powers for inspections and enforcement, Prof. Misra said that withdrawing a detailed regulatory framework without clarifying equivalent safeguards creates uncertainty over how institutional deficiencies and false disclosures will be addressed.
“Medical colleges cannot be judged merely by their buildings, equipment, or number of approved seats. The real measure of medical education is the competence of graduating doctors, the availability of qualified faculty, adequate supervised clinical exposure, and their ability to deliver safe and ethical patient care,” he said.
Prof. Misra has also written to the Union government, warning that misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk. He urged the Union Health Ministry and the NMC to clarify the enforcement mechanisms that will remain in place and to ensure that medical education standards are independently verifiable.
‘Dilution of regulatory oversight’
Babu K.V., an ophthalmologist and medical activist, said the withdrawal could dilute the penalty framework. He explained that by denotifying the stronger MSMER 2023 September regulation and retaining the June regulation, some clauses have been deleted.
“Like the clause 8(2)c, which states that monetary penalty not exceeding ₹5 lakh [will be imposed] for the faculty/Head of the Department (HoD)/Dean/Director/doctor submitting false declaration/documents/records (including patients’ records). Further, they can also be charged or penalised for misconduct under the Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations in vogue,” he said.
“This is the key regulation ,where the individual doctors are made accountable and hence deleting it is dilution of regulatory oversight,” Dr. Babu explained, refuting the NMC’s argument that there is no dilution of regulatory oversight.
‘Eliminates duplication’
However, a senior NMC official told The Hindu that the decision had been “misinterpreted”. The withdrawal followed a review by the Commission’s legal team, which recommended streamlining regulatory powers and removing overlapping responsibilities, the official said.
The Commission functions through four autonomous boards, of which two set standards for undergraduate and postgraduate medical education. Another assesses and rates medical colleges and undertakes institutional inspections and regulatory action, while the fourth oversees medical registration, professional conduct, and ethics.
The NMC maintains that the move eliminates duplication without diluting standards, and that its inspection and verification powers remain intact.
Not retrospective
The Gazette notification provides that the withdrawal will not affect actions already taken, approvals granted, or rights, obligations and liabilities accrued under MSMER-2023. Applications, proceedings, appeals and inquiries pending before the withdrawal will continue to be dealt with under the regulations, insofar as applicable. Matters arising after the withdrawal will be governed by the NMC Act and the statutory and regulatory provisions then in force.
India had 846 medical colleges, 1,39,864 MBBS seats and 86,360 postgraduate medical seats, according to government data cited in August 2026. “With medical education expanding, the key question is whether the regulatory framework that remains can ensure that colleges meet prescribed standards and face effective action when they fail to do so,’’ Dr. Babu said.

Australian sunscreen brands face stricter rules after safety scandal
- Published
Australian sunscreen manufacturers will be subject to stricter rules in the wake of a safety scandal that saw popular brands pulled off shelves.
The reforms, announced by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on Tuesday, include stronger testing and quality requirements for specific ingredients.
This comes after a bombshell report last year by consumer advocacy group Choice which found that some popular sunscreens did not provide the level of protection their manufacturers claimed.
The new proposed regulations are "about making SPF claims more reliable" and giving the agency "faster access to evidence when concerns arise", Robyn Langham, the TGA's chief medical adviser, tells the BBC.
"Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence," she said in a statement over email.
"These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation, with stronger testing requirements for the finished product consumers buy and repeat testing throughout its time on the market."
Under the new regulations proposed by the TGA, cosmetic sunscreen brands will also be limited in the skin protection factor (SPF) claims they can make.
This is to ensure "clear distinction for consumers" between sunscreens that are mainly made for UV protection and cosmetic products where UV protection is a secondary function.
Suppliers would also be required to provide their SPF testing data to the TGA when they list a sunscreen, and keep periodically testing the product throughout its shelf life.
Under current regulations, it's not mandatory for sunscreen manufacturers to provide testing data to the TGA unless requested.
The TGA said the reforms would be "implemented in stages, with further consultation where required".
The Choice report, published in June 2025, found that 16 of 20 tested sunscreens - including several premium, expensive brands - failed to live up to their advertised SPF rating.

One product, Ultra Violette's Lean Screen Skinscreen, which was voluntarily recalled last year, was marketed as having an SPF of 50+ but was found to offer only SPF 4.
The scandal sparked massive backlash in Australia, which has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world.
More than a dozen products were pulled from shelves or had their sales suspended as a result of the scandal.
The TGA proposed sweeping reforms to the sunscreen industry earlier this year, which included plans to make sunscreen labelling simpler and more oversight at testing labs.
Its statement on Tuesday said that changes to labelling would be made after further review and consultation.
Choice welcomed the reforms, saying in a statement on Tuesday that it was "pleased to see" the stricter rules proposed by the TGA.
However, the group pointed out that the TGA has not proposed to "routinely monitor and evaluate test results".
Choice also argued that that sunscreen test results should not be provided only to the TGA - as proposed by the regulator - but rather made publicly available and routinely monitored, "in the interest of transparency and public safety".
