Several companies produce animal-free egg white protein in the U.S. Some of these products have been available since 2021. The EVERY Company made its OvoPro product available to consumers in March 2026. The FDA said in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding The EVERY Company's declaration that the protein ingredient in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were omitting it from their product ingredient lists. Federal law governs what must appear on ingredients labels. An OvoPro spokesperson said the EVERY Company had not sought an exemption from OvoPro being included in ingredients lists and provided guidance to companies about how to list it.
It was also unclear whether OvoPro and products like it that are grown using yeast qualify as "lab-grown." That classification usually describes products that grow actual animal cells, which OvoPro does not.
In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that U.S. consumers could buy federally approved "lab-grown" eggs that brands were secretly including in their products.
For example, one Facebook user shared a video about the alleged lab grown eggs in which two speakers said:
Lab-grown eggs are federally approved and Walmart, alongside Target, are already selling them. The protein is squeezed out of gene-edited mold and cloned on repeat because a steel tank costs less than a hen.
They're brewing eggs with no chicken in sight and slipping them onto your breakfast plate. That egg isn't real food, it's factory fungus, spliced with the gene for egg protein then dumped into giant fermenting vats and fed on sugar until it swells into a wet, moldy soup. And it gets worse: that cloudy sludge is blasted into dust, ton after ton, padded out with plant filler and passed off as egg white, then buried in packaged foods under labels that never say so. At Walmart, two or more of these lab egg products already sit on the shelf.
The video also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). It included shots of the packaging for OvoPro, an egg protein The EVERY Company produces. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim, asking questions like, "Are there such a thing as Lab grown eggs being sold in secret?"
The claim was a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
Though it was true that egg proteins grown using yeast rather than chickens were available to U.S. consumers in October 2026, products like OvoPro were not new to the market. The EVERY Company, which produces OvoPro, also did not appear to be the only company selling animal-free egg protein to consumers in the U.S.
OvoPro was not FDA "cleared" or "approved" — the latter of which is generally a status reserved for drugs, not food. Rather, in October 2023, the FDA responded with a "no questions" letter to The EVERY Company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that retailers could decide not to list the animal-free egg protein as an ingredient in products that contained it, as some claimed. Federal legislation governs what must appear on ingredients labels. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said via email on Aug. 21 that the company had not sought to exempt OvoPro from ingredients lists.
Additionally, it was unclear whether OvoPro and other yeast-grown egg proteins could correctly be called "lab-grown," a classification that usually describes products grown from a small sample of the source, as seen with fish, poultry and meat. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said:
OvoPro is made through precision fermentation: a yeast (Komagataella phaffii) is given the genetic instructions to produce egg-white protein, and it does so during fermentation. No animal cells, and no chicken, are involved at any point.
What is egg protein grown by yeast?
According to its website, The EVERY Company uses a patented method to produce ovalbumin, the dominant protein in egg whites, through precision fermentation.
The company described this process as "programming" yeast to produce egg protein through fermentation, a process familiar from beer brewing.
It said the process eventually results in "a pure, powdered protein that is tasteless, colorless, sugar-free, and can be used to replace the functionality of eggs and egg whites in a range of applications."
The EVERY Company received its patent for its method of precision fermentation in September 2024. The company, previously known as Clara Foods, has been working to develop animal-free egg protein since at least 2021.
It unveiled EVERY ClearEgg, a predecessor to OvoPro, in October 2021. The EVERY Company received a "no questions" letter in September 2021 in response to its GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) determination for ClearEgg.
The FDA's GRAS Notification program allows companies to submit documentation that they believe their product is "safe under the conditions of its intended use." In the case of ClearEgg, the FDA said in a letter on Sept. 9, 2021, that it had "no questions," meaning The EVERY Company could market ClearEgg as "Generally Recognized as Safe."
The EVERY Company got another "no questions" letter in response to a GRAS determination for an egg white protein produced by Komagataella phaffii, a species of yeast, in October 2023. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said on Aug. 21, 2026, that this GRAS notice was for the egg-white protein in OvoPro.
Company sold animal-free eggs before 2026
OvoPro and related products have been available to consumers since at least 2021, meaning they were not new to the U.S. market in October 2026, as some claims appeared to suggest. For example, in November 2021, The Spoon, an outlet that reports on the food tech industry, reported that smoothies containing ClearEgg had hit the market.
The next year, The EVERY Company reportedly sold its EggWhite product in macarons and Every Protein (formerly ClearEgg) in juice. By January 2024, the New York Times wrote that The EVERY Company had showcased EveryEgg, a "yellow vegan plant-based liquid" that the paper said, "behaves astonishingly like a whole beaten egg."
It did not appear that The EVERY Company sold EveryEgg directly to consumers at that point, but rather distributed the product through restaurants.
The new development in 2026 appeared to be that The EVERY Company was selling OvoPro, a successor to EveryEgg, directly to consumers. The company announced on March 11, 2026, that the general public could buy OvoPro through Healthier Comforts, a food retailer, and Amazon.
The company said in June that same year that OvoPro was also available as an ingredient sold in Walmart and Target.
Brands not hiding use of animal-free egg protein
According to some claims, brands could allegedly decide for themselves whether to declare OvoPro as an ingredient in their products. The video above said that companies "buried" their "lab-grown" eggs in "packaged foods under labels that never say so"The EVERY Company's website page on OvoPro said, in reply to a frequently asked question about how the protein appears on ingredient declarations, that "Final labeling decisions are made by our customers, but we recommend labeling OvoPro™ as 'egg white protein (from fermentation),' 'egg white protein (from yeast),' or 'animal-free egg white protein.'"
That did not appear to mean that brands that used OvoPro in their products could avoid labeling them entirely. Federal law dictates that products must generally include an ingredients list, with ingredients listed in descending order according to how much of the product's weight they make up.
A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said that it had never sought to exempt OvoPro from being included in ingredients lists. Speaking via email, the spokesperson added:
"OvoPro" is the trade name we use with the manufacturers who buy the ingredient, so it typically won't appear on a retail pack — the same way most functional ingredients are listed by common name rather than by supplier brand. What appears on the label is the ingredient, named plainly.
Healthier Comforts listed OvoPro as an "animal-free egg white protein," one of The EVERY Company's suggested phrasings, on its branded version of the product.
In sum ...
Though the claims circulated in October 2026, OvoPro had actually been available to consumers since March of that year. The FDA told The EVERY Company in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding the company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was GRAS.
That letter was not the same thing as FDA approval, which is a process whereby the administration approves drugs for consumer use. Rather, they showed that the company had documented to the FDA's satisfaction that the product in question was "safe under the conditions of its intended use."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were leaving it off product ingredients lists. This appeared to be a misinterpretation by some social media users of a statement by The EVERY Company that brands had leeway in how they described the product.
OvoPro is also not the only animal-free egg white protein product available to U.S. consumers.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contained "beaver butt secretions" or whether McDonald's apple pies contained an ingredient derived from human hair.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.
Below are images of a bookstall set up by SFI-DYFI during Christmas in 2017:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2022:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2024:
Similarly, the SFI-DYFI local committee in the Khidderpore area of Kolkata organised a bookstall during Eid this year. Khidderpore has historically been home to a significant Muslim population. The bookstall was organised for two days and was featured on the Facebook page of the CPI(M) Kolkata Port Assembly Committee.
Below are glimpses of the stall set up on Eid at Khidderpore:
Further, Nasrin claimed that the Leftist bookstalls only sell books promoting atheism. However, the images on social media, posted by people who bought books from hundreds of these stalls, clearly show a vast array of books from across genres being sold in these stalls.
An Alt News correspondent visited the CPI(M) bookstall set up near Jadavpur 8B bus stand and encountered a diverse section of books, ranging from Bengali classics, poetry, history among others. Books on Ramkrishna and Vivekananda were also available at the stall.
CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh made a video, interviewing a woman who visited the stall and described herself as a devotee of spiritual leader Lalon Fakir. In the video, she shared her book haul which comprised books on Lalon Fakir, and other Hindu spiritual leaders like Nityananda Mahaprabhu, and even a cook book.
CPI(M) leader Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the 8B bookstall regularly posted pictures of the stall on his Facebook page. In one such image, physician Dr. Arjun Dasgupta was seen holding a book on Swami Vivekananda, along with a book on the Second World War.
According to Dasgupta, apart from Leftist books, the stall also contains books such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s Anandamath. “I was looking at some old pictures my family took at the Jadavpur 8B stall, and I could see Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s books behind me. His books include ‘Anandamath’, which has the song ‘Vande Mataram’. So it is simply not true that these stalls only sell books promoting atheism. These stalls are part of Bengal’s culture, and anyone who loves books should stand against efforts to shut them down,” said Dasgupta.
“We Bengalis feel that a book is a book, whether it is sold at an ISKCON stall or a CPI(M) stall. We love books and naturally gather around any stall that sells them. When we were children, these stalls introduced many of us to great books from around the world. I vividly remember my father buying me a copy of ‘Ispat’, the Bengali translation of Nikolai Ostrovsky’s ‘How the Steel Was Tempered’. I think thousands of people like me have similar memories,” he added.
Similarly, the Rashbehari-1 area committee of the CPI(M) set up a book stall near the Kalighat temple during Durga Puja. Images of the stall show stacks of books ranging from Bengali children’s classics such as Thakurmar Jhuli to literary works including ‘Ichhamati’ by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, ‘Kapalkundala’ by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, ‘Grihadaha’ and ‘Devdas’ by Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, among others. Books on Maa Sarada, and books written by Rabindranath Tagore were also visible at the stall.
Thus, the findings above show that Nasrin’s claim that Leftists organise bookstalls only during Hindu festivals such as Durga Puja is false, as there is documented evidence of Left organisations organising bookstalls during both Eid and Christmas. Her claim that books exclusively on atheism are sold at the stalls is also false, as there is documented evidence of books of various genres being sold across Left bookstalls.

The Ebola outbreak is breaking records — and just marked a grim milestone
The fastest spreading Ebola outbreak in history has surpassed another grim milestone. More than 10,000 people have been infected since the outbreak was first declared in May, according to the latest government figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
"It's a milestone that we're all surprised to be passing this quickly," says Katie Thomas-Canfield, interim Ebola response director for the International Rescue Committee. "10,000 people affected by Ebola in such a short period is really staggering," she says, noting that at this point in the West Africa outbreak of 2014-2016, only about 4,000 people had been infected. But that earlier outbreak still has the highest case count — more than 28,000 cases.
The current outbreak is also the largest ever in geographic scope, spanning Nigeria to Kenya. It is second in the death toll, with nearly 5,000 deaths compared to the previous toll of over 11,000.
About a third of those who've died in this outbreak have been kids. Children under 5, with their developing immune systems, are hit especially hard — roughly three out of four infected have died.
"Behind every figure is a life interrupted, a family mourning, a health worker under pressure and a community seeking reassurance," said Mohamed Janabi, regional director for the World Health Organization Africa, at a press conference last week. "We must reach people earlier, bring safe care closer, and strengthen trust before fear becomes a barrier to survival."
Here's a look at some of the key questions about the 2026 outbreak.
Why has the outbreak become so bad so fast?
Part of the answer lies in uncertainty over when the virus started circulating
While the outbreak was officially declared in May, more recent evidence suggests the virus likely started spreading in February or March.
"That's a really long time for things to be undetected in communities, and that means we started at a disadvantage," says Thomas-Canfield. A confluence of factors contributed to the delay.
First, there's the fact that a rarer species of Ebola is behind the outbreak — Bundibugyo. Existing tests weren't calibrated for this species, leading to delays. What's more, this region of northeastern DRC is remote and beset by conflict. And U.S. cuts to foreign aid may have slowed disease surveillance efforts, says Nahid Bhadelia, an infectious disease physician at Boston University.
In those early days, "the writing was on the wall that this would be a hard road and it would need international cooperation," says Bhadelia. International cooperation and support have been slower in coming than in previous Ebola outbreaks.
In 2014, for example, healthcare workers from around the globe traveled to West Africa to bolster the response. Bhadelia was one of them.
"I think you are seeing a lot less American or other healthcare workers coming into DRC because of U.S. policy that Americans may not be allowed back even if they're sick," says Bhadelia. That's different from the policy in the prior major outbreak. "That means that a lot of the burden is being carried by DRC and regional healthcare workers."
Despite pledges of funding from around the world, including more than $880 million from the U.S., some health workers on the ground say that money is slow to materialize. "The scale of financing that's available for this response is really a fraction of what it was in our previous response," says Thomas-Canfield. "I think the degree of international solidarity has been a lot less."
Are we making progress?
The response on the ground has improved over the past several months. There are now two dozen or so diagnostic labs and more than 50 treatment centers.
"We're up toward almost 2,000 treatment beds for Ebola, so there's been a lot of progress," says Douglas Noble, global incident manager for Ebola at UNICEF. Nonetheless, roughly two-thirds of deaths are occurring in the community, not in treatment centers — a sign that people are not coming forward with symptoms. That figure has been stubbornly constant for months and needs to improve for the outbreak to get under control, says Noble.
Part of why people aren't seeking care may be that Bundibugyo infections can seem mild at first. "Things like fever, headache, body ache, they're all symptoms of the most common and largely treatable endemic diseases in the region," says Thomas-Canfield. Those who are infected with Ebola may not decide to seek treatment until it's too late, he says.
A bigger hurdle, say many healthcare workers on the ground, is community distrust.
An October survey from the International Rescue Committee found that 85% of respondents in North Kivu — a current hotspot — say that distrust of community responders is keeping them from seeking care.
"We're constantly fighting different kinds of rumors, different kinds of misinformation," says Thomas-Canfield of the International Rescue Committee. Many community members question whether Ebola is real or believe responders are just trying to make money. Others wonder why teams come for Ebola and not other diseases that afflict the region, like malaria or typhoid.
Community health workers are working hard to rebuild that trust. "I do think that in areas where we've been able to establish a longer-term presence, we're better able to respond," says Thomas-Canfield. But the virus is rapidly spreading to new health zones. Building trust from scratch is hard, she says. That's especially true in conflict zones, where fighting makes it hard to work, and armed groups actively sow disinformation.
When trust is low, people don't seek care or engage with health officials trying to find new cases and isolate their contacts. Roughly 80% of new cases are still coming in from people who weren't on health officials' radar. Until that rate goes down, the outbreak will remain out of control, says infectious disease doctor Bhadelia.
She points to the cases in Nigeria and Kenya this month as proof of that point. "The sporadic cases that we're seeing in neighboring countries is a sign of the growth in DRC," she says. While daily case counts seem to be plateauing, she says there's likely many regions where the virus is spreading undetected. "It's so far out of control."
Is there any hope that an Ebola vaccine or better treatments could tamp down numbers?
No vaccine or treatment is licensed for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Several are in the works, but all far from being used in this response.
There is an existing vaccine for Ebola. It's called Ervebo, but it targets a different species of the disease. It hasn't been widely deployed, but healthcare workers began receiving the vaccine in late August and researchers just started a clinical trial, dubbed Tumaini after the Swahili word for hope, aimed at testing how well Ervebo works against Bundibugyo. If it proves effective, "that would be amazing, that could make a difference," says Bhadelia. But she cautions that vaccines and new treatments are not a silver bullet.
"Targeted medical countermeasures are necessary, but they are not sufficient," she says. These interventions need to be coupled with basic public health measures, like tracing all the contacts for a newly infected person and isolating and treating those who are stricken. Improving these strategies takes more work and resources, she says, and she worries that the needed support may not come fast enough.
"In this moment, the question that scares me more than anything is will the international community turn its eyes and forget about DRC?" she says. "I am worried the funding will dry out, that we will not keep paying attention to a public health disaster that is much deeper and bigger in this moment than people realize."

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.
“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.
The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.
The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.
The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.
India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.
“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.
In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.
Patents on the BPaL combination have been granted in 11 countries and are set to expire in 2036: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Spain’s high-speed train collision, which killed at least 68 people and injured more than 100, was the deadliest rail accident in the country in 2026. A Renfe train struck a stationary Iryo service in central Spain. Preliminary accounts from the Spanish transport minister have raised questions about a possible technical failure in the automatic control system and the decision to resume services before it was restored.
The train crash in Spain occurred on Wednesday morning in Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid, as two trains travelled towards Seville.
The impact derailed carriages from both trains, leaving wreckage scattered across the tracks and a nearby embankment. Investigators are examining the sequence of decisions that allowed one train to move towards another that remained stationary.
The disaster, Spain’s second major high-speed rail collision this year, has put Pedro Sánchez's railway infrastructure and operational safeguards under scrutiny.
According to Transport Minister Óscar Puente, an automatic security system malfunctioned at around 8.30 am, forcing trains operating along an affected stretch of track to stop. The disruption covered approximately 63 to 69 kilometres, according to differing initial accounts.
Spain's central railway control centre subsequently authorised a Renfe train to resume its journey, even though the safety system had not been restored. The service travelled about 25 kilometres before colliding with the stationary Iryo train at approximately 8.53 am.
The Renfe train may have been travelling at speeds of up to 200 kilometres per hour, Puente said, although its precise speed at the time of impact remained under investigation.
The minister described the decision to restart traffic as inexplicable, adding that the train should not have been allowed to proceed while a stop signal remained active. If movement had been authorised, he said, it should at least have been subject to reduced speed restrictions.
The initial account points to two critical failures in Spain's train crashes: the malfunction of the automatic control system and the subsequent decision to resume services without restoring normal safeguards.
When the system stopped working, trains were halted, and the control centre assumed responsibility for managing movements. However, according to Puente, the Renfe service was permitted to restart despite the continuing safety restriction.
The incident has raised questions about how railway staff handled the disruption, whether they knew the Iryo train had stopped on the tracks, and why the Renfe train continued towards it despite a signal telling it to stop.
Puente said the train’s drivers were not to blame, but the investigation will need to establish precisely how the malfunction and the restart authorisation combined to cause the collision. The available information does not yet establish whether additional signalling, communication or procedural failures contributed.
Aerial footage from Spain’s Civil Guard showed the extent of the destruction near Urda, in the province of Toledo, where several carriages derailed after a Renfe high-speed train struck a stationary Iryo service.
Some carriages plunged down an embankment, leaving twisted metal and wreckage scattered across the surrounding fields.
Spanish emergency services deployed firefighters, Civil Guard officers, medical teams and Civil Protection personnel to search the wreckage and assist passengers.
Ambulances and medical helicopters were among the emergency vehicles sent to the scene, while cranes were used to help rescuers reach damaged carriages and search for victims.
Spanish authorities also established an advanced medical post to treat the injured, and the regional government requested assistance from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit.
Passengers described a violent impact that sent luggage, mobile phones and people flying through the carriages. Survivors were evacuated as emergency crews and nearby residents helped those trapped in the wreckage.
The collision comes months after a January crash involving Renfe and Iryo trains killed 46 people in southern Spain. Before this year, the country's dedicated high-speed network had not experienced a fatal crash since its opening in 1992.
Spain has built one of the world's largest high-speed rail networks, with about 3,900 kilometres of track. But railway workers' representatives have questioned whether infrastructure maintenance has kept pace with increased passenger traffic and competition following the entry of private operators.
The latest disaster has prompted calls for accountability and renewed assurances on safety. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced three days of national mourning and pledged an investigation into the causes.
The central question remains whether the collision could have been prevented had the automatic system failure been handled differently.

The Bombay High Court on 26 October set aside a trial court order taking cognisance of the Enforcement Directorate's prosecution complaint against OctaFX India Private Limited, now known as Tauga Private Limited, and quashed consequential steps, including a Red Corner Notice and a non-bailable warrant against the company in the case.
Justice Milind N. Jadhav, allowing the company's writ petition on October 26, held that the cognisance order dated December 24, 2024 was not sustainable because the statutory procedure had not been followed. The case is among the more closely watched enforcement actions involving an offshore retail trading platform in the Indian market.
The Court observed that where statutory procedure must be followed scrupulously, an order taking cognisance can be passed only after the prosecution's reply has been considered and the accused has been heard. Finding that the December 2024 order had not met that requirement, the Court quashed and set it aside.
Senior Advocate Aabad Ponda appeared for the petitioner, instructed by Khaitan & Co. Advocate Ashish Mehta appeared for the Directorate of Enforcement.
The company has been directed to appear before the trial court through counsel on November 18, 2026. The trial court must hear the objections of the petitioner and the other co-accused under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and only then decide whether to take cognisance.
The ED sought a direction that the hearing be completed within eight weeks. The Court declined to fix a timeline, leaving the schedule to the trial court's discretion given its workload.
Fresh service of summons and notice under Section 223(1) of the BNSS was waived for the petitioner. The prosecution was directed to ensure the other accused are served in accordance with law.
With the cognisance order set aside, the Court directed that any consequential steps taken by the prosecution towards issuing a Red Corner Notice or a non-bailable warrant against the petitioner in this case are also quashed. The relief is limited to the petitioner and to this case.
The order does not go into the merits of the ED's allegations. The trial court must first hear objections in accordance with law and then decide whether to take cognisance afresh.
The High Court allowed and disposed of the writ petition.

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.
Types of strokes
Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.
An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.
The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.
The first few hours
There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.
In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.
Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.
How brain function is affected
The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.
Recognising warning signs
The BE FAST method is an effective means of identifying the symptoms of a stroke:
- B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance, dizziness or difficulty walking
- E – Eyes: Sudden blurred vision, double vision or loss of vision
- F – Face: One side of the face is drooping or numb
- A – Arms: One arm is weak or dropping down
- S – Speech: Slurred speech
- T – Time: Call for help immediately
Sudden changes in vision, lack of balance, confusion or even a severe headache without apparent reason might be symptoms of a stroke as well. Disappearing symptoms within a minute or two shouldn’t be considered harmless and require immediate medical examination.
After the golden hour
The ‘golden hour’ is significant to preserve as much of brain function as possible and to ensure best possible outcomes, but this does not mean medical professionals cease working after this window is over. Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.
It is worth noting that every stroke patient has his or her own path to recovery, which depends greatly on the level of injuries, the affected area of the brain, timely assistance and the patient’s health in general. For all individuals, however, it is important to understand how the brain functions, remember the signs of a stroke and seek timely help for oneself or a loved one.
(Dr. B. K. Madhusudhan is lead consultant – neurology, Aster RV Hospital, Bengaluru. madhusudhan.bk@asterhospital.in)

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

A recent debate over investors’ lack of interest in India’s hardware and deeptech bets has brought some longstanding challenges in the ecosystem back into focus. These include a lack of patient capital, pressure from limited partners (LPs) for early distributions, consensus-driven investing, and the difficulty of underwriting long development and qualification cycles. As AI infrastructure moves beyond a pure compute race to focus on the layers that determine how efficiently systems run, India stands at the cusp of a significant opportunity. However, simply adding more computing power will not be enough for the country to establish itself as a global AI leader. Instead, opportunities are emerging in the supporting infrastructure. Data centres, for instance, need more efficient power delivery, better cooling systems, and faster connections between processors and memory. These layers are becoming increasingly critical as they directly influence real-world performance and the total cost of ownership of AI infrastructure. For India, the debate and the technical opportunity converge. Rather than trying to compete across the entire AI hardware stack, the country can develop specialised technologies. To understand which of these layers offer the strongest multiplier effects and what it will take for India to own them, we spoke to VCs tracking the homegrown deeptech ecosystem. Let’s unravel what they said in this edition of The AI Shift... The Need To Power Data Centres A consensus among VCs pointed to power delivery as the first major opportunity. As AI systems become more power-dense, improving power efficiency becomes an increasingly important engineering challenge. Natasha Malpani, founder and general partner of Boundless Ventures, sees an opportunity in power electronics, grid-edge systems and cooling designed for hot and humid environments. Data centres operating in Indian cities must manage local temperature and humidity conditions, potentially creating demand for technologies that can also serve other tropical markets. “The multiplier here is integration,” she said. Power semiconductors can serve AI data centres, electric vehicles and energy infrastructure. The opportunity, therefore, is to develop components that address multiple markets instead of relying on demand from one category. Cooling is also closely connected to this opportunity. Liquid-cooling systems help manage the heat generated by high-density computing equipment, creating demand for coolant distribution units, heat exchangers and direct-to-chip cooling technology. The second opportunity lies in moving data between processors and memory. Debraj Banerjee, general partner of F2A (Fundamentum Frontier Advisors), which recently closed a ₹3,000 Cr fund for deeptech, argues that India should target the interconnect and memory layer of AI chips. This includes high-speed SerDes circuits, PCIe and CXL controllers, chiplet interconnects, and memory expansion silicon. These technologies help processors exchange data and access memory efficiently. Banerjee’s argument is that standards-based technologies can give new entrants a route into multiple chip ecosystems without requiring them to challenge established GPU platforms directly. “India shouldn’t try to win the fab race. It should own the plumbing of AI chips, the interconnect and memory layer, because that’s where the bottleneck is moving and where one design earns on every chip shipped worldwide,” he recommended. The multiplier here is the business model. Companies that own valuable semiconductor IP could license it to multiple manufacturers and potentially earn royalties across global shipments, rather than relying entirely on engineering fees. Pranav Pai, managing partner of 3one4 Capital, added a third dimension: India’s established semiconductor and systems-design talent can support demand for custom embedded-system design, verification and testing. But he argues that value capture requires moving beyond services. "The opportunity is to move deeper, into components, advanced materials, proprietary process equipment, and finally product and system IP, which is where value capture will concentrate," Pai said. For AI infrastructure, this means turning engineering capabilities into products that global customers repeatedly buy. Who’s Taming The AI Infrastructure Layer Some Indian startups are already building in these areas, although their commercial maturity and ownership of technology differ. Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors developed power-management technology for AI data centres, including multiphase controllers and smart power stages. Then, German semiconductor company Infineon completed its acquisition of C2i on October 5, 2026, strengthening its power-management capabilities and expanding its research and development footprint in India. The deal demonstrates how Indian-developed technology can attract a global strategic buyer. Ahmedabad-based KuhlTherm is addressing the thermal-management problem. It develops liquid-cooling systems for high-density computing, including rear-door heat exchangers and coolant distribution units. Its next test is to demonstrate reliability, secure customer deployments and scale beyond early stage development. In data movement, LightSpeed Photonics is developing optical interconnect technology for AI and high-performance computing. The company raised $6.5 Mn in a funding round led by pi Ventures last year. Its work highlights an emerging opportunity in using light to transmit data, although commercial adoption will depend on integration with existing systems, manufacturing readiness and customer qualification. Government support is also building the broader semiconductor design ecosystem. Earlier this year, 24 chip-design projects were supported under the Design Linked Incentive scheme, producing 16 tape-outs, six fabricated chips and 10 patents. The projects had engaged more than 1,000 specialised engineers and developed over 140 reusable semiconductor IP cores. These figures show growing design activity. However, chip-design progress is not the same as a proven position in the global AI hardware supply chain. What Comes Next? India’s challenge is to turn early technical progress into commercially competitive products. Semiconductor development involves long design and testing cycles, while cooling and power systems must demonstrate reliability under demanding operating conditions. Global customers are unlikely to switch suppliers without evidence that new products can meet performance, safety and service requirements. Banerjee of F2A said the biggest gaps are not necessarily engineering talent, but patient capital and a lack of willingness to work with first-time chip companies. His thesis points to a need for investors who understand hardware development timelines and can support businesses through product qualification, rather than expecting rapid commercial returns. Access to manufacturing and advanced packaging is another constraint. India’s design ecosystem is expanding, but startups still need to establish where their IP resides, which components can be produced domestically and where they depend on overseas suppliers. The government’s Design Linked Incentive scheme provides financial incentives and design infrastructure support, but moving from prototype to volume production is still a challenge. The next phase should be judged by commercial milestones: customer qualification, repeat orders, manufacturing scale and licensing revenue. For instance, for power and cooling startups, the test is whether their products can deliver measurable efficiency improvements and win deployments. Similarly, for semiconductor IP companies, it is whether global manufacturers adopt their designs and generate recurring revenue. Overall, VCs agree that Indian startups need to choose where their engineering strengths can translate into proprietary technology, then build the capital, manufacturing and customer relationships needed to commercialise that technology. The opportunity is visible. Whether it becomes a lasting advantage will depend on how many Indian startups can move from promising designs to products that global infrastructure providers cannot easily do without. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s Manavdeep Singh Grover, cofounder & CEO of SuperLiving, with a prompt he uses to turn an A/B test result into a clear ship, kill or keep-running decision. “You are my analytics lead, and your job is to tell me the actionables from insights, not just what happened. The A/B experiment: . Before any numbers: Check the live setup matches what I described: the split, the targeting, the pricing, and the exact wording users see in each variant. Flag any mismatch first. Judge it on one metric: total revenue per user who saw the test, across every product, and 6 month LTV projection. Not just the product we changed. Then read it honestly: Count each user in the variant they first saw, never by what they bought. Show new and existing users separately, and weight by day if the split or the traffic changed mid-test. Show the full journey for each variant: started checkout, paid, cancelled the same day, and what they bought instead. Give the difference with a range and the chance each variant is really ahead. If it’s too early, tell me how many more days you need. Tell me the break-even: how many buyers the pricier option can lose and still win. End with: Your call in one line: ship it, kill it, or keep running, and why. The one thing that could prove the call wrong, and the date we’ll know. Use plain language and a table for every comparison.” Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

(Bloomberg) -- Veteran federal judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw cases against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Archegos Capital Management family office founder Bill Hwang and litigation over the 9/11 terrorist attack, died at 92.
The Jewish Center, a synagogue in Manhattan, notified congregants that Hellerstein, a longtime member and trustee, had died. The US District Court for the Southern District of New York said the the judge passed away Wednesday morning, surrounded by family.
“Judge Hellerstein was an insightful and dedicated lawyer who, following a distinguished career in the private sector, served with distinction for over 25 years as a distinguished jurist of this court,” Chief Judge Laura Swain said in a statement. “His energetic and dedicated service to this court continued until his death.”
Hellerstein, a native New Yorker, served in the Army’s Judge Advocate General’s Corps before joining New York City law firm Stroock & Stroock & Lavan LLP in 1960. He was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1998.
Since then, he has overseen high-profile white collar prosecutions and complex litigation. Most recently, he was overseeing the narco-terrorism case against Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores.
The couple are scheduled to face trial in June. New judges will be assigned at random to the Maduro case and the other cases Hellerstein was overseeing.
During his early years on the bench, Hellerstein built his reputation overseeing yearslong litigation related to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. In 2010, he rejected a settlement for 10,000 rescue and cleanup workers who fell ill working at Ground Zero because the payouts may have been too small after attorney fees were taken out. Months later, Hellerstein approved a $712 million pact well over the original proposal.
In a separate case, he ruled against families seeking to recover human remains from the 9/11 debris.
In the courtroom, the Columbia Law School graduate was famous for interrupting lawyers who weren’t questioning witnesses to his satisfaction or losing the jury’s attention.
In the 2024 criminal trial of Hwang, whose family office meltdown caused chaos across Wall Street, Hellerstein interrupted the questioning of a witness to announce the birth of his great-grandchild. “It’s a gorgeous baby,” remarked Hellerstein as he turned his phone to bemused lawyers in the courtroom. The jury erupted in applause.
In the same trial, he chided a lawyer for boring the jury to tears.
‘Just and Measured’
He sentenced Hwang to 18 years in prison, a decision that the judge never took lightly.
In rare public comments, Hellerstein, an Orthodox Jew, has spoken about how his faith intersected with his work. He told a podcast in 2020 that he held sentencing hearings on Fridays so he could used Sabbath to reflect on the consequences of his decisions.
“I never ever have had the feeling that my punishment was just and measured,” he said. “And that’s good. I think a judge should be disconcerted with what he does. I’m taking away the liberty of someone.”
In recent years, Hellerstein oversaw trials involving Charlie Javice, the start-up founder convicted of defrauding JPMorgan Chase, as well as a human rights case against BNP Paribas.
Roger Stavis, the head of Mintz & Gold’s white collar defense practice, who’s tried cases before Hellerstein, recalled him having a sense of humor that made him likeable even when Stavis was losing.
‘Dayenu’
In one hearing in Hellerstein’s courtroom in lower Manhattan, Stavis recalled objecting to the prosecution introducing the same evidence over and over. The judge shot back at Stavis, asking him to identify the legal precedent on how many times is too many.
“I said ‘United States v. Dayenu’ — the Hebrew term for it would have been enough — and he started cracking up,” Stavis said.
