'He could be happier' - why is Estevao becoming Chelsea's forgotten man?
- Published
The last time Chelsea beat Liverpool, Estevao was the talk of the Premier League.
The Brazilian was still in his first couple of months at Stamford Bridge when his name hit the headlines after he scored the winner against the Premier League champions with practically the final kick of the match last October.
Fast forward 12 months, and Estevao is beginning to attract attention for all the wrong reasons as he struggles to force his way into Xabi Alonso's side.
The 19-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Palmeiras last summer, was conspicuous by his absence on Wednesday night as Chelsea were knocked out of the Carabao Cup following a penalty shootout loss to Liverpool at Anfield.
The Blues had taken the lead in the first half through Morgan Rogers, but they failed to kick on after Cody Gakpo quickly restored parity for the hosts.
Most concerning for Estevao, though, was that as both teams pushed for a winner in the second half, Alonso never appeared to consider the forward.
The clearest indication of just how low Estevao sits in Alonso's pecking order came midway through the second half, when Alonso made a triple substitution in an attempt to turn the game in his side's favour.
One of the three changes was Emanuel Emegha, who had yet to feature for the Blues since his summer move from Strasbourg.
Just moments after that triple change, which brought Chelsea's total number of substitutions to five, Estevao could be seen ending his warm-up and retreating to the bench.
It was another night of no action for the Brazilian.
'I'm sure Estevao will have his moment'
Sadly for Estevao, Wednesday night's situation at Anfield was nothing new for him.
The Brazilian has failed to make the starting XI in any of the eight Premier League matches since Alonso took charge of the Blues in the summer.
His total minutes for the campaign so far stand at an underwhelming 172, with 125 of those coming in the victories over Luton Town and Leeds United in the earlier rounds of the EFL Cup.
Yet even in the thrilling 6-3 win against Daniel Farke's side, which remains one of only two games he has started this campaign, he was withdrawn at half-time with Chelsea trailing 1-0.
After the fourth-round defeat by Liverpool, Alonso defended his decision not to play Estevao, hinting that the forward is still coming to grips with the physical demands of English football.
"We started with Pedro [Neto], Morgan [Rogers] and Danny Welbeck, and the game had very intense moments," said Alonso.
"We knew it was going to be physical, and Malo [Gusto] had cramps, so we were a bit forced with substitutions. The season is going to be very long, and there will be moments for everyone."
When asked directly about the Brazilian, Alonso added: "He could be happier. He wants to play. I'm sure Estevao will have his moment, it is my responsibility.
"We know the game in England is really intense, and you need to be up for it. Estevao is in his second season. The season is going to be long."
Neto's revival and attacking firepower limit Estevao's chances
One of the main reasons behind Estevao's exile has been the form of Pedro Neto.
It was only a couple of months ago that Portugal international Neto looked destined to leave Chelsea, only two years after joining from Wolverhampton Wanderers.
The 26-year-old was linked with a move to Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, but he ultimately remained at Stamford Bridge.
That decision appears to have been influenced by Alonso, who has underlined his faith in Neto by handing him seven starts in eight Premier League matches this season.
His success out on the right - which also happens to be Estevao's favoured position - has meant opportunities have been few and far between for the Brazilian.
He has primarily been deployed as a right-sided wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 system, with his Premier League experience and greater defensive solidity compared to Estevao seemingly winning over the Spaniard.
After an impressive start to the campaign, in which he has scored four goals in 11 matches, Neto was rewarded with a new six-year deal at Stamford Bridge.
"He's a player who is a little bit of a victim of the system," former Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff told Sky Sports.
"Alonso tends to play Neto in that hybrid wing-back role, expecting him to get high up the pitch as well. Maybe he doesn't feel that suits Estevao, and I don't feel it does either."
One area that has not been a problem for the Blues this season is attack, with the forward positions firmly in the hands of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Rogers, who has made a spectacular start to life at Stamford Bridge following his £117m move from Aston Villa.
Against Liverpool, though, Estevao couldn't even get a look-in despite Chelsea being without the suspended Palmer and the injured Joao Pedro.
"How Estevao has not got on the pitch tonight, I do not know," said former Crystal Palace forward Clinton Morrison.
"He must be thinking, 'What do I have to do? We have injuries to two of the star players up front, and I'm still not getting on the pitch'."
Estevao will be hoping he can follow in the footsteps of Neto and revive his Stamford Bridge career.

 over Field Marshal Asim Munir’s participation in a high-level regional security meeting in Iran, questioning why the defence minister was absent from the talks.

Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
- Published
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.
Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.
The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Von der Leyen, speaking to reporters after landing in Montreal on Wednesday, said the two sides will "start discussing how to make Canada the first associate member of the EU".
"Our ambition is to build the closest partnership we have ever had with a non-European country," she said.
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.
According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.
The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.
"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.
Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.
On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.
But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.

Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion.
The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.
The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan.
Space Force officials will closely scrutinize Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission. The Pentagon has entrusted ULA’s Vulcan rocket for roughly half of its major launches through the early 2030s. The Space Force certified the Vulcan rocket for national security launches in 2025, then flew two missions on Vulcan before its grounding after the February booster incident.
Making strides
In a statement, United Launch Alliance said engineers “made great strides” in understanding the booster anomaly that occurred in February. Engineers “have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle,” ULA said.
“To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission,” ULA said. “By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers.”

The Osmania General Hospital (OGH) in Hyderabad has established a dedicated gender-affirming surgery service in the government healthcare sector in Telangana, marking a step towards improving access to specialised healthcare for transgender persons.
The Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery has introduced the service through a multidisciplinary team of specialists from plastic surgery, anaesthesiology, endocrinology, urology, gynaecology and psychiatry, along with nursing staff and other healthcare professionals. The initiative has been developed over the past eight months, said doctors.
The team has successfully performed several procedures for transgender people, including frontal bossing reduction, autologous fat grafting for breast augmentation, breast augmentation using implants, penile inversion vaginoplasty and bilateral nipple-areola complex-sparing mastectomy. Breast implants have also been facilitated through letters of credit under the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund (CMRF).
The initiative aims to provide safe, accessible and affordable gender-affirming surgical care within the public healthcare system, particularly for individuals who face financial and logistical barriers to accessing specialised procedures.
The service follows a multidisciplinary approach, with emphasis on patient evaluation, individualised surgical planning, perioperative care and post-operative follow-up. The hospital has also received support from the Queer Badhu Parents Association, whose president, Mukunda Mala, helped facilitate the renovation of a three-bed ward for transgender patients recovering from surgery, said Dr P. Lakshmi, Professor and Head of Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.
The hospital plans to expand the range of gender-affirming procedures offered and further strengthen the multidisciplinary programme. The initiative is expected to help more transgender people access specialised surgical care through the government healthcare system while promoting inclusive, dignified and comprehensive healthcare.

Your Kindle doesn't have to be just a plain e-reader. The right Kindle accessories can transform the simple device into something that showcases your personality, makes it easier to read, or all of the above. Personally, I'm always looking for a way to hold up one less device in front of my face; I'm holding my phone enough already, thank you very much.
If you're shopping around for new Kindle accessories, I've got you covered as a fellow reader and owner of every single current Kindle model. I've tried everything from clear cases you can fill with stickers to ones with built-in straps, and have tested straps you can add to your e-reader without needing a case. Stickers? Charms? Got ’em. Hate holding your Kindle up to read? The Kindle holders and page-turning remotes are for you. This guide will give you ideas on how to improve your own reading time or gift your favorite reader.
As new Kindle models are rolling out that aren't the same size as the old, it's important to double-check what size and generation Kindle accessory you're getting. Most accessories in this guide were tested on the 2024 generation, unless otherwise noted.
Updated October 2026: I've added notes on the new Kindle Page Turn Case and Kindle Click, plus cases and grips from Bondi.
My Favorite Kindle Accessories
Kindle Cases and Covers
An easy must-have for any Kindle reader is a case or cover to protect your e-reader. Here are some of my favorites that I've tried on my various Kindles.
All of these were tested on 2024 models of the Kindle, usually the 7-inch Paperwhite or Colorsoft. The new 2026 generation has some slight size differences, so if you're shopping for accessories for a newer Kindle, double-check if there's a version for the model you have.
Kindle Straps and Grips
Looking for an easier way to hold your Kindle? Add these straps and grips right onto the Kindle or the case.
Kindle Holders
Hate holding up your Kindle? Or struggle with chronic pain that makes holding it feel terrible? These holders will literally take the weight out of your hands.
A Page Turner Made for Kindle
Page turners have been the latest item to have as an e-reader user, but while Kobo launched a remote last year, Kindle had yet to have one—until now.
Kindle announced the release of the Kindle Click, its first Bluetooth page-turning remote, in early October, and it's finally available to buy. It's a huge improvement over third-party devices that required you to have one part of the device on your Kindle so it could tap and turn the page for you, and a remote in your hand. The worst part was not just that it blocked some of the screen, but that you had to track the battery life of two separate pieces.
The Kindle Click solves these complaints, and while it launched on the same date as the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft, it's backward compatible with Kindle models from 2024. It's easy to set up: Just go into your device settings, click on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and then Bluetooth devices to sync your Kindle Click. I tried it with both a 2024 Kindle and a 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, and both devices were able to find the Click almost instantly and start working.
The Click has two buttons on the main body that move forward and backward and will move around a page you're on, too (but won't select a book for you; it'll just move through your library or homepage). There are also two buttons on the right side that let you adjust screen brightness, which is a fantastic convenience. There's also an included lanyard to attach it to your wrist. It's great to pair with a Kindle stand of any kind so you can prop up your Kindle and turn the page without lifting a finger.
Some Charger Options
If you're getting a new Kindle, you might not be thrilled to discover you need to provide your own charging block to charge it. And if you haven't already switched over your home's collection of wall chargers to USB-C, you'll be especially frustrated when you open the box and find only a USB-C cord. If you're in the market for a new wall charger to pair with your Kindle, these are a couple of our favorites.
Looking to charge on the go? You shouldn't need to with a Kindle's long battery life. But in case you're a serial battery drainer, you can try these portable power banks we love. If neither of these suit you, check out our complete guide to the Best Power Banks.
Kindle Adornments
While everything else in this guide serves a protective or convenience purpose, this section features items with a singular purpose: fun. Here are a few I've liked adding to my Kindle.
Kindle Bags and Sleeves
Looking for a bag to tote your Kindle around? These carriers have you covered with a specific size and special pockets designed to safely store your device. Sure, you could throw your Kindle in any old bag, but these will keep it secure and prevent scratches from your keys. If you'd rather use the bag you have but want a separate sleeve to keep it safe, we've got ideas for that too.
Still Need a Kindle?
If you're reading this guide and actually are still in need of a Kindle, we've got an entire guide to the best Kindles to buy and why. The newest models are (for the most part) the smartest buy, unless the older 2024 models are on sale.

Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
- Published
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.
Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".
"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".
Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."
When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days.
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for.
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage.
Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen.
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth".
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

India’s only international bullion exchange is seeing a revival in activity, driven by silver imports after a regulatory change made licences mandatory for certain categories of the metal.
The India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) recorded trades of 570 metric tonnes of silver in the three months since August, after seeing no trades over the preceding year, while spot gold imports stood at just 0.3 tonnes.
The surge follows a May decision by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) to move certain categories of silver to the restricted list, requiring importers to obtain authority's licences. As licences began to be issued, importers turned to IIBX to source the metal, with industry estimates suggesting that approvals covering about 400 tonnes of silver had been granted by mid-August, and some may have been approved after that.
“As licences began to flow, imports followed. Industry estimates suggest around 400 tonnes of licences were approved by mid-August,” said Anindya Banerjee, head of commodity and currency research at Kotak Neo. The 400 tonnes refers to the quantity of silver that could be imported under the approved licences, not the volume already imported.
India imported 1,017 metric tonnes of silver in the current fiscal year through September, according to Department of Commerce data. Of this, 283 metric tonnes, or about 27%, came through IIBX. Silver prices have fallen 11.7% since August to ₹1.92 lakh per kilogram.
What's prompting silver imports via the IIBX is how nominated banks allocate silver. Working with limited quotas, banks often favour a single large order over several smaller ones, according to officials.
“If a nominated bank has a 200 kg quota, and one client asks for the full 200 kg while 20 others ask for 10 kg each, the bank will typically give the entire amount to the first buyer,” said an industry official, who asked not to be named. “The exchange model solves this allocation issue, which is why so many importers are switching to IIBX,” the person added.
The government’s move to restrict certain categories of silver imports was aimed at curbing non-essential imports and easing pressure on the rupee, the official said. It also sought to prevent importers from exploiting a duty differential that had emerged following changes in import duties.
In May, the Centre raised the import duty on silver to 15% to curb imports. However, the India-UAE trade agreement allowed eligible importers to bring in silver at lower duty rates, creating an incentive to source the metal through the UAE. Moving certain silver categories to the restricted list made imports subject to government licensing, giving authorities greater control over the flow of silver into the country.
Second growth engine
IIBX, launched as India’s first exchange through which eligible jewellers and other buyers can directly import bullion, was expected to build its business around gold. However, a legal dispute over the allocation of quotas for importing gold at lower customs duty rates, which began in early 2025, has disrupted gold imports through the exchange. Gold and silver imports into India have traditionally been routed primarily through nominated banks.
IIBX expects silver to become a more significant part of its business. “We are hopeful of recording silver trading volumes of over 2,000 tonnes in the current financial year, subject to the availability of import licences issued by the DGFT,” said Ashok Gautam, managing director and chief executive officer of IIBX.
“We see silver becoming IIBX’s second growth engine. The exchange has already handled silver at scale, with about 1,127 tonnes in calendar 2024, roughly 16% of India’s silver imports. The market is large, with India’s silver import bill at a record $12 billion in FY26,” Banerjee said.
Sustainability
For the exchange to sustain those volumes, however, it may need to attract importers even when they can use banks and other permitted channels, according to experts.
“Traditionally, bullion imports have been concentrated among a relatively small group of banks and intermediaries. Allowing a wider range of eligible participants to import directly from the exchange can improve competition, reduce intermediary premiums and potentially deliver better pricing to end consumers,” said Hiren Chandaria, managing director for the Middle East and Asia at Monetary Metals.
Some industry participants argue that regulation could help secure a more durable flow of business for IIBX by requiring a portion of imports under each licence to be routed through the exchange.
“The DGFT could specify that a certain percentage of imports under each licence must be routed through IIBX. Suppose an importer receives a licence to import 50 tonnes of silver. The DGFT could stipulate that 10 tonnes must be imported through IIBX, while the remaining 40 tonnes could be sourced through other permitted channels like banks,” another official said.

New Delhi: India’s healthcare industry and public health experts have warned that price cuts of non-scheduled cancer medicines effective 9 November under the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s trade margin rationalization exercise are structurally flawed, legitimize profiteering and completely bypass high-cost patented drugs.
One-off, self-reported price revisions without independent verification will fail to deliver lasting relief, health groups said, demanding comprehensive, cost-based price controls covering all oncology therapies, permanent statutory margin caps across distribution channels and full scrutiny of company assistance programmes.
They also urged the government to mandate supply-chain data audits and expand public cancer care infrastructure to ensure access is determined by medical need rather than commercial pricing.
“We welcome the government’s move to cap trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs. However, the real test is whether patients benefit, without loopholes undermining the intended relief,” said Jyotsna Govil, chairperson of the Indian Cancer Society in New Delhi.
According to public health network Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India, the government's policy formula legitimizes an excessive 42.8% markup over the stockist price in supply chains involving direct hospital sales. This is much higher than the 16% retail margin under the Drug Price Control Order.
Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India noted that while prices of generic brands fell sharply—such as Palbociclib (Palbopro 125 mg) crashing from ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 and Thiotepa (Samtepa 100 mg) plunging from ₹80,072 to ₹7,150—the policy formula legitimizes high distributor markups instead of mandating cost-based price control.
“The dramatic collapse in cancer drug prices exposes the staggering exploitation of patients over the years by pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian generic manufacturers that offered inflated trade margins while families faced unaffordable treatment costs,” said Amulya Nidhi, national co-convenor of Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India. “Controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving treatment must be affordable and based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.”
Prices unchanged
An evaluation of the 24-page NPPA compliance notification and document shows that high-cost patented therapies and imported innovator brands remained completely untouched because medicines supplied free under patient assistance programmes were excluded from calculations.
Consequently, there was no price reduction for several exorbitantly priced patented therapies. Prices remained unchanged for AstraZeneca’s lung cancer therapy Osimertinib and Selumetinib, MSD’s Pembrolizumab, Roche’s breast cancer combo Phesgo, Alecensa and Avastin, Janssen’s Daratumumab, Astellas’s Gilteritinib and Padcev, Johnson & Johnson’s Rybrevant, Takeda’s Alunbrig, GSK’s Jemperli, Pfizer’s Lorbriqua and AbbVie’s Imbruvica.
“While a detailed examination is required, the prices of many original manufacturers appear to have remained unchanged. My only worry remains that the low-cost, life-saving drug should remain viable to manufacture and sell. In the past we have seen that getting affected because of price control,” said Dr. Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital in Bengaluru. “The primary impact is likely to be on drugs that have traditionally been marketed with very high profit margins. Overall, the move appears reasonable, with its long-term impact depending on how effectively it is implemented.”
Medical professionals stressed that access to newer therapies remains critical.
“We need to ensure that newer therapies and innovative medicines are also accessible, alongside transparent pricing and effective implementation. Ultimately, no patient should have to compromise on treatment because of cost,” said Dr. Aashish Chaudhry, managing director of Aakash Healthcare.
The pricing directive comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court, responding to public interest litigations challenging exorbitant markups, criticizing the vast gap between wholesale procurement rates and printed retail prices. It cited instances where an injection procured at ₹11,000 was billed to hospital patients at ₹1.3 lakh. The court asked why margin caps were selectively applied to non-scheduled cancer medicines rather than across all essential drugs.
Cancer drug market
India's anti-cancer market comprises roughly 225 drugs and 500 formulations, generating an annual turnover of ₹12,500 crore. Scheduled medicines covering 63 drugs under the National List of Essential Medicines 2022 accounted for about ₹2,250 crore under statutory ceiling prices, leaving over ₹10,250 crore non-scheduled, where uncurbed margins drive up out-of-pocket spending.
According to Govil of the Indian Cancer Society, the government’s projected annual savings are encouraging, but these must translate into measurable reductions in patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure.
“Too often, such initiatives lose their effectiveness due to inadequate monitoring and weak implementation. Regular compliance reviews, accessible grievance redressal and transparent reporting are essential,” Govil said. “Patients and patient support groups must be consulted on policy design and implementation. Affordable cancer care must also strengthen organizations providing financial, emotional and practical support to patients.”
Queries sent to the spokesperson of the NPPA and ministry of health and family welfare remained unanswered till publishing time.
Govil also called for vigilance against evergreening of patents, where minor modifications or extensions of patents could delay the entry of affordable generic alternatives.
“Strong safeguards are essential to ensure that patent protections do not become a barrier to access to life-saving cancer medicines,” Govil said.

On Tuesday, defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm announced a partnership to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027. They also announced a “long-term goal” of pushing the computer industry to create “a fully domestic supply chain.”
Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch
Palmer Luckey says it was always the goal, and now the company is committing to it.
Even a single Made-in-USA laptop would be a surprise, because no major US computer company builds its laptops here — not Apple, not Dell, not HP, not Microsoft. We’re not aware of any company that does.
But we are aware of companies that have briefly and strategically assembled computers here seemingly to appease President Donald Trump. We’re also aware of companies that have promised US jobs only to deliver empty buildings. And we’re aware of at least one fake “US” company that lied to the government about making product domestically.
That’s why we now ask pointed questions when a company says it’s committed to US manufacturing. We asked TP-Link those sorts of questions just over a week ago. On Monday, we asked Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Qualcomm president and CEO Cristiano Amon those kinds of questions.
Over the course of two days, Anduril has changed its answers.
Anduril communications VP Shannon Prior now says the company’s laptop will have at least 65 percent of its components made in the US by the time it launches in 2027. It’s an important number, and one that Anduril did not commit to earlier this week.
Luckey held a call with reporters on Monday, during which he was clear that he wants to make literally every part of a computer in the United States — and that Anduril and Qualcomm have already mapped out a plan. “We have a technical roadmap to get to 100 percent domestic over time,” he told journalists.
Luckey also suggested his laptop would be built to comply with the requirements of the military and other government agencies — and that it would meet or exceed one specific US government standard that has an exact definition.
“We are not just barely meeting the bar for Made in America. We are going hard to make this an all-American play, and not even the Buy American Act requires what we’re trying,” Luckey said.
The Buy American Act dates back to 1933, but it was updated during the Biden Administration to require that at least 65 percent of the cost of a company’s products must be made domestically for it be considered a domestic product itself. That number is going up to 75 percent in 2029.
Many products need to be made in America to those standards, or federal agencies can’t buy them without receiving a waiver — which agencies currently use en masse, Luckey himself argued on the call. “There’s a number of government agencies that are required by law to buy American-made computers [...] All of those procurements are happening under waivers of those laws,” he said.
We also noticed that Anduril’s press release specifies that its first laptop will be “designed and assembled” in the United States, not necessarily “manufactured” here (though the release does talk about future manufacturing). This was also a sticking point with router maker TP-Link, which would not confirm full manufacturing even after suggesting it in an interview with The Verge.
That’s why we asked Luckey what percent of his first laptop’s components would be made in the US. His reply was not 65 percent or 70 percent. It was “TBD.” You can read the exchange for yourself:
The Verge: When it arrives in 2027, what percent of the components in the BlueChip laptop will be made in the US?
Luckey: TBD. I’m doing my very, very best. It’s gonna be a whole mix of things based on when do certain memory fabs come online? When do certain CPU, GPU fabs come online? There’s a whole— Like, am I able to get a display line here or not? Do I have to do that after launch? I’m being totally open kimono with you here. Those questions are not settled. It is not clear if I will be able. I know the glass is gonna be made in the US, I know the frame is gonna be made in the US around that display. I know that parts of the ribbon component are gonna be made in the U.S. I don’t know if I will have successfully pulled that component in or a dozen other components. So it’s a little up in the air. I’m doing my very, very best. I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American. I think it’ll be a blend of US and allies around the world, mostly US, probably a few things from some allies, and then that’ll be in the context of conversations with those allies about bringing those components into production in the United States, and I’m being honest with the government on this too. I mean, I’ve had conversations where I’ve said, listen. I would love to give you guys an American, 100-percent American laptop right off the bat, but that is not the environment the US government has created or US industry has created. I can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
When we followed up by email to ask specifically about 65 percent, the answer was that the laptop prototype is currently at 32 percent and Anduril could not yet commit to 65 percent. Here’s Anduril spokesperson Stephanie Davis’ full reply on Tuesday:
For the prototype today, approximately 32% is U.S.-origin by component procurement cost, and more than 90% is sourced from the United States and allied countries combined.
We’re working to expand domestic sourcing and production ahead of planned availability in 2027, with the goal of eliminating foreign content and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.
The final domestic-content percentage at launch remains unsettled, so we can’t confirm above or below 65% today. That’s why we’re asking you to revise the assertion that it will be “well below” that threshold.
Today, Prior writes that Anduril can indeed commit to 65 percent. Here is the most recent statement:
Our previous response to The Verge was incorrect. The BlueChip laptop is indeed being developed to exceed the 65% U.S. domestic-content threshold at launch in 2027. Meeting that threshold is a fundamental objective of the program. The precise domestic-content percentage of the final product is still being determined as we finalize suppliers and work through prototypes, and we look forward to sharing more next year.
Today’s statement is the first time Anduril has confirmed that we, and government agencies, theoretically shouldn’t need to wait until Anduril achieves its full goals to see a laptop that meets the Buy American standard. If everything works out, Anduril’s first laptop in 2027, with Qualcomm, should be that laptop.
We invited Luckey to explain how Anduril would get to 65 percent domestic component production in a follow-up interview, but we were told he’s not currently available. On the Monday call, he told journalists that Anduril already has a US glassmaker lined up for the laptop’s cover glass, is programming FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) to serve the purpose of power management chips and other circuits it can’t normally can’t get outside China, and is developing made-in-America batteries as well.
The press release adds that the enclosure is designed “for US machining” and the laptop will use metals “that US industry can produce and machine at scale.”
As for the laptop’s Snapdragon processor, we asked Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon about that. “TSMC has a manufacturing facility in Arizona, and that’s where our chips are going to be made,” he told The Verge.

This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.
The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.
“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”
Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.
The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.
“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”
Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.
As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.
In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.
Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust, said Sutton. “They're losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”
In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.
“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there's a chemical plume coming my way, the phone's ringing, the radio's blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.
Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.
Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.
Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.
The original alert read, “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.
The new alert read: “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.
EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.
“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They're using their own personal accounts, or they're using free ones.”
It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.
“We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue.
As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.
Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.
“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.
The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test

Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: In the election for the Aurangabad Division Graduates’ Constituency of the Legislative Council, NCP-SP candidate Dr Pratapsinh Vedprakash Patil emerged victorious by a margin of 18,124 votes. He secured 85,876 votes, while Satish Bhanudasrao Chavan, the candidate of the NCP, received 67,752 votes. Following the elimination of 39 candidates based on the order of preference and the subsequent transfer of votes, Dr Patil secured the highest number of votes in the final count.
Returning Officer and Divisional Commissioner G. Sreekanth declared Dr Patil the winner at 5:10am on Thursday.
The election was held across 842 polling stations in eight districts: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Jalna, Beed, Parbhani, Hingoli, Nanded, Latur and Dharashiv. A total of 41 candidates were in the fray. Arrangements were made for 70 tables to facilitate the counting of votes.
At the beginning of the counting process, the ballot papers were verified and categorised. Subsequently, the counting of first-preference votes was completed in three rounds. By the end of the first round, 70,519 ballot papers had been counted, while the cumulative total reached 1,40,543 by the end of the second round. According to the counting data, 1,77,115 votes were declared valid, while 16,540 votes were deemed invalid. Based on the number of valid votes, the quota required for victory was set at 88,558 votes.
At the end of the first-preference vote count, Dr Pratapsinh Patil received 73,931 votes, Satish Chavan received 60,768 votes, independent candidate Raviraj alias Annasaheb Sawle-Patil received 19,835 votes, and Dilip Ghuge received 8,439 votes. Since no candidate met the required quota for victory, the prescribed election procedure was followed. Candidates with the fewest votes were eliminated in successive rounds, and their ballots were transferred based on the next available preferences marked by voters.
During the vote-transfer process, votes were reallocated among the remaining candidates according to the next available preferences indicated on the ballot papers of eliminated candidates. From the ballot papers of Dilip Ghuge, 2,285 votes were transferred to Dr Patil, while 1,881 votes were transferred to Satish Chavan. Subsequently, during the 39th round of elimination, 6,469 votes from the ballot papers of Raviraj Sawle-Patil were transferred to Dr Patil, while 3,241 votes were transferred to Satish Chavan.
After the elimination of 39 of the 41 candidates, Dr Patil and Chavan remained in the contest. At this stage, neither candidate had reached the required quota of 88,558 votes. In the final count, Dr Patil secured 85,876 votes, while Satish Chavan received 67,752 votes. Dr Patil thus won the election by a margin of 18,124 votes. Subsequently, Returning Officer G Sreekanth announced the official results and formally declared Dr Patil the winner.
The counting of votes, which began at 8am on Tuesday, October 27, continued for more than 45 consecutive hours before the final results were announced in the early hours of Thursday, October 29.

The Madhya Pradesh Government has constituted a five-member committee to investigate claims that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district, officials said on Sunday (October 25, 2026).
The panel will submit its report within 15 days, they said.
Ujjain divisional Commissioner constituted the committee after conflicting claims over the deaths.
Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16.
The district administration had earlier dismissed the claims as false and misleading. It later said viscera samples of two deceased persons have been sent to a forensic science laboratory (FSL) for examination. The cause of death would become clear after the reports are received, it added.
The administration said 10 persons died in Chandana village between October 1 and 15, but denied that any of the deaths was caused by spurious liquor. It attributed the deaths to old age, common illnesses, brain haemorrhage and "deterioration of health due to excessive alcohol consumption".
Ujjain Additional District Magistrate Pratham Kaushik will head the probe committee, which includes Mandsaur Additional Superintendent of Police Ramsanehi Mishra, Ratlam Sub-Divisional Police Officer Lekhraj Meena, Ujjain divisional flying squad Deputy Excise Commissioner Harshvardhan Rai and Regional Director of Public Health and Medical Education Dr Deepak Kumar Pippal.
The panel will conduct a detailed and impartial inquiry into the causes and circumstances of the deaths, along with the related technical and administrative aspects, and submit a factual report within 15 days, according to the Ujjain divisional Commissioner's order.
Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari has claimed that 22 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Chandana, Binjana and adjoining areas over the past month, while at least 40 people suffered damage to their eyesight.
The Opposition party leader has accused the administration of concealing the deaths and shielding the "liquor mafia".

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
One of Kathleen Tejeda's students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person.
By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school.
Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find.
There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states, according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It's now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students.
While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn't new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent?
Myths and realities about teaching special education
Let's start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don't want to do the job. "That is not the case," said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. "That has not borne out in our research at all."
Loading...
What Bettini's research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don't get paid enough to do this essential work.
"That's a very heavy weight to carry as a teacher," Bettini said.
NPR set out to hear directly from about a dozen special educators from around the United States' public schools to learn what it takes to do their jobs day to day. They have been sharing snippets of their lives through voice memos since the start of the school year, and some will open their classroom doors to NPR in the coming months.
"No teacher does this for the paycheck," said third-year high school teacher Diana Swanson, who works in Vail, Ariz., as she sat at her desk the day before her school year began in July. "Just the students, that fulfillment, seeing them fill their cup a little bit, seeing them smile, be a member of society and part of their community. That's what fulfills me."
"I feel like I was coming into this school year more prepared this time around," fourth-year elementary school teacher Danalyn Garcia said late one school night from her living room in Chicago. "Yet, I feel the needs are even greater than the year before."
"Honestly, I had no life outside of school and outside of being a teacher," said Kaori Anderson-Walker, looking back on his first year of teaching middle school in Philadelphia. Now in his fourth year, he said he has finally learned to manage his time more effectively but said the work is still never-ending. "When my students aren't performing where I want them in the classroom, my mind is just constantly moving."
Much of the day isn't spent on teaching
Being an educator of any kind is demanding and requires immense skill. Research shows that burnout among all kinds of public school teachers is high, but it's even more acute for special educators. These teachers work with students who have an incredibly diverse set of needs, including those with autism, learning disabilities such as dyslexia, developmental delays and physical disabilities.
Special educators also do a lot more than teach — in fact, one study found that they spent only about a third of their day on instruction. They spend the rest of their time tracking student goals, coordinating specialized services for students (say, speech therapy or extra reading help), training support staff and writing individualized education programs (IEPs), which are legal documents that track each special education student's needs at school.
In many states, that means teachers must have specialized certification and training, but they typically aren't paid more. In 32 states, teachers get no extra pay for the hardest-to-staff positions, including in special education, according to a recent study.
While all 13 special educators NPR has spoken to said building relationships with students is their favorite part of the work, they also described the realities of those students' needs being more complex than those of many general education students.
"Special educators have reported, 'I can't teach this kid and respond to the student's crisis simultaneously. So I'm abandoning instruction because the crisis has to take priority,'" Bettini said.
For example, Grace Fitzgerald, who teaches elementary school in Peoria, Ill., shared on a drive home from school that one of her students had an emotional crisis that forced her to evacuate the rest of her class for their safety. "It's been challenging mentally and emotionally to kind of go through that at the very end of the first quarter, my first year of teaching," she said. "No one gets a road map to deal with that kind of situation."
Several teachers shared that behavioral challenges with individual students can make it harder to meet the needs of their many other students.
Loading...
"Our school doesn't have walls. So we have six classes per grade level in one ginormous room, and it's separated by dividers," Garcia, in Chicago, said. "So when one kid is screaming and crying and begins to escalate, it disturbs the whole pod and then other kids react to it." Getting students back on track can be difficult in these kinds of situations, she said.
Essential but time-consuming paperwork
Individualized education programs are a key part of special education. These written plans, required by federal law, are managed by teachers and other school staff and serve as a kind of road map for each special education student. IEPs outline the student's unique needs and their annual goals. For example, a goal of a student with autism may be to maintain eye contact for a certain period of time.
IEPs help families hold schools accountable, and they also help enforce a primary aim of special education: to teach students in the "least restrictive environment," meaning students with disabilities are taught alongside students without disabilities as much as possible. But IEPs also require regular meetings with families, an understanding of special education law and time spent away from teaching students — time that teachers often don't have.
Then there's the work of putting the IEP into practice in the classroom. Tejeda, of Riverside County, said when she's "pushing in" to other teachers' general education classrooms, she provides targeted support without singling out special education students. "We're going to walk the classroom and check in with everybody, but at the back of our minds, we know that we need to make sure we're [making] accommodations for that particular student."
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For Anderson-Walker, in Philadelphia, "the biggest struggle" was feeling like he had to juggle IEP paperwork with teaching duties. Then, last year, his school, Boys' Latin of Philadelphia, hired staff members who are responsible for the paperwork part of IEPs, leaving teachers more time for the classroom. "Not having that stress is amazing," Anderson-Walker said.
Searching for solutions
In addition to the workload, at the core of the special education teacher shortage are pay and the sheer number of qualified people. Research shows that paying teachers more can help attract and retain them.
For example, in 2020, Hawaii raised special education teacher salaries by $10,000 annually. That cut the state's vacancies by 35%, but it wasn't enough to keep many special education teachers in their jobs. Seventeen states now pay teachers additional money to work in hard-to-staff subjects, including special education. That's down from four years ago, when 22 states did so.
The pipeline of qualified special educators is another big problem. According to education policy researcher Chad Aldeman's analysis of federal data a few years ago, about 46,000 special ed teachers leave public schools every year, while teacher preparation programs train fewer than 30,000 annually to replace those teachers.
Aldeman calls it a crude estimate but said that the rapid increase in demand for special education teachers is outpacing the supply of people trained to do those jobs. Many schools end up resorting to hiring teachers who aren't fully qualified for the work.
But research has found that "grow-your-own" programs that focus on recruiting people who already live in the community may be effective at filling special education jobs. Bettini and her research partners also found that supportive administrators and adequate planning time can help make the work feel more sustainable for teachers.
For example, Fitzgerald, the first-year teacher in Illinois, said she was feeling overwhelmed by her workload at the start of the year. So she worked with her school leadership to build more dedicated planning time into her day.
"I think that's going to be very beneficial and will hopefully lead to a decrease in time spent after school," Fitzgerald said. She uses that time to focus on lesson plans, logging data and writing IEP goals.
It allows her to be more present in the classroom, working with her students.

Despite an overall decline in tobacco consumption, disadvantaged and rural populations in India and the U.S. continue to be disproportionately affected, according to a comparative analysis presented at a national pulmonary diseases conference here.
The analysis highlighted that smokeless tobacco and bidis remain major concerns in India, while cigarettes and e-cigarettes remain public health challenges in the US.
The paper, titled "Two Countries, Two Tobacco Epidemics, One Hidden Inequality", was presented on October 25 by Akanksha Anand, assistant professor at Morgan State University's School of Community Health and Policy in the US, during the 28th National Conference on Pulmonary Diseases (NAPCON) concluded on Sunday.
The study examined tobacco-use patterns and disparities using national survey data from both countries, highlighting the role of gender, income, education and geographical location in tobacco exposure.
According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), tobacco use among adults aged 15 and above in India declined from 34.6 % in 2009-10 to 28.6% in 2016-17.
However, smokeless tobacco remained a major concern, with a prevalence of 21.4 % in 2016-17, nearly twice the 10.7 per cent prevalence of smoked tobacco.
The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) showed that 38%of men and 8.9 % of women used tobacco.
The rural-urban divide was particularly significant, with 42.7 %of rural men reporting tobacco use, compared with 28.8 % of urban men.
Among women, tobacco use stood at 10.5 % in rural areas against 5.5 % in urban areas.
The presentation noted that focusing only on cigarette smoking could overlook substantial tobacco exposure through bidis, smokeless tobacco and other products.
It also highlighted the risks associated with secondhand smoke.
In the US, data from the 2024 National Health Interview Survey showed that 9.9 %of adults smoked cigarettes, while 7 % reported using e-cigarettes.
Cigarette use was considerably higher in non-metropolitan areas at 15.4 %, compared with 8 % in central metropolitan counties.
Similarly, e-cigarette use stood at 9.2 % in non-metropolitan areas against 6.1 % in central metropolitan counties.
The analysis found that while tobacco products differed between the two countries, social and geographical inequalities remained common challenges.
Gender, wealth, education and geographical location were important factors influencing tobacco use in India, while rural residence, education and age played significant roles in the U.S.
The presentation highlighted the need for targeted public health interventions to address tobacco use among vulnerable populations and reduce associated respiratory health risks.
It also cautioned that the figures were drawn from surveys conducted in different years using different methodologies and should not be treated as directly comparable.
The analysis was based on published national estimates rather than an original combined analysis of individual-level survey data.

Park Hospitals strengthens north India footprint with Rs200 crore investment, targets 6,600 beds
The hospital is being developed in partnership with the Prayagraj Municipal Corporation under a public-private partnership (PPP) model.
Uttar Pradesh's Prayagraj is set to get a 550-bed multi-specialty hospital, which would be built with an investment of ₹200 crore over the next two years.
The project by Park Medi World Limited is part of the company’s plan to expand its hospital network across North India and improve access to healthcare in smaller cities.
The hospital is being developed in partnership with the Prayagraj Municipal Corporation under a public-private partnership (PPP) model. The hospital is expected to be completed within two years.
“The groundbreaking of our Prayagraj hospital marks an important milestone in our expansion journey. As we work towards increasing our network capacity to approximately 6,600 beds by December 2028, our focus remains on strengthening our presence across North India and expanding access to healthcare in emerging markets,” said Dr Ankit Gupta, Managing Director of Park Medi World Limited.
The company currently operates 17 hospitals with around 4,290 beds across 15 cities in six states. In Uttar Pradesh, it runs a 360-bed hospital in Agra and is preparing to open hospitals in Kanpur and Gorakhpur. The proposed Prayagraj facility will further expand its presence in the state.
The Prayagraj Municipal Corporation will reimburse ₹76.52 crore towards construction costs, covering around 38% of the project’s estimated cost. This will bring the company’s effective investment down to approximately ₹123.48 crore.
Park Medi World is expanding its network through new hospital projects, acquisitions and the addition of beds at existing facilities. According to the company, six more hospitals are being integrated into its network, while capacity is being increased at three existing hospitals. The company aims to expand its total capacity to around 6,600 beds by December 2028, with the Prayagraj hospital forming part of this plan.
Park Hospitals operates a network of 17 hospitals across North India, with facilities in Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, according to its official website. Its hospitals are located in New Delhi, Gurugram, Faridabad, Sonipat, Panipat, Karnal, Ambala and Panchkula in Haryana; Mohali, Bathinda and Patiala in Punjab; Jaipur and Behror in Rajasthan; Agra in Uttar Pradesh; and Rudrapur in Uttarakhand.

Regulatory tightening in Hong Kong sees delistings outnumber resumptions: report
Grant Thornton says 35 companies were delisted from city’s stock exchange in 12 months to August this year
The tightening of Hong Kong’s securities regulations – in the wake of property developer Evergrande’s liquidation and unrelated IPO frauds – has resulted in more delistings than resumptions for the first time in three years, according to a report by accountants Grant Thornton.
Hong Kong saw 35 delistings in the 12 months to August this year but only 21 resumptions, the report said.
“Regulators have comprehensively tightened resumption requirements,” said Barry Tong, national leader of forensic investigation services at Grant Thornton China, pointing to heightened scrutiny over asset overstatement and misappropriation, bank statement forgery and the illicit outflow of initial public offering proceeds.
